semester I (11/12/2022 - 30/04/2023)


  • Pāḷi - bhante Vijitānanda
    • Chapter 1 - Pāḷi pāṭha sikkhā - Bhante Vijitānanda
      • Lesson 1 - Alphabet
        • Pāḷi means the {{3971980407272855::dhamma taught by the Buddha}} and {{3971980407272855::the language used for teaching (māgadhī)}} - language spoken in the Kingdom of {{3971980407272855::Magadha}} (even though most modern philologers disagree with the tradition)
        • Vowels↔sara
        • Number of vowels→8 (according to grammarian Kaccāyana. Grammarian Moggallāna thinks there are 10 vowels with the short diphthongs e o)
        • Consonants↔vyañjana
        • Number of consonants→33
        • Total number of letters→41 (Kaccāyana), 43 (Moggallāna)
        • Diphthong→combination of two adjacent vowel sounds within the same syllable. ("no"). Also called gliding vowel.
        • 6 groups of consonants according to where the sound is produced
          • Gutturals
          • Palatals
          • Linguals
          • Dentals
          • Labials
          • Non-group
        • Aspirations/aspirated consonants→Mahāpāṇa
        • 1) Pāḷi language is both the language used by the buddha to teach the Dhamma and the Dhamma itself. The language is called Māgadhī as it was spoken in the Kingdom of Magadha according to traditional account.
        • 2)
          • Sara (vowels)
            • a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o
          • Vyañjana (consonants)
            • k, kh, g, gh, ṅ
            • c, ch, j, jh, ñ
            • ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ
            • t, th, d, dh, n
            • p, ph, b, bh, m
            • y, r, l, v, s, h, ḷ, ṁ (niggahīta)

      • Lesson 3 - Noun stems and case-endings
        • Noun stem (morpheme without a case ending)↔liṅga
          • Morpheme (not pāḷi grammar)→a meaningful morphological unit of a language that cannot be further divided (e.g. in, come, -ing, forming incoming ). A morphological element considered in respect of its functional relations in a linguistic system.
        • 7 Case-endings/nominal endings ({{615237359689851::nāma vibhatti}}) (suffixes added to a stem)
          • Paṭhamā vibhatti (nominative case)
          • Dutiyā vibhatti (accusative case)
          • Tatiyā vibhatti (instrumental case)
          • Catutthā vibhatti (dative case)
          • Pañcamā vibhatti (ablative case)
          • Chaṭṭhī vibhatti (genitive case)
          • Sattamī vibhatti (locative case)
        • Mentioned agent (mentioned by the verb)↔utta kattu
        • Utta↔something that has been said

      • Lesson 6 - Gender and Addressing
        • Ultimate gender↔atthaliṅga
        • Grammatical gender↔saddaliṅga
        • 3 atthaliṅga
          • purisa (male)
          • itthi (female)
          • napuṁsaka (eunuch)
        • 6 saddaliṅga
          • purisaliṅgika
          • itthiliṅgika
          • napuṁsakaliṅgika
          • diliṅgika (two genders such as geha ⇒ geho / gehaṁ)
          • tiliṅgika (three genders such as uttama ⇒ uttamo / uttamaṁ / uttamā
          • aliṅgika
        • According to some grammarians the grammatical gender of a noun is decided on {{9517482104774693::certain characteristics of the sound that is produced while uttering that particular noun}}. It does not necessarily corresponds to the ultimate gender of the thing it refers to.

          • ālapana ekavacana―bho purisa, bho purisā
          • ālapana bahuvacana―bhonto purisā

      • Lesson 8 - Genitive and Location
        • What indicates the possessor is called genitive↔sambandha
          • sambandha (m.)↔connection, join, tie, (grammar) relationship, construction
          • The sambandha (genitive) is expressed by the→chaṭṭhī vibhatti
          • sāmī sambandha↔Owner relationship such as between a farmer who possesses an ox (the ox of the farmer runs)
          • sāmī (m.)↔owner, master, husband, lord, ruler, sir
          • Chaṭṭhī vibhatti (purisa)―purisassa / purisānaṁ
        • The place where an action takes place is the location, in pāḷi called↔okāsa, avakāsa or ādhāra
          • The okāsa is expressed by the locative case―Sattamī vibhatti
          • Sattamī vibhatti (purisa)―purise, purisasmiṁ, purisamhi / purisesu
        • What is the main component of a sentence?→the verb

        • declension of purisa (purisādigaṇa)
          • nom. puriso / purisā
          • voc. (bho) purisa, purisā / (bhonto) "
          • acc. purisaṁ / purise
          • ins. purisena / purisehi, purisebhi
          • dat./gen. purisassa / purisānaṁ

              • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
        • Declension (English definition)→the inflection of nouns and pronouns and adjectives
        • Declination (English definition)→a condition inferior to an earlier condition; a gradual falling off from a better state; a downward slope or bend; a polite refusal of an invitation.
        • what does the nominative case express?→the meaning of the noun stem (liṅgattha)
        • sampadānaṁ (nt.)↔handing down, handing over, passing on (scriptures), (gram.) dative case, supplying, making ready
        • apādānaṁ (nt.)↔(gram) separating; ablation (ablative); taking away
        • Purisādi gaṇa: masculine gender nouns ending in "a"
        • In traditional grammar there are no stems ending in consonants. Modern scholars use consonant ending stems (satthār, guṇavant, gacchant...)

      • Lesson 10 - Verbs
        • 4 parts of speech / groups of words (pada)
          • nāmapada: morphemes / stems to which case-endings / nominal suffixes are added; they are declined in liṅga (genders), vibhatti (cases) and vacana (number) and perform the functions of subjects, nouns, adjectives, certain actions and so on
          • ākhyātapada (Verbs): morphemes together with verbal terminations/suffixes. Verbs are formed by adding verbal suffixes to {{97794712674967::roots}}
          • avyaya / abyaya
            • nipātapada (Indeclinable particles)
            • upasaggapada (Prefixes)
          • mem aid: nānu
        • avyaya / abyaya↔does not change
        • Roots→a collection of letters that represent an action. Roots cannot be used in a sentence without having added verbal suffixes.
          • some roots
            • /pac↔cooks
            • /khād↔eats
            • /yā↔goes
            • /gam↔goes
            • /paṭh↔reads
        • there are {{6143297111351387::8}} types of verbal tenses
        • vattamāna vibhatti↔present tense
        • 3 grammatical persons and their vattamāna vibhatti terminations
          • Paṭhama purisa (third person): ti / nti
          • Majjhima purisa (second person): si / tha
          • Uttama purisa (first person): mi / ma
        • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • Paṭhati↔reads
          • Pada (nt.)↔word (as in nāmap.), part of a word, suffix, foot, path, track, way, (poetry) line, phrase, sentence, saying, place, position, reason, cause, part, component, footprint
          • Pivati↔drinks, imbibes
          • Māreti↔kills (s.w/ m)
          • Daṇḍa (m.)↔stick, truncheon, nightstick, club, walking stick, staff, violence, punishment, fine, (nt.) Jain word for kamma
          • Makkaṭa (m.)↔monkey, ape
        • The vowel that stands before the terminations{{3232747810025389:: "mi" and "ma"}} in vattamāna vibhatti is lengthened
        • 10.2. Indeclinable particles and prefixes
          • Indeclinable particles (nipātapada) are words that {{6903244714454406::are declined but do not undergo any changes}}.
          • how to say: from under the bed? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • Evaṁ (nipāta)↔thus, in this manner
            • Heṭṭhā (nipāta)↔under (Sunakho mañcassa h. niddāyati)
            • Niddāyati↔sleeps (s.w. n)
            • Ajja (nipāta)↔today
            • Puna (nipāta)↔again
            • Chāyā (f.)↔shade, shadow, reflection, reflected image
            • na (nip.)―no, not, nor, neither
            • āma (nip.)↔yes, certainly
            • have (nip.)↔truly; really; indeed; surely (s.w. h)
            • yato (ind.)↔from where; from which; wherever
            • ca (nip.)↔and
            • eva (nip.)↔only, just, even, exclusively
            • vā (nip.)↔or
            • he (nip.)↔hey!, oh!
            • ambho (nip.)↔hey! yo! look here!
            • sayaṁ (nip.)↔by one's own, oneself, one's own (s.w/ s)
            • saddhiṁ (nip.)→together with, with
            • iti (nip.)↔thus, like this, this is, and so (s.w. i)
            • pāto (nip.)↔early, in the morning
            • suve (nip.)↔tomorrow
            • yāva (nip.)↔as long as, as far as, so much so, (s.w. y)
            • tāva (nip.)↔that much, that far, to that extent, until,
            • tattha (nip.)↔there
            • kho (nip.)↔indeed, surely, certainly, truly (s.w. k)
            • alaṁ (nip.)↔suitable, proper, enough
            • api (nip.)↔just, only, even, even then, if
            • upari (nip.)↔above, overhead, on top
          • Prefixes also do not undergo any changes in declension. In most cases they are added to the beginning of a root or a noun to change their meaning. There are {{1644163642144869::20}} upasagga (prefixes) in pāḷi

            • ati, api, apa, upa

      • Lesson 2 - Past Tense Verbs
        • 8 types of verbal vibhatti
          • Vattamāna vibhatti (present simple, present continuous, present emphatic)
          • Pañcamī (Imperative)
          • Sattamī (Optative)
          • Ajjatanī (past simple - more common)
          • Bhavissantī (future tense)
          • Kālātipatti
          • Hiyattanī (past tense - less common)
          • Parokkhā
        • In the case of nouns the suffixes added to the stems are referred to as {{717191794582799::case endings}} and in the case of verbs the suffixes added to the roots are referred to as {{717191794582799::verbal terminations.}}
        • A verbal base is the (English definition) {{7314671417667677::morpheme constructed by adding a conjugational sign to a root}}.
        • The vibhatti used to indicate an action that has occurred but not directly witnesses by the speaker is {{9977655939926109::parokkhā vibhatti}}
        • To augment is to {{0940968146763177::insert an extra letter }}and the pāḷi term for it is {{0940968146763177::āgama.}}
          • Majjhima purisa, bahuvacana, ajjatanī of the root paṭh (reads)→paṭhittha (augmented i)
        • "a" is not added to the beginning of verbs in the sense of {{4232895891399402::negation ("not")}}.
        • The ending of the root gam often changes into {{218087290976956::cch.}}
        • Ajjatanī vibhatti (terminations)
          • ī, i, / uṁ, iṁsu o, (i) / ttha iṁ / mhā, mha
        • in ajjatanī vibhatti when the verbal termination ends with a {{8478839989957856::consonant}} and the first letter of the verbal termination is also a consonant, the vowel {{8478839989957856::"i"}} is augmented in between

            • by (Brazil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
            • 1)
              • Modifier (visesana)
                • The adjective or word that acts as a qualifier to a noun modifying it is called visesana such as:
                  • Rasso pāṇo sadā paṇṇe bhuñji.
                    • Rasso (visesana pada) modifies the noun pāṇo giving more information about it and agreeing in gender, case and number (purisaliṅga, paṭhamā vibhatti, ekavacana).
                  • Bālā dārakā uṇhaṁ aggiṁ upagacchiṁsu.
                    • Bālā (visesana pada) modifies the noun dārakā also agreeing in gender, case and number (purisaliṅga, paṭhamā vibhatti, bahuvacana) and uṇhaṁ does the same to the object aggiṁ (purisaliṅga, dutiyāvibhatti, ekavacana)
              • Modified (visesya)
                • The noun that is modified by the adjective is in turn named visesya (modified) and is that which the adjective qualifies giving it more qualities. Example:
                  • Sīghā meghā vehāse caliṁsu.
                    • In this case the noun meghā (visesya) is modified by sīghā specifying what type of clouds.
                  • Migo vane santaṁ sambuddhaṁ olokī.
                    • In this sentence santaṁ qualifies the noun sambuddhaṁ which is acting as object.

      • Lesson 5 - Gerund
        • The Pāḷi rendering of gerund is ‘{{9617969436539673::pubbakāla kiriyā’}}
        • "So gehaṁ pavisitvā mañce asayi". Of these two verbs which one is the main one?→Both are equally important but the main emphasis is on the final verb "asayi".
        • What is the definition of a gerund? (In English)→The word that expresses an action which had occurred prior to the final action.
        • How are pubbakālakiriyā (gerunds) constructed?→They are constructed by adding the suffix ‘tvā’ or ‘tvāna’ to the end of roots or verbal bases.
        • In which of the 4 groups of nouns are gerund considered to be?→Gerunds are considered as indeclinable particles.
        • Less common suffixes used for gerunds→the suffixes -tuna (khādituna, labhituna) and -ya (nikkhamma, āgamma).
          • -ya (only some cases)
            • How is the gerund āgamma and nikkhamma formed?
              • Root gam: +ya (āgamya) ⇒ āgamma
              • Root kam: +ya (nikkhamiya) ⇒ nikkhamya ⇒ nikkhamma
        • When a gerund suffix is added to a root the vowel {{9726961184932477::‘i’}} may be augmented (āgama) before it.
        • The gerund can also express {{2041098481713659::samānakāla }}{{2041098481713659::(an action occuring simultaneously with the main verb)}} apart from the pubbakāla sometimes

      • Lesson 7 - Guṇavādigaṇa
        • How are nouns like guṇavant constructed? {{05131114365768541::adding the suffix -vant / -mant to the noun stem}}
        • The suffix -vantu / -mantu indicate {{2114729441789689::the possessor of something}}.
        • These nouns from guṇavādigaṇa can be declined in which genders?→all three genders
        • There is another suffix -mantu which has a similar meaning to that of -vantu. They are also in guṇavādigaṇa and are declined similarly.
        • Nouns belonging to this group can be used as stand-alone nouns and also as modifiers (adjectives) of other nouns.
        • In traditional grammar the suffix is -vantu but since u does not appear in any declension, modern scholars use -vant.
        • After akāranta and ākāranta nouns the suffix added is {{5737564847941865::-vantu}}, and after nouns ending in other vowels the suffix added is {{5737564847941865::-mantu}}.
        • Extra suffix that is used apart from -vantu and -mantu: {{047249204676201195::imantu (candimā, puttimā)}}
        • When a letter is removed it is called (in English) {{6336744868072028::elision (to elide)}}
        • Nouns stems can end in 8 letters: {{8657703074744934::a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, o, ṁ}}
        • *declension of guṇavantu (m.) (guṇavādigaṇa)
          • guṇavā, guṇavanto / guṇavanto, guṇavantā
          • (bho) guṇavaṁ, guṇava, guṇavā / (bhonto) "
          • guṇavaṁ, guṇavantaṁ / guṇavante
          • guṇavatā, guṇavantena / guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi
          • guṇavato, guṇavassa, guṇavantassa / guṇavataṁ, guṇavantānaṁ

          • nom. guṇavaṁ, (guṇavantaṁ [nrt])/ guṇavantā, guṇavantāni, guṇavanti
          • voc. / "
          • acc. / guṇavante, guṇavantāni, guṇavanti

        • declension of guṇavantu f. (guṇavādigaṇa)
          • guṇavantī (the same as itthī)
        • According to Rūpasiddhi, only himavantu has two forms as himavā, himavanto in nominative singular. Other stems in this group only have one form in nominative singular as guṇavā, sīlavā, dhanavā etc.
        • According to Rūpasiddhi, only the stems satimantu and bandhumantu have satimaṃ, bandhumaṃ in accusative singular and satimassa, bandhumassa in dative/gentivie singular. Other stems do not have such forms.
        • The suffix used in guṇavā, sīlavā, and himavā is vantu. In satimā and bandhumā, the suffix is mantu. In bhuttavā, it is tavantu. In ettāvā, it is tāvantu. In yāvā, it is āvantu and in candimā, it is imantu.

      • Lesson 9 - Missaka kiriyā and gacchantādigaṇa
        • Actions that are done simultaneously with the main action of a sentence are called {{15214689404309434::missaka-kiriyā}}
        • In Pāḷi, missaka-kiriyās are constructed by {{44803151389458784::adding the suffixes ‘anta’ and ‘māna’ to roots or verbal bases}}
        • In which genders can Missakakiriyās be declined? {{9252273199699421::in all three genders}}
        • Words ending in -māna when declined in masculine gender are declined similar to the noun {{2807839594229995::purisa}}. When they refer to a feminine noun they are declined as the noun {{2807839594229995::kaññā}}. When they refer to a neuter noun they are declined like the noun {{2807839594229995::citta}}. Words ending with the suffix -anta have a different declension but similar to guṇavādigaṇa with one exception in the nominative singular case.
        • *declension of gacchanta m. (gacchantādigaṇa)
          • nom. gacchaṃ, gacchanto / gacchantā, gacchanto
          • (the rest as guṇavantu)
          • mem aid:
            • apart from gacchaṁ, the rest is the same as guṇavantu
          • note:
            • arahanta and mahanta both have arahā and mahā as nominative singular
            • santa has sabbhi as ins./abl. plural as well
            • why are they 2 groups?
              • suffixes are different
                • guṇavādi: ending in -u, similar meanings
                • gacchanta: -anta
              • though the declension is mostly similar, some words have different forms (karonta, mahanta, arahanta...)
        • *declension of gacchanta nt. (gacchantādigaṇa)↓
          • nom. gacchaṃ, gacchantaṁ / gacchantā, gacchantāni, gacchanti
          • acc. gacchaṁ, gacchantaṁ / gacchante, gacchantāni, gacchanti
          • (the rest as m.)
          • mem aid:
            • close to citta
            • nom. gacchantaṁ, -nti
        • declension of karonta m. (gacchantādigaṇa)
          • nom. karaṁ, karonto / karontā, karonto
          • voc. (bho) karonta, karontā / karontā, karonto
          • acc. karontaṁ / karonte
          • dat. karoto, karontassa / karotaṁ, karontānaṁ
          • mem aid:
            • like gacchanta but with 'o' and long forms
            • voc., acc., longer forms
            • dat. no short form as gacchassa
        • 3 main functions of missakakiriyā:
          • as missakakiriyā
          • as stand-alone nouns
          • as adjectives
        • vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • pariyatti (f.)↔the scriptures
          • paṭipatti (f.)↔the practice
          • pūreti↔fills, fulfills
          • thāmavā↔one who has strength; strong
          • yodho (m.)↔soldier
          • cetiyaṁ (nt.)↔pagoda
          • saṅgāmo (m.)↔battle
          • dhamma+desanā+kālo (m.)―the time of preaching Dhamma
          • olambati↔hangs down
          • vigatamiddha (adj.)↔one who is not sleepy/drowsy
          • Api /pi (nip.)↔and (s.w. a/p)
          • yāvatā (nip.)↔as far as (s.w. y)
          • tāvatā (nip.)↔so long (s.w. t)
          • hutvā √hū↔(+nom) having been; having become
          • pasaṃsā (f.) √saṃs↔(+instr) praise (by); approval (of); commendation (of)
          • annaṁ (nt.)↔food; lit. eaten (s.w. a)
          • pānaṁ (nt.)↔drink, beverage
          • atītaṁ (nt.)↔past
          • anāgato (m.)↔future
          • nisinnaṁ (nt.)↔(nt.) sitting, (pp.) seated
          • sayāna (prp.) √sī↔lying down (s.w. s)
          • pūrayiṁ (pūreti ⇒ pūresiṁ ⇒ pūrayiṁ)↔I fulfilled
          • mahaṃ↔one who is honouring, that which is big/great
          • saṃ↔that which is existing, a good person
            • In instrumental and ablative plural of santa, there is an additional form sabbhi. Therefore, the declension should be santehi, santebhi, sabbhi.
        • "{{42407943476207044::a}}" may be augmented between the root and the suffix -māna (pac + māna ⇒ {{42407943476207044::pacamāna}})
        • e may change to {{09153962737905297::aya}}: (deseti ⇒ {{09153962737905297::desayati}})
        • missakakiriyās are under which of the 4 main divisions of words?→nāmapada (nouns)
        • Other parts of the sentence, not only the verb, can also have objects, instruments and so on (guṇavā buddhaṁ namassanto tiṭṭhati - buddhaṁ is the object of namassanto)
      • Lesson 10 - Infinitive and pronouns
        • tumanta→(tuṁ + anta) infinitive
        • In Pāḷi, infinitives are called tumanta and are made by {{21880385070444053::adding the suffix ‘tuṃ’ to roots or verbal bases.}} Infinitives are that form of the verbs which {{21880385070444053::merely name the action}} such as 'to go', 'to do' and so on.
        • In most of the cases, when the infinitive suffix is added to the root, the vowel ‘{{5701759514629918::i}}’ is augmented between the root and the vowel
        • Why are pronouns called sabbanāma?→because most of them can be declined in any gender (tiliṅgika)
        • Morphemes that can refer to nouns of all genders are called {{46873606261595957::sabbanāma (pronouns)}} in Pāḷi
        • There are {{15538637604921823::twenty-seven}} sabbanāmas in Pāḷi. Some of them are sabba, katara, katama, ubhaya, itara, añña and amha. They are all categorized under the nominal group of sabbanāmagaṇa. It is one of the thirteen nominal groups.
        • 11 / 13 nāmagaṇas (nominal groups)
          • purisādigaṇa (m., akāranta)
          • cittādigaṇa (nt., akāranta)
          • kaññādigaṇa (f., ākāranta)
          • manādigaṇa (mix gender, akaranta)
          • pumādigaṇa (m., akāranta)
          • rājādigaṇa (m., akāranta)
          • satthādigaṇa (m., ukāranta)
          • guṇavantādigaṇa (m., nt., ukāranta)
          • gacchantādigaṇa (m., ukāranta)
          • rattādigaṇa (mixed gender, ikāranta)
            • nadādigaṇa (īkāranta)
            • gahapatādigaṇa (inīkāranta)
          • sabbanāmagaṇa
          • mem aid: a man thinks of a woman who thinks of a man who is a king who wants to pay respect to a teacher who has qualities; (the king) goes during the night to the river together with his house-lady who knows all names
        • declension of the pronoun 'amha' (sabbanāmagaṇa) (aliṅgika)
          • nom. ahaṃ / mayaṃ, amhe, no
          • acc. maṃ, mamaṃ / amhe, amhākaṃ, no
          • ins. mayā, me / amhehi, amhebhi, no
          • dat./gen. mama, mamaṁ, mayhaṃ, me, amhaṃ / amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ, no
          • abl. mayā / amhehi, amhebhi
          • loc. mayi / amhesu
          • note: vo, no, te, me in the declensions of tumha and amha are never used in the beginning of a sentence - they are used at least after one term
        • Most of the declensions of sabbanāma do not have the {{5262245050913308::vocative}} case
        • Vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • sīhāsanaṁ (nt.)↔throne
          • turago (m.)↔horse (s.w. t, not turaṅga)
          • khaggo (m.)↔sword
          • kasā (f.)↔whip
          • vāraṇo (m.)↔elephant (s.w. v)
          • vaḷavā (f.)↔mare
          • hatthāroho (m.)↔elephant rider, mahout
          • sandano (m.)↔chariot (s.w. s)
          • dāruṇa (adj) √dar↔brutal; savage; vicious; cruel
          • mānuso (m.)↔human being (s.w. m, not manussa)
        • declension of the pronoun 'tumha' (sabbanāmagaṇa) (aliṅgika)
          • nom. tvaṃ, tuvaṃ / tumhe, vo
          • acc. taṃ, tavaṃ, tvaṃ, tuvaṃ / tumhe, tumhākaṃ, vo
          • ins. tayā, tvayā, te / tumhehi, -bhi, vo
          • dat./gen. tava, tuyhaṃ, te, tumhaṃ / tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ, vo
          • abl. tayā, tvayā / tumhehi, -bhi
          • loc. tayi, tvayi / tumhesu
          • note: vo, no, te, me in the declensions of tumha and amha are never used in the beginning of a sentence - they are used at least after one term
        • me, te, no, and vo should not be at {{5040143082560318::the beginning of a sentence, not even at the beginning of a line of a verse}}
      • Lesson 11 - Optative mood
        • Permission (anumati) and assumption (parikappa) are expressed through the {{18021228213296725::sattamī vibhatti}} verbs in Pāḷi. This mood is translated as {{18021228213296725::optative.}}
        • Anumati↔permission
        • parikappa↔assumption
        • Sattamī vibhatti
          • eyya, eyyuṃ,
          • eyyāsi, eyyātha,
          • eyyāmi, eyyāma
        • gam – sattamī vibhatti
          • gaccheyya / gaccheyyuṃ
          • gaccheyyāsi / gaccheyyātha
          • gaccheyyāmi / gaccheyyāma
        • {{15931291243335144::Sattamī vibhatti}} is used to express supposition, doubt, possibility, mild command, request, invitation, courteous question and also a prayer. These verbs may be translated into English by using the auxiliary verbs {{15931291243335144::‘may, might, should’ or ‘would}}.

          • dat./gen. rañño, rājino / raññaṃ, rājānaṃ, rājūnaṃ
          • abl. raññā (, rājasmā, rājamhā) / rājehi, rājebhi, rājūhi, rājūbhi
          • loc. raññe, rājini / rājesu, rājūsu
          • note: rājasmā, rājamhā are only found in Niruttidīpanī

      • Lesson 13 - Nominal groups of nadī (nadādigaṇa) and gahapatānī (gahapatādi gaṇa)
        • Nominal groups of nadī and gahapatānī contains only nouns of the {{6764934666339979::feminine}} gender ending in ‘{{6764934666339979::ī}}’. Their declensions are {{6764934666339979::identical}}. They are recognized as two different nominal groups due to the {{6764934666339979::difference of formation of nouns in these groups}}. Feminine nouns of the group nadādi are constructed by {{6764934666339979::adding the suffix ‘ī’}}, whereas the suffix {{6764934666339979::‘inī’}} is added to construct nouns pertaining to the nominal group gahapatādi.
        • Long vowels are not shortened and short vowels may be lengthened.
        • *declension of itthī (f.) (rattādigaṇa / nadādigaṇa)
          • nom. itthī / itthī, itthiyo
          • voc. (bhoti) itthi / (bhotiyo) "
          • acc. itthiṃ, itthiyaṃ / "
          • ins./abl. itthiyā / itthīhi, itthībhi
          • dat./gen. " / itthīnaṃ
          • loc. ", itthiyaṃ / itthīsu
          • mem aid: as ratti but with itthiyaṁ as acc. and no short forms
          • note:
            • paṭhavī has the short forms pathabyā and pathabyaṃ where it applies
            • nadī has the short forms najjo, najjā, najjaṁ where it applies
            • pokkharaṇī has pokkharañño in plural of paṭhamā, ālapana, and dutiyā, pokkharaññā in singular of tatiyā and pokkharaññaṃ in singular of sattamī
        • The declension of nouns pertaining to the group of gahapatānī is similar to that of nouns of the {{347305133595738::nadī}} group.
        • There are three suffixes used to construct feminine nouns: {{9307544416219982::‘ā’, ‘ī’ and ‘inī’}}.

          • i. Gerunds are:>Gerunds (pubbakālakiriyā) are the nipātapada which express an action done before the final action of a sentence. They are constructed by adding the suffix -tvā (in most cases) to the verbal root/base
          • ii. Missaka-kiriyā are→nāmapadas formed by adding the suffix -anta / -māna to verbal bases / roots that can be declined in the three genders and can perform the three functions of missakakiriyā (expressing an action performed simultaneously with the main action), stand-alone nouns or nāmavisesanas (adjectives)
          • iii. visesana and visesya are→nāmapadas declined in the same liṅga (gender), vibhatti (case) and vacana (number) and that act as noun modifiers (visesana) and the nouns that are modified (visesya)
          • iv. Anumati and parikappa→Anumati (permission) is one of the functions of the sattamī vibhatti of the ākhyātapadas. Parikappa is the other function which is to {{5080527187522037::express assumptions.}} They are both constructed by adding the verbal terminations (such as eyya, eyyuṁ...) to verbal bases/roots.

        • 2.1 Grammar
          • declension of the pronoun ‘ta’ (sabbanāmagaṇa)
            • masculine declension
              • Nom. so / te, ne
              • Acc. taṃ, naṃ / te, ne
              • Ins. tena, nena / tehi, tebhi, nehi, nebhi
              • Dat/gen. tassa, nassa, assa / tesaṃ, tesānaṃ, nesaṃ, nesānaṃ
              • Abl. tasmā, nasmā, asmā, tamhā, namhā / tehi, tebhi, nehi, nebhi
              • Loc. tasmiṃ, nasmiṁ, asmiṃ, tamhi, namhi / tesu, nesu
              • memory aid:
                • 1 - t ⇒ n
                • 2 - sa, sma, smiṁ: ta ⇒ a
            • neuter declension
              • Nom./Acc. taṁ, naṃ / te, tāni, ne, nāni
              • (the rest as masculine)
            • feminine declension
              • Nom. sā / tā, tāyo, nā, nāyo
              • Acc. taṃ, naṃ / tā, tāyo, nā, nāyo
              • Ins. / Abl. tāya, nāya / tāhi, tābhi, nāhi, nābhi
              • Dat/gen. tāya, nāya - tassā, nassā, assā, tissā - tassāya, nassāya, assāya, tissāya / tāsaṃ, tāsānaṃ, nāsaṃ, nāsānaṃ
              • Loc. tāyaṃ, nāyaṃ, tassaṃ, nassaṃ, assaṃ, tissaṃ / tāsu, nāsu
              • memory aid:
                • 1 - t ⇒ n
                • 2 - sa, smā, smiṁ, sā, saṁ: ta ⇒ a
                • 3 - dat. gen.: ending in sā: add ya
                • 4 - ta ⇒ ti, sa ⇒ saṁ
          • sandhi↔euphonic combination
          • what is a sandhi (euphonic combinations)? (English definition)→The linguistic act of combining two words (actually letters) for the sake of an easier pronunciation
          • saññā (f.) (grammar) √ñā↔(gram) grammatical term; technical term; definition; lit. name
            • 1.Forty-one letters (41) starting with ‘a’ and ending with ‘ṃ’ are the {{03930858487714595::letters – akkhara}}.
            • 2. Out of the 41 letters, first eight letters: ‘a’, ‘ā’, ‘i’, ‘ī’, ‘u’, ‘ū’, ‘e’ and ‘o’, are {{5903710234419932::vowels – sara}}.
            • 3. Among vowels, three vowels, ‘a’, ‘i’ and ‘u’ are called {{27557109756554143::short vowels – rassa sara}}.
            • 4. The remaining five letters, ‘ā’, ‘ī’, ‘ū’, ‘e’ and ‘o’ are called {{24881204349786334::long vowels – dīgha sara}}.
            • 5. Thirty-three (33) letters starting from ‘k’ till ‘ṃ’ are called {{6514651385913395::consonants – vyañjana/byañjana}}.
            • 6. Out of the consonants, twenty-five letters starting from ‘k’ and ending with ‘m’ are called {{1757153654156589::group letters – vaggakkhara}}
            • 7. Vagga letters are divided into five groups: {{5022266000075137::ka-vagga, ca-vagga, ṭa-vagga, ta vaggga and pa-vagga}}
            • 8. Last letter of each vagga (group) is called {{5557973562087928::group-endings – vagganta}}. There are{{5557973562087928:: five vagganta letters: ‘ṅ’, ‘ñ’, ‘ṇ’, ‘n’ and ‘m’.}}
            • 9.The last consonant of the alphabet is called {{518548251015269::niggahīta (ṁ)}}
            • 9 saññās under sandhi:
              • 41 letters – akkhara
              • 8 vowels – sara
                • 3 short vowels – rassa sara
                • 5 long vowels – dīgha sara (be careful: vuddhis are only ā, e, o)
              • 33 consonants – vyañjana / byañjana
              • 25 group letters – vaggakkhara
                • 5 groups: ka-vagga, ca-vagga, ṭa-vagga, ta vaggga and pa-vagga
                • group-endings – vagganta ‘ṅ’, ‘ñ’, ‘ṇ’, ‘n’ and ‘m’
              • mem aid: akkhara, saras, vyañjana, vagga
          • 3 types of sandhi
            • sara sandhi: letter + vowel (yassa + indriyāni ⇒ yassindriyāni)
            • vyañjana / byañjana sandhi: letter + consonant (ava+vādo = ovādo)
            • niggahīta sandhi: ṁ + letter / the insertion of niggahīta is also included in niggahītasandhi (yaṁ+hi=yañhi)
          • two consonants together are called a {{6065806196803576::saṁyoga / saññoga (conjunct)}}
          • the vowels {{6255338059360125::e and o}} are shortened before double consonants (conjunct) but the remaining vowels may remain long
          • when two words are separated it is called {{6304834061382858::visandhi (disjoining)}}
          • 3 grammar traditions
            • Kaccāyana
            • Moggallāna
            • Saddanīti (Myanmar)

        • 2.1. Reading
          • Tasmiṃ khaṇe nesādo taṃ ekappahāreneva vijjhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Atha so kālaṃ katvā tattheva vihāre vasantassa mahābhayattherassa kaṇiṭṭhikāya kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā dasamāsaddhamāsaccayena mātukucchito nikkhamitvā kamena abhivaḍḍhanto sattavassiko ahosi. Tato taṃ mātāpitaro abhayattherassa santikaṃ nesuṃ. So na cirena kālena pabbājesi. So pana kumāro pubbe migabhūtenattanā dhammasavaṇānubhāvena khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.
        • The suffix ‘-to’ in the word matukucchito is a suffix with which meaning? {{8296795504243739::the ablative meaning (most often)}}. It can be used in both singular and plural according to the context. It is a suffix, not a case ending. It turns the noun into a {{8296795504243739::nipāta}}.

        • 2.2 Grammar
          • declension of the pronoun 'kiṁ' (sabbanāmagaṇa)
            • masculine
              • Nom. ko / ke
              • Acc. kaṁ / "
              • Ins. kena / kehi, kebhi
              • Dat/Gen. kassa, kissa / kesaṁ, kesānaṁ
              • Abl. kasmā, kamhā / kehi, kebhi
              • Loc. kasmiṁ, kismiṁ, kamhi, kimhi / kesu
              • mem aid: extra 'i' form, but not in abl.
            • neuter
              • Nom./Acc. kaṁ, kiṁ / ke, kāni
              • (the rest as the masculine)
            • feminine
              • Nom. kā / kā, kāyo
              • Acc. kaṁ / "
              • Ins./Abl. kāya / kāhi, kābhi
              • Dat/Gen. kāya, kassā / kāsaṁ, kāsānaṁ
              • Loc. kāyaṁ, kassaṁ / kāsu
              • note: no 'i' form, 'a' takes over
            • If one does not know which gender the word kiṁ refers to the gender used is {{13904412465489324::neuter kiṁ}}.
          • Sara sandhi is further divided into following categories.
            • 1). Lopa (elision) – Elision of a vowel
              • pubba sara lopa sandhi (elision of the previous vowel)
                • paññā + indriyaṁ ⇒ paññindriyaṁ
                • loka + aggo ⇒ lokaggo
                  • In traditional Pāḷi grammar, on most of such occasions the combination is considered to have happened by eliding the previous vowel (pubbasara)
              • para sara lopa sandhi (elision of the following vowel / succeeding vowel) It only occurs between dissimilar vowels. Dissimilarity of vowels is based on the difference of sounds. (a and ā, i and ī, u and ū are similar; the others are dissimilar)
                • cattāro + ime ⇒ cattārome
                • saññā + iti ⇒ saññāti
            • 2) Ādesa – substitution
            • 4) Dīgha – lengthening
            • 3) Āgama – augmentation or insertion

          • Tassa pana mātulatthero paṭiladdhapañcābhiñño appattaarahattamaggaphalo ahosi. Athekasmiṃ divase sāmaṇero padoseva upajjhāyassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Athassa upajjhāyo hatthaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pāṇinā candamaṇḍalaṃ parimaddanto aṭṭhāsi. Sāmaṇero taṃ disvā “Bhante, etaṃ rakkhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Thero pana tassa aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ajānanto tassa vacanaṃ na sammā manasākāsi. Atha sāmaṇero iddhiyā candasahassaṃ āharitvā therassa dassetvā “Bhante, candasataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā satasahassaṃ vā āharaṇaṃ na bhāriyaṃ.               • jaladhi (m.)↔sea
              • gahapati (m.)↔householder
              • samādhi (m.)↔concentration
              • maṇi (m.)↔gem
              • giri (m.)↔mountain (s.w. g)
              • ravi (m.)↔sun
              • asi (m.)↔khagga
              • nidhi (m.)↔treasure

              • atithi (m.)↔(m.) āgantuko, visitor
          • Dhātugaṇa (root groups)
            • Roots ({{7969412836027532::dhātu}}) are the fundamental sounds (morphemes) which have verbal meanings. Verbs are made by{{7969412836027532:: adding a vikaraṇa paccaya (conjugational sign) and a verbal termination to the roots}}. All the roots in Pāḷi are classified into {{7969412836027532::eight }}groups called {{7969412836027532::dhātugaṇa}}. They are classified according to {{7969412836027532::conjugational signs (vikaraṇa paccaya)}}.
            • The suffix added between the dhātu and the verbal termination is called {{8107451289781471::the conjugational sign – vikaraṇa paccaya}}. There are {{8107451289781471::thirteen}} such signs in Pāḷi.
            • Following are the eight dhātugaṇa together with their vikaraṇa paccaya
              • 1. bhūvādigaṇa – a (most common)
              • 2. rudhādigaṇa – ṃ … a
              • 3. divādigaṇa – ya
              • 4. svādigaṇa (√su) – ṇā, ṇu, uṇā
              • 5. kiyādigaṇa – nā
              • 6. gahādigaṇa – ṇhā, ppa
              • 7. tanādigaṇa – o, yira
              • 8. curādigaṇa – (ṇ)e, (ṇ)aya (2nd most common)
              • mem aid: the ghost (bhū) cries (rudh), the deva (div) is happy (su), the kiṇṇara (ki) holds (gah) with stretched (tan) paws the thief (cur)
            • Curādi group
              • Though it is mentioned in traditional Pāḷi books that the conjugational sign of the curādi group is ‘ṇe’ and ‘ṇaya’ the actual signs are {{21822081392744397::‘e’ and ‘aya’.}} The lingual ‘ṇ’ is just an indicator called {{21822081392744397::anubandha}}. It indicates that when the conjugational sign is added to the root{{21822081392744397:: the first vowel gets strengthened (vuddhi)}}. After that {{21822081392744397::the anubandha sign ‘ṇ’ is dropped.}}
              • During the process of vowel strengthening ({{6395027069312367::vuddhi}}) a light vowel turns into its corresponding heavy vowel: a > {{6395027069312367::ā}}, i and ī > {{6395027069312367::e}}, u and ū > {{6395027069312367::o}} When a light vowel is followed by {{6395027069312367::a double consonant (saññoga)}} vuddhi normally does not occur
              • A few roots belonging to the curādigaṇa
                • cinteti / cintayati↔thinks
                • peseti / pesayati↔sends
                • pāleti / pālayati √pāl↔protects
                • poseti / posayati↔nourishes, brings up
                • vedeti / vedayati↔knows
      • Lesson 4 - declension of 'daṇḍī', bhikkhu, sayambhū
        • 4.1. Reading
          • Taṃ sutvā thero vipassitvā tadaheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha dutiyadivase therakaṇiṭṭhikā sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ theraṃ nimantesi. Thero bhaginiṃ evamāha. “Upāsike, tayājja bahū bhikkhū disvā cittaṃ pasādetabbaṃ. Paṭivīso pana dvinnaṃyeva hotū”ti taṃ pesetvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya bahūhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ agamāsi. Tesaṃ ānubhāvena dvinnaṃyeva paṭiyāditaṃ sūpabyañjanādi sabbaṃ bahūnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pahonakaṃ ahosi. Bhuttāvasāne kho upāsikā bhuttānumodanatthaṃ sāmaṇerassa pattaṃ gaṇhi. Sopi tesaṃ majjhe madhurabhāratiṃ nicchārento dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāvasāne mātāpitaro ādiṃ katvā bahū sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Bahuno janassa sā desanā sātthikā ahosi.

      • Lesson 5 - declension of 'atta', bhavalakkhaṇa, pubbasaradīghasandhi
        • 5.1. Reading
          • Atīte jambudīpe ajitaraṭṭhe eko gopālako vasi. Tassa gehe eko paccekabuddho nibaddhaṃ bhuñjati. Tasmiṃ gehe eko kukkuro ca ahosi. Paccekabuddho bhuñjanto tassa nibaddhaṃ ekaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ adāsi. So tena paccekabuddhe (loc.sg) sinehamakāsi. Gopālako divasassa dve vāre paccekabuddhassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchi. Sunakhopi tena saddhiṃ gacchi. Gopālo ekadivasaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ āha: “Yadā me bhante, okāso na bhavissati, tadā imaṃ sunakhaṃ pesessāmi. Tena saññāṇena āgaccheyyāthā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya anokāsadivase sunakhaṃ pesesi. So ekavacaneneva pakkhanditvā paccekabuddhassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tikkhattuṃ bhussitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā ekamantaṃ nipajji. Paccekabuddhe velaṃ sallakkhetvā nikkhante bhussanto purato gacchi. Paccekabuddho taṃ vīmaṃsanto ekadivasaṃ aññaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Atha sunakho purato tiriyaṃ ṭhatvā bhussitvā itaramaggameva naṃ āropesi.
          • English translation:
            • In the past in the island of Jambudīpa in a country called Ajita dwelt a herdsman. In his house a silent Buddha regularly ate. In that house there was also a dog. The silent buddha would frequently give a lump of food to it. The dog because of that became fond of the silent buddha. The herdsman twice a day would go to silent buddha for serving him. The dog as well would go with him. One day the herdsman said to the silent buddha: "Whenever, bhante, I have no opportunity (to come) I will send this dog. By this sign may bhante come". From then onwards whenever he had no opportunity to go he would send the dog. The dog would spring forward on a single command and after having approached the dwelling place of the private buddha would bark thrice to make known its presence and lie down at a side. When the private buddha departed after having considered the time it would go ahead while barking. The private buddha one day took a different path in order to test the dog. Then the dog stood horizontally and while barking got the silent buddha back on the right path.
          • Vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]

          • In Pāḷi adverbs are called {{10983049870057693::kiriyā visesana}} – {{10983049870057693::verb modifiers}}. They are adjectives mostly written in {{10983049870057693::neuter gender accusative singular form or sometimes instrumental}}. There are also some nipātas which function as adverbs as well.

The main verb of the sentence could be in different verbal tenses

      • Lesson 6 - declension of 'eta', causative, niggahītasandhi
        • 6.1. Reading
          • Athekadivasaṃ aññaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā sunakhe tiriyaṃ ṭhatvā vārentepi anivattitvā taṃ pādena apanetvā pāyāsi. Sunakho tassa anivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā nivāsanakaṇṇe ḍaṃsitvā ākaḍḍhanto gantabbamaggameva pāpesi. Evaṃ so sunakho tasmiṃ paccekabuddhe balavasinehaṃ uppādesi. Aparabhāge paccekabuddhassa cīvaraṃ jīri. Athassa gopālako cīvaravatthāni adāsi. Paccekabuddho “Phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā cīvaraṃ kāressāmī”ti gopālakaṃ āha. Sopi “Bhante mā ciraṃ bahi vasitthā”ti avadi. Sunakhopi tesaṃ kathaṃ suṇanto aṭṭhāsi. Paccekabuddhe vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā gacchante bhuṅkaritvā ṭhitassa sunakhassa hadayaṃ phali. Tiracchānā nāmete ujujātikā honti akuṭilā. Manussā pana aññaṃ cintenti, aññaṃ vadanti.
          • English translation:
            • Then, one day after following another path when the dog 🐶 stood sideways preventing him he went on without stopping moving it away with his foot. The dog realizing he did not stop bit the edge of his robe and while dragging him made him reach the right path. In this way that dog gave rise to strong affection for the private buddha. Afterwards the private buddha's robe got worn out. Then the herdsman offered him cloth for a robe. The paccekabuddha said to the herdsman: "I will go to a comfortable place and have a robe made" and the herdsman said thus: "Bhante, may bhante not dwell away for long". The dog too stood listening to their conversation. When the private buddha rose up in the sky and was going away the dog barked and its heart was broken. Such animals are of an honest nature, not crooked, but humans think one thing and say another.
          • Vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]

          • the particle mā goes with either {{42663216527004::pañcamī vibhatti or ajjatanī vibhatti (mā vasatha / mā vasittha). }}In both cases it has the same meaning (the {{42663216527004::past}} meaning is not applied). On occasions where respect should be shown plural nouns and verbs are used instead of singular.
        • 6.2 Grammar
          • declension of the pronoun "eta" (sabbanāmagaṇa)
            • masculine declension
              • Nom. eso / ete
              • Acc etaṃ, enaṁ / ete
              • Ins. etena / etehi, etebhi
              • Dat/gen. etassa / etesaṃ, etesānaṃ
              • Abl. etasmā, etamhā / etehi, etebhi
              • Loc. etasmiṃ, etamhi / etesu
              • note: only one 'n' version - enaṁ (not in neuter)
            • neuter declension
              • Nom. etaṃ / ete, etāni
              • Acc etaṃ / ete, etāni
              • (the rest as masculine)
              • note: no 'enaṁ' as masculine
            • feminine declension
              • Nom. esā / etā, etāyo
              • Acc. etaṃ / etā, etāyo
              • Ins./Abl. etāya / etāhi, etābhi
              • Dat/Gen. etāya, etissā, etissāya / etāsaṃ, etāsānaṃ
              • Loc. etāyaṃ, etissaṃ / etāsu
              • note:
                • neither 'na' nor 'a' versions as with 'ta'
                • no 'enaṁ' as with masculine 'eta'
                • 'i' versions as with 'ta'
                • dat./gen. like 'ta' but only the tā- and ti- versions
          • Causative actions and verbs (kārita kiriyā / payojja kiriyā / hetu kiriyā)
            • an action made to be done by someone else is called {{1620647690656032::kārita kiriyā / payojja kiriyā / hetu kiriyā}}{{1620647690656032:: (causative actions)}} ; verbs used to indicate such actions are called {{1620647690656032::kārita kiriyā pada }}{{1620647690656032::(causative verbs)}} #[[final exam pāḷi]]
              • payojja = "combine"
              • can the verbs also be called pajojja kiriyā pada and hetu kiriyā pada? #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • 4 causative suffixes used to construct kārita kiriyā pada (causative verbs): #[[final exam pāḷi]]
              • 1. (ṇ)e
              • 2. (ṇ)aya
              • 3. (ṇ)āpe
              • 4. (ṇ)āpaya

            • vuddhi is traditionally explained as {{18132284856943226::being the vowels }}{{18132284856943226::ā}}{{18132284856943226::, }}{{18132284856943226::e}}{{18132284856943226:: and }}{{18132284856943226::o}}{{18132284856943226:: }}and modern teachers teach it as {{18132284856943226::the act of strengthening a vowel: a ⇒ ā i, ī ⇒ e u, ū ⇒ o }} note: if followed by a double consonant, vuddhi does not occur
              • even though long vowels do not change are they considered strengthened in such cases? is there a strengthening of a long vowel? #q🙋🏼‍♂

            • 2 types of niggahīta sandhi according to the letter that substitutes ṁ when followed by a vowel (ṁ + vowel)
              • makāra ādesa sandhi (substitution of ṁ for m): gantabbamaggaṃ + eva = gantabbamaggameva
              • dakāra ādesa sandhi (substitution of ṁ for d): this happens only with the pronouns:
                • ya (yaṁ + idaṁ = yadidaṁ)
                • ta (taṁ + eva = tadeva)
                • eta (etaṁ + ahosi = etadahosi)
                • note: philologically, this is the recurrence of the ending consonant d of those pronouns found in Sanskrit (yad, tad, etad)
            • ādeso (m.) √dis↔(gram) substitution; replacement; change
      • Lesson 7 - saṅkhyānāma, tulyatthaliṅgatthavākya, yākārādi āgamasandhi, dvebhāvasandhi
        • 7.1. Reading
          • Kūṭavāṇija Jātakaṃ – 1 Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ vāṇijakule nibbatti. Nāmaggahaṇadivase assa paṇḍitoti nāmamakaṃsu. So vayappatto aññena vāṇijena saddhiṃ ekato hutvā vāṇijjaṃ karoti. Tassa atipaṇḍitoti nāmaṃ ahosi. Te bārāṇasito pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya janapadaṃ gantvā vaṇijjaṃ katvā laddhalābhā puna bārāṇasiṃ āgamiṃsu. Atha tesaṃ bhaṇḍabhājanakāle atipaṇḍito āha: “Mayā dve koṭṭhāsā laddhabbā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā?”ti. “Tvaṃ paṇḍito, ahaṃ atipaṇḍito, paṇḍito ekaṃ laddhuṃ arahati, atipaṇḍito dve”ti. Nanu amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ bhaṇḍamūlampi goṇādayopi samasamāyeva. Kasmā tvaṃ dve koṭṭhāse laddhuṃ arahasī?”ti. “Atipaṇḍitabhāvenā”ti. Evaṃ te kathaṃ vaḍḍhetvā kalahaṃ akaṃsu.
          • Quick English translation:
            • In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the bodhisatta was born in a family of merchants. In his naming day he was given the name Paṇḍita. After growing up he joined another merchant in business whose name was Atipaṇḍita. After taking goods from Bārāṇāsī with five hundred carts they went to the countryside, did business and after making profit came back to Bārāṇasī. Then when it was the time for sharing the goods Atipaṇḍito said: "I should receive two portions", "for what reason?" asked Paṇḍita. "You are Paṇḍita and I am Atipaṇḍita. Paṇḍita deserves one share while Atipaṇḍita deserves two". "Isn't our investments, oxen and so on, the same indeed?

          • Sentences which have nouns in the place of verbs are called {{27744513744441224::tulyattha liṅgattha }}{{27744513744441224::vākya ("same meaning stem meaning sentences")}} It is also fine to say that they are sentences with either {{27744513744441224::predicate }}{{27744513744441224::nominatives}} (Tvaṃ paṇḍito) or {{27744513744441224::predicate }}{{27744513744441224::adjectives}} (Mayā dve koṭṭhāsā laddhabbā) #[[final exam pāḷi]]

          • sarasandi
            • yakārādi āgama sandhi (augmentation of consonants ‘y’ and so on):
              • sandhi in which the following consonants are augmented when followed by a vowel:
              • y - pari + esati > pariyesati
              • v - ti + aṅgikaṃ > tivaṅgikaṃ
              • m - idha + āhu > idhamāhu
              • d - u + ayo > udayo
              • n - ito + āyati > ito nāyati
              • t - tasmā + iha > tasmātiha (tasmātiha bhikkhave evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ)
              • r - ni + antaraṃ > nirantaraṃ
              • ḷ - cha + abhiññā > chaḷabhiññā
                • if pāḷi is a spoken language how can l and ḷ be the same sound? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • From Kaccāyana: "yavamadanataralā cāgamā" > yava (as long as) mada (one is intoxicated) na (one cannot) Tara (cross) la (there)
          • dvebhāva sandhi
            • sometimes the consonant in the beginning of the second word is duplicated, which is called augmentation of a consonant; the consonant that is thus augmented is called {{7724796027804757::dvebhāva}}
              • philologically, most of such doubling is due to the assimilation of the two beginning consonants of the Sanskrit counterpart of those words. For example, vaya + prāpta > vayaprāpta > vayappātta > vayappatta; nāma + grahaṇa + divasa > nāmagrahaṇadivasa > nāmaggahaṇadivasa
            • dvebhāva sandhi is twofold:
              • sadisa dvebhāva sandhi (similar augmented consonant): pp, gg
                • sappuriso
                • duggati
              • asadisa dvebhāva sandhi (dissimilar augmented consonants): bbh, pph
                • when the beginning letter of the second word is an aspiration (kh, gh, ch, jh, ṭh, ḍh, th, dh, ph, bh), the augmented consonant is its non-aspirated counterpart (k, g, c, j, t, d, p, b) since in pāḷi two aspirated consonants never come close to each other without a vowel in between them

        • 8.1. Reading
          • Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka - 2 Tato atipaṇḍito ‘Attheko upāyo’ti cintetvā attano pitaraṃ ekasmiṃ susirarukkhe pavesetvā “Tvaṃ amhesu āgatesu ‘Atipaṇḍito dve koṭṭhāse laddhuṃ arahatī’ti vadeyyāsī”ti vatvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “Samma, mayhaṃ dvinnaṃ koṭṭhāsānaṃ yuttabhāvaṃ vā ayuttabhāvaṃ vā esā rukkhadevatā jānāti. Ehi naṃ pucchissāmā”ti taṃ tattha netvā “Ayye rukkhadevate, amhākaṃ aṭṭaṃ pacchindā”ti āha. Athassa pitā saraṃ parivattetvā “Tena hi kathethā”ti āha. “Ayye, ayaṃ paṇḍito, ahaṃ atipaṇḍito. Amhehi ekato vohāro kato. Tattha kena kiṃ laddhabba”nti. “Paṇḍitena eko koṭṭhāso. Atipaṇḍitena dve laddhabbā”ti. Bodhisatto evaṃ vinicchitaṃ aṭṭaṃ sutvā “Idāni devatābhāvaṃ vā adevatābhāvaṃ vā jānissāmī”ti palālaṃ āharitvā susiraṃ pūretvā aggiṃ adāsi. Atipaṇḍitassa pitā jālāya phuṭṭhakāle addhajjhāmena sarīrena upari āruyha sākhaṃ gahetvā olambanto bhūmiyaṃ pati.

            • ins. pitunā, pitarā, (petyā [gāthā]) / pitūhi, pitūbhi, pitarehi, pitarebhi

            • note:
              • same for bhātā (brother)
              • *word formation under rattādigaṇa
          • Passive voice sentences
            • In passive voice sentences the subject is written in the {{38520074737646737::instrumental}} case whereas the object is written in the {{38520074737646737::nominative}} case because the word that indicates the verb refers to the object. The object is {{38520074737646737::utta kamma}} (as opposed to utta kattu). The word referred to by the verb or the verbal-word should always be written in the {{38520074737646737::nominative}} case.
            • if a word made in the passive meaning is in the place of a verb the question that should be asked must be {{07703764988392736::passive}}. if a word made in the active meaning is in the place of a verb the question that should be asked must be {{07703764988392736::active}}. One cannot ask an active voice question regarding a passively constructed word which is in the place of a verb and vice-versa.
            • Sentences in which the {{8994412315158447::object}} is expressed by either the verb or the verbal word are called {{82531144759819::passive}} voice sentences Sentences in which the {{8994412315158447::subject}} is expressed either by the verb or by the verbal word are called {{82531144759819::active}} voice sentences
            • Syntax
              • Subject (kattu): Said by the verb or verbal-word (utta): {{8748818175640989::nominative}} Unsaid by the verb or verbal-word (anutta): {{8748818175640989::instrumental}} Object (kamma): Said by the verb or verbal-word (utta): {{8748818175640989::nominative}} Unsaid by the verb or verbal-word (anutta): {{8748818175640989::accusative}}
            • Niggahīta sandhi
              • Parassara lopa sandhi
                • When niggahīta is followed by a vowel sometimes {{9553217544931532::the vowel is elided (tvaṃ + asi > tvaṃsi (tvaṃsi ācariyo mama)}}
              • vaggantādesa sandhi
                • When a niggahīta is followed by a group-letter (vaggakkhara), the niggahīta is substituted by {{7067650030317205::the ending letter of the group (vagganta byañjana) to which that group-consonant belongs.}} (taṇhaṅkaro > taṇhaṃ + karo)
      • Lesson 9 - manogaṇa, pumādigaṇa
        • 9.1. Reading
          • Nāmasiddhi Jātaka - 1 Atīte takkasilāyaṃ bodhisatto disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañcamāṇavakasatāni mante vācesi. Tasseko māṇavo ‘Pāpako’ nāma nāmena. So ‘Ehi pāpaka, yāhi pāpakā”ti vuccamāno cintesi: mayhaṃ nāmaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ. Aññaṃ nāmaṃ āharāpessāmīti. So ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “Ācariya, mayhaṃ nāmaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ. Aññamme nāmaṃ karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ ācariyo “Gaccha tāta, janapadacārikaṃ caritvā attano abhirucitaṃ ekaṃ maṅgalaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā ehi. Āgatassa te nāmaṃ parivattetvā aññaṃ nāmaṃ karissāmī”ti. So “Sādhū”ti pātheyyaṃ gahetvā nikkhanto gāmena gāmaṃ caranto ekaṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha ceko puriso kālakato jīvako nāma nāmena. So taṃ ñātijanena āḷāhanaṃ nīyamānaṃ disvā “Ko nāmesa puriso?”ti pucchi. “Jīvako nāmeso”ti. “Jīvako’pi maratī?”ti. “Jīvako’pi marati. Ajīvako’pi marati. Nāmaṃ nāma paññattimattaṃ. Tvaṃ bāloti maññe”ti. So taṃ kathaṃ sutvā nāme majjhatto hutvā antonagaraṃ pāvisi.

            • *declension of mana (manādigaṇa)
              • Nom. mano, manaṃ / manā, manāni

                • ahani, ahu, raho
              • mem aid:
                • simplified method: purisa + citta + o / sā / so / - / si
                • exceptions:
                  • ahani, ahu
                  • raho
                  • thāma is fake ukāranta
              • note:
                • another list: "mano tamo tapo tejo rajo ojo uro siro ayo vayo payo vāso raho ceto saro yaso chando icchādayo nāma manogaṇo'ti vuccare"
                  • there are 2 lists, some words in this group do not share all 3 characteristics
                  • vayo belongs to purisādi group when its meaning is destruction as in ‘udayavaya’
                  • saro belongs to purisādi group when its meaning is arrow or vowel
                  • raho is found as a nipāta as well
                  • rajo has 2 characteristics: sa so si, o in samāsa
                • 3 characteristics shared by most words of manogaṇa
                  • 1: o as accusative
                  • 2: sā, so, -, si
                  • 3: o in samāsas and taddhitas
                    • samāsa: manoseṭṭhā, vayovuḍḍho, tejodhātu, tapovanaṃ
                    • taddhita: manomayā, ayomayaṃ

So antaravīthiyā gacchanto taṃ pothiyamānaṃ disvā “Kasmā imaṃ pothethā”ti pucchi. “Bhatiṃ dātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Kimpanassā nāma”nti. “Dhanapālī nāmā”ti. “Nāmena dhanapālī samānāpi bhatimattaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Dhanapāliyopi adhanapāliyopi duggatā honti. Nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ. Tvaṃ pana bālo maññe”ti. So nāme majjhattataro hutvā nagarā nikkhamma maggaṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge maggamūḷhaṃ purisaṃ disvā “Ambho, kiṃ karonto vicarasī”ti pucchi. "maggamūḷhomhi sāmī”ti. “Kimpana te nāma”nti. “Panthako nāmā”ti. “Panthakāpi magge mūḷhā hontī”ti. “Panthakopi apanthakopi maggamūḷho hoti. Nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ. Tvaṃ bālo maññe”ti. So nāme atimajjhatto hutvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “Kiṃ tāta, nāmaṃ rocetvā āgatosī”ti ca vutte “Ācariya, jīvakāpi nāma maranti ajīvakāpi. Dhanapāliyopi duggatā honti adhanapāliyopi. Panthakāpi maggamūḷhā honti apanthakāpi. Nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ. Nāmena siddhi natthi. Kammeneva siddhi. Alaṃ mayhaṃ aññena nāmena. Tadeva me nāmaṃ hotū”ti āha. Bodhisatto tena diṭṭhañca katañca saṃsandetvā imaṃ gāthamāha. Jīvakañca mataṃ disvā, dhanapāliñca duggataṃ Panthakañca vane mūḷhaṃ, pāpako punarāgato.
          • Nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ. Nāmena siddhi natthi. Kammeneva siddhi.
          • English translation: #editing
            • Then the owners of a female slave who did not give the money back made her sit down by the door and were hitting her with a whip. Her name was "The one who protects wealth". Walking on the middle of the road he saw her being beaten and asked: "why are you beating her?", "She did not give back the money", "What is her name?", "The name is The one who protects wealth", "Even being named "The one who protects wealth" she is not able to give back a mere fee". "Those (who are named) those who protect wealth as well as those who are named those who do not protect wealth can be poor. The name is just a designation. I think you are a fool". Becoming more indifferent to his name he left the city, took the road and on it saw a man who had lost his way and asked him "Hey there, what are you doing wandering around?", "I have lost my way, sir", "What is your name?", "'One who knows the way' is my name", "Even those named 'One who knows the way' can also lose their way", "Those named 'one who knows the way' as well as those who are named 'one who does not know the way' can both lose their way. The name is just a designation. I think you are a fool!". Becoming more indifferent to his name he went to the presence of the future-buddha who said: " ...only by deeds there is success. Enough of other names for me. May this indeed be my name". The future-buddha comparing what was seen and done by him uttered the verse: "Having seen the one who lives dead, the wealthy-one poor, the skilled in the way lost in the woods, pāpaka came back"

      • attha #edited
        • attha chart

        • what is attha?
          • realities; any objects that can be known by the mind (anything, including ultimate realities and concepts)
            • how do we know the mind can know everything? #q🙋🏼‍♂
        • when an attha is known by the mind, it is felt as existing
        • 2 main ways the mind knows atthas
          • diṭṭhavasena: when encountering objects of the 5 senses
          • sutavasena: when hearing / reading words / signs
        • hīnattha
          • what are hīnatthas?
            • mind-made: realities that are created by certain types of cittas
            • cittanimitta: mental ideas / signs
            • subjective: do not really exist objectively, but depend on the subject / observer for their existence
            • reducible: they can be reduced into components
            • e.g.: meanings, concepts, words, ideas
          • parikappanā / vikappanā
            • process of production of hīnatthas by the mind
              • Sesānīti pañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchana dvayato sesāni santīraṇa mahāvipākāni. Sabbathāpi kāmāvacarā lambaṇānevāti paṭisandhādīhi nānākiccehi rūpādīsu nānārammaṇesu pavattena sabba pakārenapi kāmāvacarālambaṇikāniyeva. Tāni hi sabbaññubuddhānaṃ uppannānipi vikappasattirahitattā avijjamāne paññattidhammeca sukhume mahaggatadhammeca gambhīre lokuttaradhammeca ālambituṃ na sakkontīti. (Prd. 138.).
          • why are they called so?
            • lower degree of existence: what is known by the mind is experienced as real, but among what is experienced as so, some are independently real and have, therefore, a higher degree of existence, while others are dependently real and have, therefore, a lower (hīna) degree of existence (attha)
            • subjective: their existence depends on the observer
          • simile for hīnatthas
            • like a spinning firebrand that appears as a circle, though the circle does not exist
          • renderings for hīnattha
            • concepts, subjective realities, conceptual realities, ideas, conceptual natures
          • 2 types of hīnattha (paññatti)
            • atthapaññatti (concepts-as-meanings): meanings conveyed by names; that which is made known
              • saṇṭhānapaññatti (formal / structural-concepts): correspond to the form or configuration of things: (land, mountain...)
              • samūhapaññatti (collective-concept): correspond to a collection or group of things (house, chariot, village...)
              • disāpaññatti (local-concepts): correspond to a locality or direction (east, west...)
              • kālapaññatti (temporal-concepts): correspond to periods or units of time (morning, noon, week, month...)
              • ākāsapaññatti (spatial-concepts): correspond to spatial regions void of perceptible matter (well, cave...)
              • nimittapaññatti (sign-concepts): correspond to mental signs gained by meditative development
              • vocab:
                • saṇṭhānaṁ (nt.)↔form, configuration, position; composition, nature, shape #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
                • samūho (m.)↔multitude, mass, aggregation #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • nāmapaññatti (concepts-as-names): names that convey meanings; that which makes something known
              • vijjamānapaññatti (concept of the real): a concept which refers to a reality such as rūpa, citta...
              • avijjamānapaññatti (concept of the unreal): a concept which refers to something that is not real such as land, mountain...These concepts are based on ultimate entities but the meanings they convey are not things that are themselves ultimate entities since they do not correspond to things that exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva)
              • vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti (a concept of the unreal by means of the real): possessor of sixfold direct knowledge (possessor: unreal, knowledge: real)
              • avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti (a concept of the real by means of the unreal): woman's voice (woman: unreal, voice: real)
              • vijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti (a concept of the real by means of the real): eye-consciousness (both real)
              • avijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti (a concept of the unreal by means of the unreal): king's son (both unreal)
          • kevalañhi samādhilābhino upaṭṭhānākāramattaṃ saññajametanti (hīnatthas are all born of perception, a mere appearance) (vsm)
            • if only saññaja were mentioned, it could lead to the idea that paññattis have intrinsic nature
          • do hīnatthas perform the funtion of being an object due to their own ability?
            • no, hīnatthas do not have kiccarasa, only up
        • paramattha
          • what are paramatthas?
            • objective: realities that exist without depending on a subject, therefore objectively
            • verifiable: their actual state of existence can be verified by intellectual investigation
            • irreducible: they cannot be reduced into components
            • intrinsic nature: possess their own intrinsic nature
            • functions: they are able to perform tasks / actions / functions, therefore can be called energies / forces
            • eg: cittas, cetasikas, rūpas and Nibbāna, khandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, etc.
          • renderings for paramattha
            • actualities, realities, ultimate realities, phenomena, dhammas, objective realities, natures, entities, dhātus, āyatanas, khandhas
            • sārattha
              • essential realities: the real core of the observed objects
              • other meanings: masc. heart of the goal; essence of welfare
            • mūlattha
              • root realities: being root ingredients of things
          • what is an objective reality?
            • a reality that does not depend on a subject / observer (mind) for its existence
            • note: it does mean that they exist without causes; they depend on other paramatthas for their existence
          • 2 types of paramatthas
            • saṅkhata (formed): citta, cetasikas and rūpas‒4 types
              • paramatthadhammā (ultimate realities)
              • paramatthajātikā (underlying defilements)
              • anuppannadhammā (unarisen realities)
              • uppādino dhammā (arisen realities): realities which are set to arise in the future as result of kamma
              • notes:
                • jātika [√jan + ti + ka]↔adj. of nature; of type; of class; of category; lit. of birth; 2 adj. descended from; born from; produced by; lit. of birth; 3 adj. belonging to clan, or nation of
            • asaṅkhata (unformed): Nibbāna
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
          • note:
            • paramatthas, by themselves, are neither 3D nor 2D
            • there is no dichotomy between the reality and its intrinsic nature
        • methods for differentiating hīnatthas from paramatthas
          • reduction / reductionism: dividing things into smaller components
            • hīnattha: can be reduced into components
            • paramattha: can't
          • functions done towards the Noble Truths
            • pariññā: knowing a reality with its specific and general characteristics
              • hīnatthas: cannot be known with pariññā
              • paramatthas: can
              • 2 types
                • abhiññā (higher knowledge): knowing a reality with its specific characteristics, intrinsic nature
                • pariññā (full knowledge): knowing a reality with its general characteristics (anicca, dukkha, anatta);
                • note: Nibbāna can be pariññā in the sense that one sees the characteristic of santilakkhaṇa (is this more specifically abhiññā?) #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • pahāna: abandoning, eradicating
              • hīnattha: cannot be abandoned, eradicated
              • paramattha: can; only realities can be eradicated
            • sacchikaraṇa: knowing, obtaining, attaining
              • hīnattha: cannot be attained
              • paramattha: can
              • extra notes:
                • 3 types
                  • ārammaṇakaraṇasacchikaraṇa (experiencing as knowing directly) (can hīnatthas be said to be known in this aspect?) #q🙋🏼‍♂
                  • paṭilabhasacchikaraṇa (experiencing as obtaining): equal to bhāvanā such as making magga arise
                  • adhigamasacchikaraṇa (experiencing as attaining): attainment of Nibbāna (clarify difference between paṭilabha and adhigama) #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • bhāvanā: developing
              • hīnattha: cannot be developed
              • paramattha: can
          • productive force: ability to produce a result
            • hīnattha: cannot
            • paramattha: some can
          • possessing lakkhaṇa, rasa, phalapaccupaṭṭhāna, and padaṭṭhāna
            • hīnatthas: only possess upaṭṭhānākārapaccupaṭṭhāna
              • though they do not have padaṭṭhāna, in suttas, its cause is given as
                • the 4 mahābhūtā becase many hīnatthas are based on them
                • or, in a way, citta is their cause, since hīnatthas are produced by it
            • paramatthas: possess all (but Nibbāna does not have padaṭṭhāna)
          • sabhāva: intrinsic nature
            • hīnatthas: do not possess it
            • paramatthas: do
              • jātaṁ rūpaṁ sabhāvena suññāṁ (rūpa which has arisen is empty of sabhāva [here, it means a self])
                • based on this, some believe that rūpa has no sabhāva
                • jātaṁ rūpaṁ: how could something that came into existence not exist?
          • (could we say having paccayasatti?)
        • 2 types of bhāva #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • ekattabhāva (unity, oneness)
          • nānattabhāva (plurality) (are they the same as ekattanaya and nānattanaya?) #q🙋🏼‍♂
        • 5 dhammatās (universal laws) with examples
          • bījaniyāma (natural law of plants and seeds): mango seed only producing a mango tree, sunflower facing the sun, coconut having 3 eyes
          • utuniyāma (natural law of seasons and weather): it explains the occurrence of buds, flowers and fruits in specific types of plants during the same season
          • kammaniyāma (natural law of volitional actions and their results): describes how results manifest in accordance with the nature of the actions they are associated with
          • dhammaniyāma (natural law of dhammas): It encompasses all other natural phenomena, such as the appearance of signs like earthquakes during significant moments like conception, birth, enlightenment of a bodhisattva, or the delivery of the first sermon
            • yoniniyāma: what mainly influences appearance, not so much the kamma itself, which mainly influences the destination
              • citta ⇒ kamma ⇒ gati ⇒ yoni ⇒ appearance
          • cittaniyāma (natural law of consciousness): it pertains to the arising of successive generations of consciousness in a particular sequence without external intervention when objects, such as visible forms, impact the senses
        • realities, collective realities, and concepts
          • group of realities taken as one thing is a {{07785267296081688::concept}}, when not taken as one thing but as a group of realities is {{07785267296081688::collective realities (not a concept)}}
        • 2 saccas
          • paramatthasacca
          • sammutisacca

                  • Kenaṭṭhena anantaro, kenaṭṭhena paccayoti. Attano anantare attasadisassa dhammantarassa uppādanaṭṭhena anantaro, upakārakaṭṭhena paccayo. Tattha 14 attasadisassāti sārammaṇa bhāvena attanā sadisassa. Sārammaṇabhāvenāti ca yo dhammo ārammaṇena vinā na pavattati, so sārammaṇo nāma, evaṃ sārammaṇabhāvena. Dhammantarassa uppādanaṭṭhenāti purimasmiṃ citte niruddhepi tassa cintanakiriyāvego na vūpasammati, pacchimaṃ cittaṃ uppādetvā eva vūpasammati, evaṃ pacchimassa dhammantarassa uppādanaṭṭhena. (Pāṭṭh-ud-dī. 473.).
                    • "Why is it 'proximate' (anantara), and why is it a 'condition' (paccaya)? It is 'proximate' because of the production of another phenomenon (dhammantara) similar to itself immediately following it, and it is a 'condition' because of its supportive nature. Here, 'similar to itself' (attasadisassa) refers to being similar to itself in terms of having an object (sārammaṇa bhāvena). And 'in terms of having an object' (sārammaṇabhāvena) means that a phenomenon which does not occur without an object is called 'having an object' (sārammaṇa); thus, it is 'in terms of having an object.' As for 'because of the production of another phenomenon' (dhammantarassa uppādanaṭṭhena): even when the preceding thought (citta) has ceased, its momentum of cognitive activity (cintanakiriyāvego) does not subside; it subsides only after giving rise to the subsequent thought (pacchimaṃ cittaṃ). Thus, it is 'because of the production of the subsequent other phenomenon' (pacchimassa dhammantarassa uppādanaṭṭhena)." (Pāṭṭh-ud-dī. 473.)

                      • dhammantara→"another phenomenon" (often referring to a subsequent mental state)
                      • uppādanaṭṭha→"because of production" or "in the sense of giving rise to."

            • 4 definitions of akusala?

                • ārammaṇarasa is technically iṭṭha or aniṭṭha, the vipākacitta is either kusala- or akusala-vipāka and the vedanā can be dukkha (taking aniṭṭha), sukha (taking iṭṭha) or adukkhamasukha (taking slightly desirable or slightly undesirable ones)

              • What is pleasant feeling?
                • Pleasant feeling is the nature of experiencing/feeling the desirable (iṭṭha) taste of the object (ārammaṇarasa).
              • What is equanimous feeling?
                • Equanimous/Neutral feeling is the nature of experiencing/feeling the neutral (majjhatta) taste of the object.
              • What is wrong view?
                • A wrong view (diṭṭhi / micchādiṭṭhi / diṭṭhigata) is a belief that is not in accordance with the real nature of the object such as the belief that there is no result of good and bad actions. The heaviest wrong views are Ahetukadiṭṭhi (causeless view), Akiriyadiṭṭhi (the view of non-action) and Natthidiṭṭhi (nihilism view).
              • What is meant by unprompted consciousness?
                • An unprompted consciousness is one that arises naturally without any encouragement or hesitation.
              • What is meant by prompted consciousness?
                • Those consciousnesses that do arise but with hesitation after having been encouraged or prompted are referred to as prompted.

            • Lesson 8 - Two anger rooted consciousness: dosamūlacitta - Assignment
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • 1. What is hatred?
                • That which opposes, resists, dislikes, fears or hates the object is dosa (hatred). Hatred is just one general rendering of the word dosa. Dosa is the first unwholesome root to be completely eradicated from the mental continuum. This eradication takes place at the moment of the third Noble Path (anāgāmimagga). The kammaṭṭhāna most indicated for the weakening of dosa from the side of samatha is mettābhāvana.
              • 2. How many feelings does the hate rooted consciousness consist of?
                • The feeling associated with all dosamūlacittas is unpleasant feeling (domanassa vedanā) which experiences the unpleasant flavor of the object (ārammaṇarasa).
              • 3. What is sorrow?
                • Soka (sorrow) is not dosa cetasika but the domanassa vedanā associated with it in those occasions when one experiences a great loss such as the loss of someone as a mother, a father or a child, or a disaster as it is mentioned in mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta: "katamo ca, bhikkhave, soko? yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa soko socanā socitattaṃ antosoko antoparisoko, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, soko.
              • 4. What are the unwholesome courses of action that could result due to hate rooted consciousnesses?
                • Ten in number are the akusalakammapathas (unwholesome courses of action) and those which can be committed with a dosamūlacitta are as follows: pāṇātipāta (killing living beings), adinnādāna (stealing), musāvāda (lying), pisuṇavācā (slandering), pharusavācā (harsh speech), samphappalāpa (vain talk) and byāpāda (wishing others’ death). The remaining ones, namely kāmesumicchācāra (sexual misconduct), abhijjhā (covetousness) and micchādiṭṭhi (wrong view) are not associated with dosa but lobha.
              • 5. What is the consciousness that arises when expressing other’s faults?
                • Righteous criticism at the proper time can be done with an undefiled mind but most often in the world it is done with a dosamūlacitta.
              • 6. What is the consciousness that arises when feeling sorry?
                • In those situations when one has committed a mistake if one has wrong attention one will feel sorry. Such consciousness is a dosamūlacitta accompanied by kukkucca (remorse). Kukkucca may arise due to having done something perceived as bad (commission) or due to not having done something perceived as good (omission).
              • 7. In what type of people do many hate rooted consciousnesses arise during one day?
                • Those people who experience many hatred consciousness are those who often pay attention to others bad qualities. It may also be added according to Vsm.III.83 that those who's janakakamma, the main kamma that is producing the present life, was surrounded by dosamūlacittas at the time of accumulation may have as result a prominence of dosa. According to the Elder Upatissa in Vimuttimagga the hating temperament has its source in previous habit. Those who have recently emerged from several lives in apāya or niraya may also have such hating tendency due to all the dosamūlacittas that would habitually arise in such destinations.
                • Macchariya (stinginess) is the term used to refer to one of the three inconstant dhammas that arise occasionally accompanying dosa. It only occurs when taking one's own attained or yet-to-attain good fortune as object. The preception of "mine" towards the object is a condition for it to arise. Attachment is meant. Macchariya shrinks from sharing such good object with others. It hides it like a child might hide a new toy in order to prevent others from using it. It is regarded as mental disfigurement.
              • 8. What is the consciousness that can arise when giving something to get over the bother of someone who asks for something?

            • Lesson 9 - Two delusion rooted consciousnesses: mohamūlacitta - Assignment
              • by (Brazil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu 04/01/2023
              • 1. What is delusion?
                • Delusion is the dhamma which darkens the mind and is perplexed about the real nature of the objects. It vacillates on making a decision about the object due to superficiality.
              • 2. What is skeptical doubt?
                • The doubt that arises when pondering on subjects which are beyond ordinary thought is vicikicchā. Those subjects are 8: The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, the Sikkhā, previous lives, future lives, previous and future lives' continuity (kamma - vipāka) and causality (paṭiccasamuppāda).
              • 3. What is restlessness?
                • The agitation, shaking, wavering, unsteadiness of the mind that opposes tranquility is restlessness. It is present in every unwholesome mind to some extent and is prominent in the second mohamūlacitta.
              • 4. According to what is the delusion rooted consciousness divided?
                • Since the deluded minds are always equanimous and unprompted they are divided in two according to association with either skepticism or restlessness.
              • 5. Why do the delusion-rooted consciousnesses not have neither pleasant nor unpleasant feeling?
                • The equanimous feeling (upekkhā vedanā) is the only feeling associated with mohamūlacittas due to delusion concealing the nature of the object, vicikicchā being uncertain about it and uddhacca being restless and shaky. Therefore vedanā is unable to experience the object's flavor clearly.
              • 6. Why does the delusion rooted consciousness not become prompted or unprompted?
                • No encouragement affects such minds since doubt and restlessness are natures that only arise naturally in beings.
              • 7. How can skeptical doubt be removed?
                • {{4963064829445156::Faith }}is the counterpart of skepticism therefore developing it removes perplexity about the eight objects which lie beyond ordinary thought. Another means is by developing {{4963064829445156::the }}{{4963064829445156::understanding }}{{4963064829445156::about the differences between oneself and great beings like Buddhas.}}
              • 8. What are the reasons for the arising of skeptical doubt?
                • Skeptical doubt arises and increases by criticizing, pondering with wrong attention to, or listening to vain criticisms about those eight objects mentioned above.
              • 9. What is the weakest unwholesome consciousness?
                • Of all twelve unwholesome cittas eleven are capable of producing rebirth in hell except the deluded citta accompanied by restlessness which is the weakest of all and therefore incapable of taking the role of janaka kamma.
