            • Lesson 10 - The eighteen consciousnesses without roots - Questions
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • Are these consciousnesses said to be without roots because they arise automatically or is it because of some other reason?
                • The work hetu could mean cause or root. In this case it should be understood as root not cause, since these ahetuka cittas are without root, not without cause.
              • What are the dhammas which are referred to as roots?
                • The dhammas which are called roots are the three unwholesome ones: lobha, dosa and moha; and their wholesome counterparts alobha, adosa and amoha.
              • What are resultant consciousnesses? Give the definition.
                • vipākacittas are those that
                  • arise as a result of past ku / aku kamma due to kammasatti
              • Based on what the consciousnesses without roots have been named?
                • They have been named firstly according to {{25989850152880445::vatthu (base) (eye, ear, nose, tongue and body)}} and since there are various consciousnesses that arise based on the heart-base they have been named according to {{25989850152880445::kicca (function) (receiving, investigating, five-door adverting, mind-door adverting / deciding and smile producing).}}
              • Do unwholesome consciousnesses produce results with roots as well?
                • All unwholesome consciousness are relatively weak due to restlessness and even though they have unwholesome roots their resultant consciousnesses do not accompany any roots and are therefore rootless. No being has unwholesome roots in their bhavaṅga citta.
              • What are the differences between unwholesome resultant consciousnesses and wholesome resultant consciousnesses?
                • The differences are:
                  • Object: unwholesome resultants experience unpleasant objects while wholesome resultant experience pleasant ones.
                  • Feeling: unwholesome resultants are accompanied by either equanimous feeling (eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, receiving- and investigating- consciousnesses) or painful feeling (body-consciousness) while wholesome ones are accompanied by equanimous feeling (eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, receiving- and investigating-consciousnesses) or pleasant feeling (body- and investigating-consciousnesses). The investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasant feeling occurs when a very pleasant object strikes the doors of the senses. In the case of pleasant and neutral objects it accompanies equanimous feeling.

            • Lesson 11 - The three functional consciousnesses without roots - Questions
              • by (Brazil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • What type of consciousnesses are referred to as functional consciousnesses?
                • All consciousnesses perform a function. Those that produce bad results are called akusala. Those that produce good results are kusala. The resultant consciousnesses are known as vipāka. The rest of the consciousnesses are called kiriyā. Kiriyā cittas neither produce results nor are results themselves.
              • Based on what the rootless functional consciousnesses have been named?
                • The 3 rootless functional ones have been named according to the door they advert to (five-doors or mind-door) and the last one was named because it produces a smile in those without defilements. There are other cittas which produce smile but this one only performs this function and has no roots.
              • What are the two types of smiles produced by the hasituppāda consciousness?
                • Sita and hasita. Sita is the name given to the smile that only slightly opens the eyes and is only appreciated by an onlooker if attention is paid to the face. Hasita on the other hand produces a more evident smile that shows the tip of the teeth. In both cases no sound is produced.
              • In whom does this (hasituppāda) consciousness arise?
                • This citta only uccurs to those free from cankers.
              • How many non-bright consciousnesses are there?
                • There are a total of 30. 12 akusalas and 18 rootless.
              • How many consciousnesses with pleasant feeling (somanassa) are there among the non-beautiful consciousnesses?
                • 1 kusalavipākas
                  • somanassasahagataṁ santīraṇacittaṁ
                • 1 ahetukakiriyā
                  • somanassasahagataṁ hasituppādacittaṁ
                • Altogether 2 cittas.
              • How many equanimous consciousnesses are there among the non-beautiful consciousnesses?
                • 6 akusala vipākas, the exception being the dukkhasahagataṁ kāyaviññāṇaṁ.
                • 6 kusalavipākas, except the sukhasahagataṁ kāyaviññāṇaṁ and somanassasahagataṁ santīraṇacittaṁ.
                • 2 ahetukakiriyās. The exception being the hasituppāda.
                • Altogether 14.
              • How many consciousnesses with unpleasant feeling are there among the non-beautiful consciousnesses?
                • There is only one which is accompanied by painful feeling. It is akusala vipāka: Dukkhasahagataṁ kāyaviññāṇaṁ.
              • How many unprompted consciousnesses are there among the non-beautiful consciousnesses?
                • Due to their weakness all 18 are considered to be unprompted.
              • How many prompted consciousnesses are there among the non-beautiful consciousnesses?
                • Not a single one since all are unprompted.

            • Lesson 12 - The eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sensuous sphere - Questions
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • What is wholesome consciousness?
                • It is a citta which has the capacity to produce good results in the future. It also associates the wholesome roots alobha, adosa and occasionally amoha. It tranquilizes the mental stream suppressing defilements. It also produces higher quality materiality which supports physical health.
              • According to what matters are the wholesome consciousnesses of the sensuous sphere divided.
                • They are divided according to feeling (somanassa or upekkhāsahagata), sampayoga (ñāṇasampayutta or ñāṇavipayutta) and according to saṅkhāra (asaṅkhārika or sasaṅkhārika).
              • What is the other name for the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere?
                • They are collectively called mahākusalacittas because they are the kusalacittas that arise most frequently in beings.
              • What are the factors that make wholesome consciousness stronger?
                • The greatness of a kusalacitta varies according to vedanā (somanassa being superior), saṅkhāra (asaṅkhārika being superior), cetanā (stronger cetanā being superior) and above all, the association with kammassakatañāṇa (ñāṇasampayutta).
              • How does the wholesome action of the sensuous sphere vary with volition?
                • The intensity of the volition affects the strength of the citta but they can also be divided according to which of the ten bases of merit volition is directed towards: dāna, sīla, bhāvanā, apacāyana, veyyāvacca, pattidāna, pattānumodanā, dhammassavaṇa, dhammadesanā and diṭṭhujukamma. When divided thus the mahākusalas amount to 80.
              • How is the strength of a wholesome action measured? Explain based on volition and knowledge.
                • Volition: the stronger the volition the stronger is the citta and the merit accumulated. A weaker volition arises when engaging in one of the ten bases of merit such as dāna with weak intent such as when giving little when one could give plenty. A strong volition arises when giving plenty.
                • Knowledge: knowledge meant here is the knowledge of kamma and its result. When engaging in meritorious acts such as undertaking sīla knowledge is not present if one does not know his act of undertaking precepts produces good future results. If done so with this understanding (right view) the merit is much superior. This is the most important factor in determining the strength of a wholesome deed.

            • jhānaṅgas
              • vicāra investigates {{8141122930131199::shallow}} characteristics of the object, while wisdom investigates {{8141122930131199::deep}} characteristics.
              • ekaggata: eko aggo
              • 5 jhānaṅgas + 1
                • vitakka (applied thought)
                • vicāra (sustained thought)
                • pīti (joy)
                • sukha (happiness)
                • ekaggata (one-pointedness): the main factor
                • (+paññā): about the disadvantages of sense objects)
              • the functions of each jhānaṅga
                • vitakka: directs the mind to the object, mounts it, ascends it, strikes it
                • vicāra: rubs, holds, sustains the object, investigates shallow characteristics (while wisdom investigates deep ones)
                • pīti: blossoms, refreshes the mind, likes the object
                • sukha: produces enjoyment, ease, comfort, pleasure
                • ekaggata: concentrates solely on one aspect of the object without distraction for a long period of time
              • 5 jhānaṅgas and opposing factors
                • vitakka ⇒ thinamiddha
                • vicāra ⇒ vicikicchā (about the path towards jhāna, about the object)
                • pīti ⇒ byāpāda (arati, boredom, dislike towards meditation)
                • sukha ⇒ uddhaccakukkucca
                • ekaggata ⇒ kāmacchanda
              • 3 types of samādhi according to the presence of vitakka and vicāra
                • savitakkasavicārasamādhi (11 1st jhāna cittas)
                • avitakkavicāramattasamādhi (11 2nd jhāna cittas [in the fivefold method])
                • avitakkāvicārasamādhi (45 cittas: 3rd, 4th and 5th jhāna cittas [in the fivefold method]; 2nd, 3rd and 4th jhānas [in the fourfold method])
              • 5 jhānas and their jhānaṅgas
                • paṭhamajjhāna: vitakka, vicāra, pīti, sukha, ekaggata
                • dutiyajjhāna: vicāra, pīti, sukha, ekaggata
                • tatiyajjhāna: pīti, sukha, ekaggata
                • catutthajjhāna: sukha, ekaggata
                • pañcamajjhāna: upekkhā, ekaggata
            • nīvaraṇas
              • 5 / 6 nīvaraṇas (hindrances)
                • kāmachanda (sense desire)
                  • gross for sex
                  • subtler for other sense objects
                • byāpāda (aversion)
                • thīnamiddha (sloth and torpor)
                • uddhaccakukkucca (restlessness and remorse)
                • vicikicchā (doubt)
                • (+avijjā): about sense objects not being a hindrance
                  • avijjā as a hindrance appers in paṭhamatajjhānasutta. Jhāna wisdom suppresses this avijjā
              • 2 types of hindrances according to what they hinder

            • Lesson 15 - arūpāvacaracittas - Questions
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • How can cittas exist without a corporeal body?
                • In pañcavokārabhāva citta depends on a material base but the cittas that have been developed by distancing it from rūpa and rūpanimitta can occur without a material base and can produce results which do not depend on a material base.
                  • can kāmāvacaracittas arise in arūpabhūmi? if so, how can they arise without a material base? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • Why does the life with no corporeal body become good?
                • From the perspective affected by sense craving the immaterial life may seem unpleasant but for those who have put aside sense craving and developed disenchantment towards rūpa their immaterial life and the immaterial jhānas are seen as good, peaceful and pleasant. It is noteworthy that even though the immaterial existences are pleasant and peaceful they are considered as bad destinations by the Buddha since they do not provide the conditions to listen and practice the Dhamma.
              • Why do arahats who have no future birth develop immaterial absorptions?
                • They may have them as maggasiddhajhānas or they may develop them in order to dwell in these immaterial absorptions, attain nirodha samāpatti and use mundane psychic powers.
              • How many mundane cittas are there? What are they?
                • There are 81 lokiyacittas: 12 akusalas, 18 ahetukas, 24 kāmasobhanas, 15 rūpāvacaras and 12 arūpāvacaras.
              • How many mundane results are there? what are they?
                • There are 32 lokiya vipākas: 15 ahetukas, 8 kāmasobhanas, 5 rūpāvacaras, 4 arūpāvacaras. This is said according to the lokiyas. If lokuttaras are added they amount to 36 or 52.
              • How many functional cittas are there? what are they?
                • There are 20 kiriyās: 3 ahetukakiriyās, 8 kāmasobhanas, 5 rūpāvacaras and 4 arūpāvacaras.
              • Why can't higher jhānas be achieved before the lower ones? why can't the arūpas be achieved before the rūpas?
                • each jhānaṅga is necessary for suppressing the hindrances so one cannot attain a higher jhāna without having attained the first one
                • if two factors can be removed at a single time, making them 4 jhānas, can more be removed? #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • why can't one remove the kasiṇa after the first jhāna and develop the first arūpa? #q🙋🏼‍♂

            • Lesson 16 - Questions
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • What is the supramundane path?
                • The lokuttaramagga is the collection of 8 well developed mental factors of the Fourth Noble Truth (sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati and sammāsamādhi).
              • What is the supramundane citta?
                • Lokuttaracitta is the consciousness that associates the lokuttaramagga and phala. It takes Nibbāna as object.
              • What is the other name for the lokuttara vipākacitta?
                • Instead of the term vipāka what is most used to refer to the resultant supramundane mind is phala (fruit / fruition).
              • How many cittas are there in total?
                • 89 according to the brief method and 121 according to the detailed one.
              • How many sobhanas and asobhanacittas are there?
                • There are 59 / 91 sobhanas: 24 kāmāvacaras, 15 rūpāvacaras, 12 arūpāvacaras and 8/40 lokuttaras.
              • Classify the 89 cittas based on their jāti (nature: kusala, akusala, vipāka and kiriyā)
                • akusalas (12): 8 lobhamūlacittas, 2 dosamūlacittas and 2 mohamūlacittas
                • kusalas (21): 8 kāmāvacaras, 5 rūpāvacaras, 4 arūpāvacaras and 4 lokuttaras
                • vipākas (36): 7 akusalas, 8 kusalas, 8 kāmāvacaras, 5 rūpāvacaras, 4 arūpāvacaras and 4 lokuttaras
                • kiriyās (20): 3 ahetukakiriyās, 8 kāmāvacaras, 5 rūpāvacaras and 4 arūpāvacaras
          • lokuttaracittas in the detailed method

            • For the meditator who does not possess lokiyajjhānas (mahaggatacittas) (suddhavipassakayānika) the magga and phala is {{8435609168546361::of the 1st jhāna}}. For those who possess jhānas (samathayānika) their magga and phala may be any {{8435609168546361::of the 5 jhānas depending on their practice}}.

              • pādakajjhāna (foundational jhāna): the jhāna used as a basis for abhiññās or before the vipassanā practice
              • sammasitajjhāna (the jhāna meditated on): the jhāna that is used as an object
              • ajjhāyasa (inclination): it will depend on the inclination of the meditator

            • Lesson 17 - lokuttaracittas in the detailed method - Questions
              • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
              • How does it become forty supramundane cittas?
                • The original 8 lokuttaracittas become 40 when divided according to the 5 jhānas.
              • What absorption will be contained in the lokuttaracitta of those who have not attained absorptions of the rūpāvacara?
                • It will certainly be of the 1st jhāna.
              • How many lokuttaracittas of the 1st jhāna and the like are there?
                • There are 8 lokuttaracittas with each jhāna.
              • How many cittas such as those of the 1st jhāna are there among the 121?
                • There are 11 1st jhāna cittas: 3 rūpāvacaras and 8 lokuttaras
                • Likewise for the second, third and fourth jhānas.
                • There are 23 5th jhānacittas: 3 rūpāvacaras, 12 arūpāvacaras and 8 lokuttaras.
              • How many kusalacittas are there according to the brief and detailed methods?
                • There are 21 or 37 kusalacittas: 8 kāmāvacaras, 5 rūpāvacaras, 4 arūpāvacaras and 4 or 20 lokuttaras.
              • How many resultants cittas are there?
                • There are 36 or 52 vipākacittas: 7 akusalas, 8 kusalas, 8 kāmāvacaras, 5 rūpāvacaras, 4 arūpāvacaras and 4 or 20 lokuttaras.
              • How many glad minded cittas are there?
                • There are 63 glad minded cittas: 4 lobhamūlas, 1 kāyaviññāṇa, 1 santīraṇa, 1 hasituppāda, 12 kāmāvacaras, 12 rūpāvacaras and 32 lokuttaras.
              • How many equanimous cittas are there?
                • There are 55: 4 lobhamūlas, 2 mohamūlas, 6 akusalavipākas, 6 kusalavipākas, 2 ahetukakiriyās, 12 kāmāvacaras, 3 rūpāvacaras, 12 arūpāvacaras and 8 lokuttaras.

          • saṁsaṭṭha ‒ what it is and an example
            • citta and cetasikas are different realities but appear as a single reality throughout their existence
            • example: phassa and citta are different realities but appear as a single reality or as 2 aspects of the same reality
            • note:
              • not essential to separate them for liberation
              • only applicable to nāmas
              • ekībhāvupagamana: does not mean they are the same; two properties of the same thing
              • vocab:
                • ekībhāva [eka + bhāva] 1↔masc. unity; harmony; lit. one state; 2 masc. solitude; being along; lit. one state
          • visaṁsaṭṭha means
            • nāmas and rūpas are different realities and do not appear as one
              • essential to separate them for liberation
            • nāma and Nibbāna are so
            • rupa and Nibbāna are never suspected to be saṁsaṭṭha
            • doubt can only occur on nāma with regard to other nāmas, rūpa or Nibbāna
          • saṃsaṭṭha √saj (pp.)↔(+instr) mixed (with); combined (with); (+instr) closely associated (with); stuck to; clinging to; joined; connected; originated together; lit. mixed together. Nāmas + nāmas: are different realities but appear as one
          • what aññāsamānacetasikas are↔cetasikas that are ethically variable (13)
          • sobhanacetasikas are divided into 4 groups: {{9810207040576713::sobhanasādhāraṇa (19), virati (3), appamaññā (2) and paññindriya}}
          • 52 cetasikas and English definition
            • Phassa (contact)↔"phusatīti phasso" The nature of impacting with the object
            • Vedanā (feeling)↔The nature of experiencing the good, bad or neutral quality (known as the taste or flavor) of the object.
            • Saññā (perception)↔The nature which becomes sensitive to the uniqueness of an object.
            • Cetanā (volition)→cetayatīti cetanā / cetetīti cetanā (it exerts) The effort involved in seeing - hearing - eating - drinking - going - coming - giving
            • Ekaggatā (one-pointedness)↔The nature of fixing the mind on an object in an unshakable manner
            • Jīvitindriya (life-faculty)↔The power of life, that is to say the strength to live of the consciousnesses and mental factors. life force
            • Manasikāra (attention)↔The dhamma that repeatedly directs the consciousness towards an object without allowing it to go away.
            • Vitakka (initial application)↔The nature of going towards and climbing onto the object
            • Vicāra (sustained application)↔The nature of caressing the already arrived object
            • Adhimokkha (determination/decision)↔The nature of judging the object
            • Viriya (energy)↔The nature of not retreating and going forward until the completion of an activity
            • Pīti (zest / rapture)↔The nature of happiness of mind – blooming like a flower
            • Chanda (desire)↔The willingness, desire to do various things
            • Moha (delusion)↔The nature of concealing the actual status of the object
            • Ahirika (moral shamelessness)↔The nature of not detesting / not being ashamed of / not shrinking away from unwholesomeness
            • Anottappa (moral fearlessness)↔The nature of not being afraid of unwholesomeness
            • Uddhacca (restlessness)↔Restlessness of the mind and the nature of not properly establishing on the object
            • Lobha (greed)↔Considering the object to be something good and attaching to it
            • Diṭṭhi (wrong view)↔The nature of seeing incorrectly and the nature of taking objects incorrectly
            • Māna (Conceit)↔The nature of assessing oneself as “I am a great person” and the like
            • Dosa (hatred)↔The opposition to the object
            • Issā (envy / jealousy)―The opposition to the happiness and prosperity of others
            • Macchariya (avarice)↔The nature of not being able to bear up someone else acquiring what belongs to one’s own self, someone else gaining benefit from what one owns, another acquiring a prospaerity similar to one’s own and concealing one’s own prosperity
            • Kukkucca (worry / regret)↔The nature of worrying about unwholesome action performed and wholesome action not performed
            • Thīna Middha (sloth and torpor)↔The weakness of the mind/consciousness, lack of the power of consciousness and laziness of the mind and the weakness and laziness of mental factors.
            • Vicikicchā (Skeptical doubt)↔Doubt and lack of confidence about the object
            • Saddhā (faith)↔The belief in the Buddha and the like and the nature of accepting the virtues of the Buddha and the like
            • Sati (mindfulness)―mindfulness
            • Hiri Ottappa (moral shame and moral dread)↔The nature of detesting and being ashamed of unwholesome action and the nature of being afraid of unwholesomeness
            • Alobha (non-greed)―The nature of non-attachment to an object
            • Adosa (non-hatred)←non-hatred
            • Tatramajjhattatā (neutrality of mind)↔The nature of maintaining the balance of mentalities in a [beautiful] mental cluster
            • Kāyapassaddhi and cittapassaddhi↔The tranquility of mental factors and the tranquility of consciousness
            • Kāyalahutā and cittalahutā↔The lightness of mental factors and the lightness of consciousness
            • Kāyamudutā and cittamudutā↔The softness of mental factors and the softness of consciousness
            • Kāyakammaññatā and cittakammaññatā↔The wieldiness of mental factors and the wieldiness of consciousness
            • Kāyapāguññatā and cittapāguññatā↔The proficiency of mental factors in various wholesome activities and the proficiency of consciousness
            • Kayujjukatā and cittujjukatā↔The uprightness of mental factors and the uprightness of consciousness
            • Sammāvācā―The nature of abstaining from the four verbal unwholesome actions of lying, slandering, harsh speech and vain talk
            • Sammākammanta↔The nature of abstaining from the three bodily unwholesome actions of killing living beings, stealing and sexual misconduct
            • Sammā-ājīva↔The nature of abstaining from bodily and verbal bad behavior done for the sake of livelihood
            • Karuṇā (compassion)↔The nature of dislike of suffering of others and the willingness to release others from suffering
            • Muditā (appreciative joy)―The nature of feeling happy about the success of others
            • Paññindriya (Wisdom faculty)↔The nature of seeing objects in a clearer and deeper manner than knowing with mind

          • Lesson 2.1 Fifty-two mental factors - Questions
            • 2. What is the meaning of sampayoga?
              • Sampayoga refers to the association of immaterial dhammas in such a way that they cannot be separated with the 4 characteristic mentioned above. In arūpabhūmi the last characteristic does not apply.
            • 3. Why do all the mental factors not arise in a single consciousness?
              • Some mental factors are counterparts of each other being incompatible within one cittuppāda. Depending on the function that has to be performed by the mind more or less cetasikas will be required.
            • 4. Do mental factors exist after the extinction of the consciousness?
              • They arise together with consciousness and perish together with it.
            • 5. Can the mental factors go into extinction prior to the consciousness?
              • No, they all vanish together (ekanirodha)
            • 6. How many mental factors are there?
              • There are 52 cetasikas.
            • 7. What are the three main groups of mental factors?
              • They are aññasamāna cetasikas (13), akusalacetasikas (14) and sobhanacetasikas (25)
        • sabbacittasādhāraṇa cetasikas
          • Phassa (contact)
            • Why is phassa essential in every cittuppāda?→because the mind can only see what it touches or what touches it. This contact is essential for cognition.
          • vedanā
            • as jhāna factor (sukha [somanassa])
              • upabrūhana↔nt. increase, augmentation
            • why vedanā is given as characteristic vedayita (being felt)? it sounds like vedanā feels itself or that something else feels vedanā #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • Saññā (perception)
            • the word sañjānana covers both the aspects of {{39849438319791286::recognition and identification}}. Therefore the rendering "recognition" does not fully cover the meaning of saññā.
            • 3 functions #tbc🕵
              • identify
              • punasañjānana nimittakaraṇaṁ (recognizing again the signs)
              • paccābhiññāṇa (recognizing again)
          • Cetanā (volition)
            • Like the general of an army
            • 3 functions:
              • āyūhana (gathering (?), accumulating) #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • saṁvidahanaṃ (organizing, arranging, giving orders)
              • ussahana (putting effort)
              • mem aid: like a general who gathers, organizes the army and puts effort towards a goal
            • In the act of {{41020632322533057::cognition}} citta is foremost, in the act of {{41020632322533057::performing actions}} cetanā is foremost.
          • ekaggatā
            • ekaggatā and uddhacca are opposed realities but occur together
              • cittas that oppose each other but occur together #editing
                • ekaggatā and uddhacca
                  • what vikkhepa and avikkhepa are
                    • vikkhepa: uddhacca and vicikicchā
                    • avikkhepa: kusalekaggatā (kiriya as well?) #q🙋🏼‍♂
                    • they oppose each other and cannot arise together
                  • 2 aspects of ekaggatā
                    • kusalekaggatā:mentality required for the mind stream to be on one object for a long time
                    • mentality that is required to focus on one facet of the object
                      • essential in any citta
                      • with uddhacca is like riding on horse back; one can stay on the back of the horse but shaking
                • ekaggatā and vicikicchā
            • What one pointedness does is to {{22210399708704376::establish the mind in one aspect of the object}}
            • as a jhāna factor
              • ekaggatā: that which holds the mind on a single object without allowing it to wander among diverse objects; it is the most prominent jhāna factor
              • ekaggatā establishes the mind and its associated mental factors evenly (samaṃ) (connected to the balancing of faculties) and properly (sammā) on the meditation object (placing the mind on the object, distancing it from opposing defilements
              • With the strength of ekaggatā, the mind can remain focused on the meditation object without scattering among various objects
            • why is ekaggatā essential for cognition?→As objects have many aspects the mind cannot take in an object without focusing on one of those aspects which is done by ekaggatā
              • since this point (of it taking an aspect of the object) is not the principal explanation of ekaggatā, what would be the reason why it is essential for congnition? cognition requires a certain degree of stability on the object? #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • citta focuses on {{21669808535790547::one object }}while ekaggatā focuses on {{21669808535790547::one aspect of the object}}
            • ekārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ samaṃ sammā ca ādhānaṃ ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hoti (vsdm) the even and right placement / fixation of the mind and mental factors in one object
          • Jīvitindriya (life-faculty)
            • that which helps / protects / supports the generation of consciousnesses
            • āyusaṅkhāra
              • 2 types of phalasamāpatti #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • normal
                • with special vipassanā before it (jīvitasaṅkhāratappanaphalasamāpatti) #tbc🕵
          • Manasikāra (attention)
            • At every moment citta breaks up and goes away from the object. It is said that the generation of consciousnesses which breaks up and goes away from the object at every moment from re-birth (conception) re-establishes in the object because of this mental factor.
          • extra information:
            • 2 types of adhikaraṇa #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • samānādhikaraṇa
              • bhinnādhikaraṇa
          • class

        • pakiṇṇaka cetasikas
          • vitakka
            • that which brings consciousness and mental factors to the object
            • directs the mind and associated cetasikas towards an object, approaches it (ānayana) and ascends it (abhiniropaṇa), allowing it to remain on the object
          • vicāra
            • repeatedly “rubs” the object mentally (parimajjana), the object becomes vivid to the cittuppāda as the sun at noon. The mind becomes well-established on the object, and the connection between the mind and the object remains intact (anubandhana)
            • vicāra ties the mind to the object
            • vitakka and vicāra are collectively called→payogasampatti
          • Adhimokkha (determination/decision)
          • Viriya (energy)
            • There are two forms of energy
              • physical energy: The strength of the body. It is not a mental factor (related to vāyodhātu and paṭhavī dhātu)
              • mental energy: cetasika
          • pīti
            • pīti also pervades pleasant mind-born matter throughout the body, generating tranquility (passaddhi). Tranquility then leads to bliss (sukha). At this point, anger subsides, and the mind remains well-composed on the meditation object
            • when meditation succeeds with the proper functioning of vitakka and vicāra (payoga sampatti), the mind begins to delight in the meditation object (pīti).
          • Chanda (desire)
        • akusala cetasikas
          • Moha (delusion)
          • Ahirika (moral shamelessness)
          • Anottappa (moral fearlessness)
          • Uddhacca (restlessness)
            • opposed to ekaggatā
            • explained in two ways
              • an outcome of unwholesomeness (due to the burning of unwholesome states restlessness arise)
              • a support for unwholesomeness (akusaladhammas arise because of restlessness)
          • Lobha (greed)
          • Diṭṭhi (wrong view)
            • (table) diṭṭhis according to what they obstruct (āvaraṇa) #Table90
              • sagga
                • magga
                • type of diṭṭhi
              • X
                • X
                • niyatāmicchādiṭṭhi
              • X
                • V
                • does not exist
              • OK
                • X
                • antaggāhikadiṭṭhi
              • OK
                • OK
                • sakkāyadiṭṭhi
          • Māna (Conceit)
            • diṭṭhi have ideas about the self, māna compares it. Both have self as object.
            • 3/9 types of māna
              • seyyamāna / atimāna (obs: the "best" of the three since it may lead to shame and wholesomeness)
                • seyya seyyamāna
                • seyya sadisamāna
                • seyya hīnamāna
              • sadisamāna / māna
                • sadisa seyyamāna
                • sadisa sadisamāna
                • sadisa hīnamāṇa
              • hīnamāna / omāna / avamāna
                • hīna seyyamāna
                • hīna sadisamāna
                • hīna hīnamāna
            • kusalataṇhā: the type of craving that leads to good things
            • kusalamāna: the pride that leads to good things
            • taṇhaṁ nissāya taṇhaṁ pajānāti, mānaṁ nissāya mānaṁ pajānāti
            • not all comparison is unwholesome. samānattatā is related to it.
          • dosa
            • as a hindrance
              • dislikes the object (strikes against it) and cannot remain on it
              • The nature of the mind is to avoid disliked objects.
              • when arati (a mode of vyāpāda) arises, the mind tends to reject every object and falls into a joyless mood. At such times, the mind resists focusing on a single object
              • opposed by pīti
          • Issā (envy / jealousy)
            • issā and macchariya are considered very low cetasikas and are said to be destroyed in the first path
            • 2 types of parihāni #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • pattaparihāni
              • appattaparihāni
          • Macchariya (avarice)
            • (dhammasaṅgaṇī) 5 types of macchariya
              • 1. Āvāsa macchariya (avarice related to residence)
              • 2. Kula macchariya (avarice related to devotees)
              • 3. Lābha macchariya (avarice related to gain)
              • 4. Vaṇṇa macchariya (avarice related to beauty)
              • 5. Dhamma macchariya (avarice related to what has been learned)
                • gurumuṭṭhi↔the stinginess of some teachers about what they know
                • if one feels the student is going to harm himself or others one can decide not to teach something
            • dhammamacchariya
            • kadariyatā↔high level of macchariya that even prevents others from giving because they dislike others getting something
              • "Kadariyo pāpasaṅkappo, micchādiṭṭhi anādaro; dadamānaṃ nivāreti, yācamānāna bhojananti."
            • Ariyas never have macchariya towards their attainments
          • Kukkucca (worry / regret)
            • not so mean, destroyed by anāgāmiphala
            • 2 types
              • wrong things we have done (comissions)
              • good things we have not done (omissions)
            • ekanta atītārammaṇa (Ledi Sayadaw's opinion): kukkucca always take a past object
            • types of kukkucca #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • yāthāvakukkucca
              • ayāthāvakukkucca
              • yāvatāvakukkucca
              • yāthāva: adj. perfectly true; real; definite; certain [yathā + vant + a]
              • • ayāthāvamāna: masc. unfounded conceit; overestimation ✗
              • • ayāthāva: adj. false; wrong; incorrect ✗
          • thīna and middha
            • makes the mind inactive and unsuitable for meditation (akammañña)
            • neither reaches nor ascends the meditation object, appearing as though it is sinking or submerging. When thīna-middha becomes strong, the flow of consciousness may even lapse into sleep.
            • Contrasted with vitakka, which approaches and ascends the object
          • vicikicchā
            • as a hindrance
              • doubt about their meditation methods. They may question, “Is this the correct way to attain jhāna by contemplating the kasiṇa nimitta as ‘earth, earth (paṭhavi, paṭhavi)’? Or is there another way?”.18
              • contrasted with vicāra, which investigates the object making it vivid
        • sobhana cetasikas
          • why they are sādhāraṇa:
            • difficult to answer
            • strong cittas (J) are either on the good or bad side, and for them to be good, they need those 19 cetasikas to keep them from going to the bad side
            • ahetukas are not in the strong position (exc. hasituppāda which is a byproduct of other good cittas)
          • 1.Saddhā – faith
            • saddahati↔accepts
            • saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṁ
            • it makes the mind pure / clear by subduing the defilements (like the water-clearing gem💎)
            • What is the saddhā that arises in ordinary beings when making some meritorious deed?→it is what purifies the mind by subduing defilements
            • saddhā occurs in the beginning of sobhanacetasikas because it is the most important as a condition for the others to arise
          • 2. Sati – mindfulness
            • This mental factor prevents the mind from falling into the unwholesome side and establishes it in the wholesome side
            • recalling the past in term of vipassanā contemplation
          • 3. Hiri – moral shame
          • 4. Ottappa – moral fear / moral dread
            • fear in the sense of {{6942370534288498::knowing the danger and avoiding it}}
          • 5. Alobha – non-greed
          • 6. Adosa – non-hatred
          • 7. Tatramajjhattatā – neutrality of mind
          • 8. Kayapassaddhi – tranquility of the (mental) body
            • 4 perspectives to apply to each of the 6 pairs of cetasikas starting with passaddhi
              • characteristic
              • opposing factor
              • how is the mind affected when it is weak?
              • how is the mind affected when it is strong?
            • characteristic: tranquility of the mind, appeases the mind
            • opposed to→uddhacca
          • 9. Cittapassaddhi – tranquility of consciousness
          • 10. Kayalahutā – lightness of the (mental) body
            • characteristic: lightness of the mind
            • opposed to→thīnamiddha
          • 11. Cittalahutā - lightness of consciousness
          • 12. Kāyamudutā – malleability of the (mental) body
            • characteristic: malleability, flexibility
            • opposed to:>diṭṭhi and māna
          • 13. Cittamudutā – malleability of consciousness
          • 14. Kāyakammaññatā – wieldiness of the (mental) body
            • ready for anything
            • opposed to→nīvaraṇas
          • 15. Cittakammaññatā – wieldiness of consciousness
          • 16. Kāyapāguññatā – proficiency of the (mental) body
            • opposed to:>vicikicchā
            • weak: like being in water without knowing how to swim
            • strong: can practice for a long time
          • 17. Cittapāguññatā – proficiency of consciousness
          • 18. Kāyujjukatā – rectitude (uprightness) of the (mental body)
            • opposed to→māyā (concealing faults), sāṭheyya (showing non existing qualities) and 4 akusala sādhāraṇa
            • ujumagga (straight path) / vaṅka (crooked)
          • 19. Cittujjukatā – rectitude (uprightness) of consciousness
        • sobhana asādhāraṇa cetasikas
          • sobhana asādhāraṇa cetasikas amount to {{7529464713547585::6}} and are divided into: {{7529464713547585::3 virati, 2 appamaññā and 1 paññindriya }}

                  • does it also arise when abstaining from breaking the laws ⚖? #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • in the case of monks there are other various wrong means of livelihood

            • karuṇā
              • "para hiṁsa kampati"
            • muditā
          • Paññindriya
    • part II
      • sampayoganaya (methods of association) #edited
        • 19 sampayoganaya
          • aññasamānacetasikas
            • sabbacittasādhāraṇa (1 sampayoga)
              • arises in 89 cittas
            • pakiṇṇaka (6 sampayogas)
              • vitakka
                • arises in 55 cittas (54 kāmāvacara - 10 viññāṇa + 11 1st jhānas)
                • does not arise in 66 cittas
                • note:
                  • why there is no vitakka in dvipañcaviññāṇa and jhānas above the 1st?
                    • dvipañcaviññāṇa:
                      • the objects have already reached the location where these consciousnesses arise (?), therefore there is no necessity of vitakka to mount the object;
                      • because these consciousnesses are redimentary and do not require the presence of more complex cetasikas to perform their functions
                    • higher jhānas: because they have been developed by meditation in a manner that it is possible to remain with the object without vitakka
              • vicāra
                • arises in 66 cittas (55 savitakka + 11 2nd jhānas)
                • does not arise in 55 cittas
              • adhimokkha
                • arises in 78 cittas (89 - 10 viññāṇa - 1 vicikicchāsampayutta)
                • does not arise in 11 cittas
              • vīriya
                • arises in 73 cittas (89 - first 16 ahetukas (weaker cittas))
                • does not arise in 16 cittas
              • pīti
                • arises in 51 cittas (62 somanassa - 11 4th jhānas)
                • does not arise in 70 cittas
                • note:
                  • why pīti does not occur in sukhasahagata kāyaviññāṇa?→because of its weakness
              • chanda
                • arises in 69 cittas (89 - 18 ahetuka - 2 mohamūla)
                • does not arise in 20 cittas (weak)
                • note:
                  • why does chanda not arise in ahetuka and mohamūlacittas?→because ahetukas and mohamūlas are devoid of the willingness to perform actions
              • chasaṭṭhi pañcapaññāsa, ekādasa ca soḷasa. sattati vīsati ceva, pakiṇṇakavivajjitā. 66 55, 11 16, 70 and 20 indeed, are free from the occasionals
              • pañcapaññāsa chasaṭṭhi(a)ṭṭhasattati tisattati; ekapaññāsa cekūnasattati sapakiṇṇakā 55 66 72 73, 51 and 69 with occasionals
          • akusalacetasikas (8 sampayogas)
            • akusalasādhāraṇas (moha, ahirika, anottappa, uddhacca)
              • arise in all 12 akusalacittas
              • do not arise in 77 cittas
              • note:
                • why do the akusalasādhāraṇas arise in all akusalacittas?→because it requires the presence of delusion (moha) which conceals the consequences of akusala, ahirika which has no moral shame, anotappa which has no moral dread and uddhacca which shakes
                • akusalacittas will not arise if one has:
                  • amoha which sees the faults of unwholesomeness
                  • hiri which detests unwholesomeness
                  • ottappa which dreads unwholesomeness
                  • ekaggatā which is well-established and concentrated in wholesome deeds
                  • moha ⇔ amoha ahirika ⇔ hiri anottappa ⇔ ottappa uddhacca ⇔ ekaggatā (or maybe passaddhi?) #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • lobha
              • arises in 8 lobhamūlacittas
            • diṭṭhi
              • arises in 4 diṭṭhigatasampayutta
            • māna
              • arises in 4 diṭṭhigatavippayutta (sometimes)
              • note:
                • why does diṭṭhi and māna not occur together?→because they have incompatible functions with regard to the idea of a self; diṭṭhi makes considerations about the self as permanent, created by god and so on while māna compares it
            • dosa
              • arises in 2 dosamūla
            • issā, macchariya, kukkucca
              • arise in 2 dosamūla (sometimes, separately)
              • note:
                • macchariya arises because of greed about one’s own property; yet, as it arises as the inability to bear up one’s own wealth being used by another, it occurs with hatred and not greed
            • thīna, middha
              • arise in 5 akusala sasaṅkhārikas (sometimes, together)
            • vicikicchā
              • arises in 1 vicikicchāsampayutta
            • "sabbāpuññesu cattāro, lobhamūle tayo gatā, dosamūlesu cattāro, sasaṅkhāre dvayaṃ tathā vicikicchā vicikicchā-citte cāti catuddasa, dvādasākulesveva, sampayujjanti pañcadhā" (in all akusalas four, in greed-rooted 3, in hatred-rooted 4, in prompted 2, and doubt in doubtful mind, 14 in twelve akusalas associated in five ways)
          • sobhanacetasikas (4 sampayoga)
            • sobhanasādhāraṇas (saddhā, sati...)
              • arise in all 59 sobhanacittas
              • do not arise in 30 cittas
            • virati (sammāvācā, sammākammanta, sammāājīva)
              • arise in 16 cittas (8 mahākusala: sometimes, separately; 8 lokuttara: always, together)
              • do not arise in 73 cittas
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
              • note:
                • kāmāvacara kusalas can produce vipākas which differ in terms of cetasikas (such as ñāṇavipayuttakusalacitta which may produce ñāṇavipayuttavipākacitta); but mahaggata- and lokuttara-kusalas always produce a mirror image with the same cetasikas
                • viratis do not occur in wholesome consciousnesses which cause alms giving, veneration, delivery of Dhamma, listening to Dhamma and the like. They occur only on occasions in which one {{763627598504282::refrains from unwholesome actions and undertakes morality;}}{{763627598504282:: }} moreover, refraining from all four verbal actions does not happen at the same time; when refraining from lying with the mental factor of right speech (sammāvācā), there is no abstinence from vain talk and the like
                • why do viratis not arise in mahaggata cittas?→because such consciousnesses do not arise as refraining from improper behavior
                • why do all viratis occur simultaneously in lokuttara maggas and phalas? #q🙋🏼‍♂
                  • because they cause the removal of the possibilities of wrong-doing by helping pañña destroy defilements; in phalacitta, viratis arise as a result of the cetanā of the maggacitta and perform the function of appeasing the mind stream (paṭipassaddhi pahāna)
            • appamaññā
              • arise in 28 cittas (8 mahākusalas + 8 mahākiriyā + 12 lokiya sukhasahagatajhānas (sometimes, separately))
              • do not arise in 61 cittas
            • paññindriya
              • arises in 47 ñāṇasampayutta cittas (12 ñāṇasampayutta kāmasobhanas + 35 appanā)
              • does not arise in 42 cittas
        • there are altogether {{20797901776983707::19}} sampayoganayas, {{20797901776983707::1}} for sabbacittasādhāraṇas, {{20797901776983707::6}} for pakiṇṇakas, {{20797901776983707::8}} for akusalacetasikas and {{20797901776983707::4}} for sobhanacetasikas

        • niyatayogī↔cetasikas that arise always ‘fixed adjuncts’

              • somanassasahagataṁ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṁ sasaṅkhārikaṁ cittaṁ: 7 + 6 + 4 + lobha + māna (sometimes) + thīnamiddha (sometimes, together) = 18/19/20/21
              • upekkhāsahagataṁ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṁ asaṅkhārikaṁ cittaṁ: 7 + 5 (no pīti) + 4 + lobha + diṭṭhi = 18
              • upekkhāsahagataṁ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṁ sasaṅkhārikaṁ cittaṁ: 7 + 5 (no pīti) + 4 + lobha + diṭṭhi + thinamiddha (sometimes, together) = 18/20

              • domanassasahagataṁ paṭighasampayuttaṁ sasaṅkhārikaṁ cittaṁ 7 + 5 (no pīti) + 4 + dosa + issā/macchariya/kukkucca (sometimes, separately) + thinamiddha (sometimes, together) = 17/18/19/20

          • how many cetasikas in total may arise in mohamūlacittas?→7 scs + 4 pakiṇṇaka + 4 aku sādhāraṇa + thīnamiddha + vicikicchā = 18

            • vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ paṭhamajjhānakusalacittaṃ vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ paṭhamajjhānavipākacittaṃ vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ paṭhamajjhānakiriyācittaṃ
              • 7 + 6 + 19 + 2 appamaññā (sometimes, separately) + paññā = 33/34
            • vicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ dutiyajjhānakusalacittaṃ vicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ dutiyajjhānavipākacittaṃ vicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ dutiyajjhānakiriyācittaṃ
              • 7 + 5 + 19 + 2 appamaññā (sometimes, separately) + paññā = 32/33
            • pītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ tatiyajjhānakusalacittaṃ pītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ tatiyajjhānavipākacittaṃ pītisukhekaggatāsahitaṃ tatiyajjhānakiriyācittaṃ
              • 7 + 4 + 19 + 2 appamaññā (sometimes, separately) + paññā = 31/32
            • sukhekaggatāsahitaṃ catutthajjhānakusalacittaṃ sukhekaggatāsahitaṃ catutthajjhānavipākacittaṃ sukhekaggatāsahitaṃ catutthajjhānakiriyācittaṃ
              • 7 + 3 + 19 + 2 appamaññā (sometimes, separately) + paññā = 30/31

          • 5 saṅgahanaya of the lokuttaracittas
            • 1st jhāna: 4 magga + 4 phala
              • 7 + 6 + 19 + 3 virati (always, together) + paññā = 36
            • 2nd jhāna: 4 magga + 4 phala
              • 7 + 5 + 19 + 3 virati (always, together)+ paññā = 35
            • 3rd jhāna: 4 magga + 4 phala
              • 7 + 4 + 19 + 3 virati (always, together) + paññā = 34
            • 4th jhāna: 4 magga + 4 phala
              • 7 + 3 + 19 + 3 virati (always, together) + paññā = 33 (somanassavedanā)
            • 5th jhāna: 4 magga + 4 phala
              • 7 + 3 + 19 + 3 virati (always, together)+ paññā = 33 (upekkhāvedanā)

          • vedanāsaṅgaha #edited
            • 2 bheda (divisions) of vedanā
              • anubhavanabheda: division according to how vedanā experiences the ārammaṇarasa (as iṭṭha, aniṭṭha or majjhatta)
              • indriyabheda: indriya is the lord who rules over others and keeps them under his authority. Likewise, with regard to the function of tasting the ārammaṇarasa, vedanā is the the lord who rules and influences other mentalities. In this regard vedanā is fivefold.
              • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
            • vedanāsaṅgaha
              • anubhavanabheda:
                • dukkhasahagatacittas (3)
                  • dukkhāsahagataṁ akusalavipākaṁ kāyaviññāṇaṁ
                  • 2 dosamūlacittas
                • sukhasahagatacitta (63)
                  • 62 somanassasahagatacittas
                  • 1 sukhasahagata kāyaviññāṇa
                • adukkhamasukhasahagatacittas (55)
              • indriyabheda:
                • dukkhasahagatacitta (1)

          • hetusaṅgaha #edited
            • 6 hetus (roots)
              • akusala hetus
                • akusala asādhāraṇa hetu
                  • lobha – greed
                  • dosa – hatred
                • akusala sādhāraṇa hetu
                  • moha – delusion
              • sobhana hetu (bright roots)
                • sobhana sādhāraṇa hetus
                  • alobha – non-greed
                  • adosa – non-hate
                • sobhana asādhāraṇa hetu
                  • amoha (paññindriya) – non-delusion
              • (mūla)hetu↔ cetasikas that assist the associating mentalities to remain fixed on the object (or that act as cause for wholesomeness / unwholesomeness ‒ confirm) #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • why they are called hetu
                • not in the sense of causes for the production of something (janakahetu), but because they help citta and cetasikas to be well established on the object they cognize, as roots assist trees in remaining upright on the ground🎄
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
              • what are sahetuka or ahetuka dhammas?→they refer to dhammas associated or not with any of the mūla hetus in terms of sampayoga lakkhaṇa
              • how does each root help the citta and cetasikas to be well established on the object?
                • the akusala hetus
                  • strongly sink into their respective objects (lobhanīya-, dosanīya- and mohanīyārammaṇas) - as a result, their associated citta and cetasikas become firmly established on the object without wavering
                    • how to conciliate the two seemingly opposed aspects of mohamūlacittas wavering due to restlessness/doubt and the root aspect of being firmly established on the object?→the firmness / non-wavering facet of mohahetu is the fact that it is repeatedly deluded about the object in a way that is difficult to change; another perspective is that it is a root in the sense of root-cause for unwholesomeness
                      • moha as a root cause for unwholesomeness would fall under which of the 4 types of hetu? #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • the sobhana hetus:
                  • suppress their opposing counterparts and increase the akusalavivekarasa (bliss / taste of seclusion from unwholesomeness) of the mind stream which is threefold: lobhavivekarasa, dosavivekarasa and mohavivekarasa; as a result, their associated citta and cetasikas become firmly established on the object without wavering
              • classification of objects according to the caṅkīsutta:
                • lobhanīyārammaṇa↔objects which are supportive to craving
                • dosanīyārammaṇa↔objects which are supportive to anger
                • mohanīyārammaṇa↔objects which are supportive to delusion
                • only {{9475615387378094::lokiyadhammas }}{{9475615387378094::and }}{{9475615387378094::paññattis}} can be lobhanīya-, dosanīya- or mohanīyārammaṇas
              • other extra classifications of objects
                • alobhanīyārammaṇa↔objects which are not supportive of craving such as monkhood or a paṁsukūlacīvara
                • saddheyyavatthu↔faith-inspiring objects such as the triple gem, kamma and vipāka, rebirth and paṭiccasamuppāda since they are real
            • hetusaṅgaha
              • ahetukacittas (18)
              • sahetukacittas (71)
                • ekahetukacittas (2 mohamūlacittas)
                • duhetukacittas (22)
                  • 8 lobhamūlacittas (lobha & moha)
                  • 2 dosamūlacittas (dosa & moha)
                  • 12 kāmasobhana ñāṇavippayuttacittas (alobha & amoha)
                • tihetukacittas (47)
                  • 12 kāmasobhana ñāṇasampayuttacittas
                  • 15 rūpāvacaracittas
                  • 12 arūpāvacaracittas
                  • 8 lokuttaracittas
            • note:
              • why there are no ekahetuka cittas among the sobhanacittas?→because of the universality of alobha and adosa in the sphere of sobhanas
              • why are there no ekahetukacittas among the akusalacittas with lobha or dosa as hetu?→because of the universality of moha in the sphere of akusalas
              • hetus can also be classified as kusalahetus (those that arise in kusalacittas) (in one passage the Buddha is said to have kusalasīla in the sense of pure or skilful), vipākahetus, kiriyahetus, and abyākatahetus (vipāka and kiriya)
          • kiccasaṅgaha #edited
            • what is the kicca meant here?
              • the function performed by the whole cittuppāda collectively
            • 14 kiccas of citta
              • paṭisandhikicca (rebirth-linking): connecting the present life with the future life without allowing the generation of consciousnesses to cease with death
              • bhavaṅgakicca (life-continuum): maintaining the continuity of consciousnesses after paṭisandhi acting as the default / root citta in the santati; it is called so since it maintains existence by arising repeatedly
              • āvajjanakicca (adverting) directing or turning towards an object in order to initiate a mind process
              • dassanakicca (seeing): knowing visible data/forms
              • savanakicca (hearing): knowing sounds
              • ghāyanakicca (smelling): knowing odors
              • sāyanakicca (tasting): knowing tastes
              • phusanakicca (contacting): knowing tangibles
              • sampaṭicchanakicca (receiving): retaking the objects taken by the ten viññāṇas
              • santīraṇakicca (investigating): investigating the objects received by sampaṭicchanacitta
              • voṭṭhabbanakicca (determining): deciding the nature of the object investigated. It adverts and determines. Yoniso manasikāra is related to this
                • how do we differentiate between the determining function of the cittuppāda and the determining function of adhimokkha? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • javanakicca (dynamic / impulsion): the strong power of the consciousness in cognizing objects well and performing verbal, physical and mental activities such as walking, talking and meditating. It is the main section of consciousness. Cittavīthis occur for the sake of javanas
                • what is kamma?→cetanā in kusala / akusala javanacittas
                • what is the only vipāka which performs the javana function?→phalacittas
                • note: even arahants have to maintain a mental balance to enter phalasamāpatti, they need some development. Due to compassionate thoughts an arahat could not enter phalasamāpatti for a whole vassa
              • tadārammaṇakicca (registration / retaking): retaking the object taken by the javanas
              • cutikicca (dying): ending life
            • kiccasaṅgaha
              • paṭisandhikicca, bhavaṅgakicca and cutikicca: 19 cittas
                • 1 upekkhāsahagataṁ akusalavipāka santīraṇa

                • note: pañcadvārāvajjana only adverts while manodvārāvajjana adverts in the manodvāravīthi and determines in the pañcadvāravīthi #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • note: according to the suttanta method yoniso manasikāra has ñāṇa because {{5574525268062855::it refers to the whole vīthi}}
                  • is the determination that arises in voṭṭhabbana that leads to dvihetuka kusala cittas also called yoniso manasikāra? #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • note:
                  • what is the difference between the function of adhimokkha cetasika and the voṭṭhabbana function of the whole cittuppāda?→adhimokkha cetasika takes the object firmly while the voṭṭhabbana function of the cittuppāda decides how to react / treat the object
                  • how to conciliate the determining function of voṭṭhabbana with the vicikicchāsahagatacitta which may follow it which cannot make a decision on the object? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • javanakicca: 55 cittas
                • 29 kāmajavanas
                  • 12 akusalajavanas
                  • 1 hasituppādajavana
                  • 8 mahākusalajavanas
                  • 8 mahākiriyājavanas
                • 26 appaṇājavanas
                  • 5 rupāvacarakusalajavanas

                • pañcadvārika javanas (javanas that occur in pañcadvāravīthis) can only be {{09110535154583088::kāmajavanas (29)}}, while manodvārika javanas can be {{09110535154583088::all 55 javanacittas}}
              • tadārammaṇakicca: 11 cittas
                • 3 santīraṇas
                • 8 mahāvipākas
            • types of paṭisandhi
              • 20 types of paṭisandhi
                • 19 cittas which can perform the paṭisandhikicca
                • 1 rūpapaṭisandhi (asaññasatta)
              • 3 types of paṭisandhi according to the presence/abscence of nāmarūpa
                • nāmapaṭisandhi (4 arūpabhāva)
                • rūpapaṭisandhi (1 asaññāsatta)
                • nāmarūpapaṭisandhi (15)
            • classification of cittas according to how many kiccas they perform:
              • pañcakicca (5 functions): 2 cittas – 2 upekkhāsahagata santīraṇacittas can perform the functions of paṭisandhi, bhavaṅga, cuti, santīraṇa and tadārammaṇa
              • catukicca (4 functions): 8 cittas – 8 mahāvipākacittas can perform paṭisandhi, bhavaṅga, cuti, and tadārammaṇa functions
              • tikicca (3 functions): 9 cittas – 9 mahaggata vipākacittas can perform paṭisandhi, bhavaṅga and cuti functions.
              • dukicca (2 functions): 2 cittas
                • somanassasahagata santīraṇacitta can perform santīraṇa and tadārammaṇa functions
                • manodvārāvajjana citta can perform āvajjana and voṭṭhapana functions

            • 6 dvāra (doors)
              • material doors
                • cakkhudvāra (eye door): it is the eye-sensitivity (cakkhuppasāda)
                  • In the middle of the pupil of the eye-ball there is a place, said to be the size of a louse's head, where images of forms fall on to (?). It is said to be the size of a louse’s head
                    • (according to medical science the images of visible forms appear in the retina which is located on the back wall of the eyeball)
                • sotadvāra (ear door): it is the ear-sensitivity (sotappasāda)
                • ghānadvāra (nose door): it is the nose-sensitivity (ghānappasāda)
                • jivhādvāra (tongue door): it is the tongue-sensitivity (jivhāppasāda)
                • kāyadvāra (body door): it is the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda) and it arises spread all over the body
              • immaterial door
                • manodvāra (mind door): it is the bhavaṅgacitta
                  • the mind door assists in cognizing the objects of the sense doors and its own objects; when objects strike at the mind door, that strike is not a physical contact like in five sense doors

            • ārammaṇa is↔that which is known / captured by the mind
            • kālabheda - classification of ārammaṇas according to time
              • atīta (past) - any reality that has arisen and already perished
              • anāgata (future) - any reality that has not arisen yet
              • paccupanna (present) - any reality that has arisen but not perished yet
              • kālamuttaka (nibbāna and paññatti) - anything that does not arise / not connected with arising and perishing
                • vijjamāna kālamuttaka: nibbāna is a reality that exists but does not arise or perish
                • avijjamāna kālamuttaka: paññattis do not exist in realty hence they do not arise
              • notes:
                • past, future and present are used as adjectives to the realities
                • paramatthajātika (anusaya)
                  • appahīna↔not erradicated
                  • avatthā (f.)↔occasion, opportunity, position, stage
                  • atītalobha arose because it was appahīna; paccuppanna lobha is also appahīna; anāgatalobha is also appahīna
                  • potencies are tekālikajātika, not bound to one time, therefore are atīta, anagata and paccuppanna
                  • tekālikajātika↔not bound to one time (potencies) (Buddhavisaya)
                  • the anusaya kilesa is not a different reality from the manifested kilesa

          • vatthusaṅgaha #edited
            • vatthu→materiality upon which citta depends; all vatthus are material
            • 6 vatthu
              • cakkhuvatthu (eye base)
                • related words from anatomy: retina, fovea, macula, visual cells, retinal cells, retinal cone, retinal rod
              • sotavatthu (ear base)
              • ghānavatthu (nose base)
              • jivhāvatthu (tongue base)
              • kāyavatthu (body base)
              • hadayavatthu / vatthurūpa / hadayavatthurūpa (heart base)
                • it is a subtle element which exists in the blood found inside the heart muscle; it is neither seen by the eye nor felt by the hand; it is not found in the dead; although the blood inside the heart muscle flows out, this heart-base which helps in the arising of consciousnesses does not go out from the heart muscle; most of the consciousnesses arise with the heart-base as base, threfore it is the most prominent base
              • the first five bases are identical with the first five doors. 1. Cakkhu vatthu is the cakkhuppasāda 2. Sota vatthu is the sotappasāda 3. Ghāna vatthu is the ghānappasāda 4. Jivhā vatthu is the jivhāppasāda 5. Kāya vatthu is the kāyappasāda
              • note: the first five bases are identical with the first five doors (cakkhuvatthu is cakkhudvāra...)
            • does manoviññāṇa always associate hadayavatthu?→in realms other than the 4 arūpa realms, yes
            • the presence of vatthus according to realms
              • kāma bhūmi beings with complete faculties have all six bases
              • rūpa bhūmi beings do not have nose-, tongue- and body-bases
                • they do not have the sensitivities but do have nose, tongue and body in appearance
                • the three bases of nose, tongue and body are of no use other than the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and do not occur in brahmas who are born with the power of meditation that suppresses sensual desire; the eye and ear bases on the other hand, are useful for mental purification and occur in brahmas for the purpose of sighting the Buddha and listening to Dhamma
                • what about asaññasatta beings?→they do not possess any of the 6 vatthurūpas
              • arūpa bhūmi beings do not have any of the bases
            • sotāpattimagga can arise for 2 reasons
              • sayambhū sotāpattimagga (arises by oneself without the help of another)
                • only sammāsambuddhas and paccekabuddhas that only arise in the human realm
              • paratoghosa sotāpattimagga (due to the sound of another)
                • "to" has mostly ablative meaning but it may have all other cases except dative; in this case it has genitive meaning
              • note: therefore sotāpattimagga never arises in arūpa bhūmi (sotāpattiphala can arise because a sotāpanna may be reborn in the arūpa realm and enter phalasamāpatti; a sotāpanna may also practice vipassanā and attain higher maggas and phalas in the arūpa bhūmi)
            • vatthusaṅgaha
              • according to each base
                • cakkhuvatthu - 2 cakkhuviññāṇas always
                • sotavatthu - 2 sotaviññāṇa always
                • ghānavatthu - 2 ghānaviññāṇa always
                • jivhāvatthu - 2 jivhāviññāṇa always
                • kāyavatthu - 2 kāyaviññāṇa always
                • hadayavatthu - 75 cittas (-10 viññāṇa and 4 arūpa vipāka)
                  • always: 33 cittas
                  • sometimes: 42 cittas
                • no vatthu - 4 arūpavipākacittas always
              • cittas according to whether they associate a base or not
                • cittas that always associate a base (they never arise in arūpabhūmi)
                  • 2 dosamūla
                  • 17 ahetukas (- Ma)
                  • 8 mvip
                  • 15 rūpāvacara
                  • 1 sotāpattimagga
                  • Total: 43
                • cittas that sometimes associate a base (they may or may not arise in arūpabhūmi)
                  • 10 aku (exc. dosamūla)
                  • 1 Ma
                  • 8 mku
                  • 8 mki
                  • 4 aru ku
                  • 4 aru ki
                  • 7 lokuttara (exc. sotāpattimagga)
                  • Total: 42
                  • they arise in association with the heart base when occurring in the pañcavokāra realms, and arise without a base in the catuvokāra (arūpa) realm
                • cittas that never associate a base (they only arise in the arūpabhūmi)
                  • 4 arūpāvacara vipāka cittas
            • notes:

                • cittas overcome by each magga & phala (TBC, WIP) #wip🚧
