          • kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṁ
            • background
              • once the Buddha was residing at the {{9227898525620388::Veḷuvana}}{{9227898525620388:: monastery near }}{{9227898525620388::Rājagaha}}; monks in the city of {{9227898525620388::Āḷavī}} were (doing what?) {{9227898525620388::constructing oversized kuṭis with difficulty }}{{9227898525620388::without sponsors}} and due excessive asking lay people were afraid to meet them and evaded them, while some even left their villages; one day {{9227898525620388::Ven. Mahākassapa}} came to the city and stayed in the {{9227898525620388::pagoda called }}{{9227898525620388::Aggālava}}; while wandering for alms he noticed the strange behavior of the lay people and asked the monks about it; the monks explained the situation to him who later informed the situation to the Buddha when he came to the city; the Buddha then promulgated the rule
            • saññācikakuṭi↔a kuṭi constructed by a bhikkhu without a sponsor (assāmika), for his own use (attuddesa), using construction material and support from an aññātaka appavārita dāyaka (unrelated and uninvited devotee)
              • assāmika↔a kuṭi built by the bhikkhu without a sponsor
              • attuddesa↔intended for oneself
            • characteristics of the devotees involved
              • aññātaka↔one who is not a blood relative
              • appavārita dāyaka↔a devotee who has not invited a monk to ask for requisites when needed
            • units of measure / distances / conversions / ratios
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
            • size of kuṭis
              • minimum size for a building to be considered a kuṭi
                • minimum width→4 majjhimapurisavidatthi (measured between the inner side of the walls)
                  • building such a small building in which a bed of {{820432723327519::9 pakati vidatthi}} in length cannot be maneuvered is→anāpatti
                    • can such a small buiding be considered a monk's dwelling? is it enough for spending vassa? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • maximum size of a saññācika kuṭi
                • maximum length: {{03809523250489599::12 }}{{03809523250489599::Sugatavidatthi }}{{03809523250489599::(handspans)}}measured from {{03809523250489599::the }}{{03809523250489599::outside edges}}{{03809523250489599:: of the walls}} maximum width: {{03809523250489599::7 }}{{03809523250489599::Sugatavidatthi}} measured from {{03809523250489599::the }}{{03809523250489599::internal edges}}{{03809523250489599:: of the walls}}
                • 12 sugatavidatthi (handspans) = {{016882780255645935::36}} majjhimapurisavidatthi = {{016882780255645935::54}} pakatipurisavidatthi 7 sugatavidatthi = {{016882780255645935::21}} majjhimapurisavidatthi = {{016882780255645935::31 1/2}} pakatipurisavidatthi
                • 3 ways the kuṭi size may exceed the maximum size
                  • only length exceeds the maximum
                  • only the width exceeds the maximum
                  • both length and width exceed the maximum
            • plastering and painting
              • {{8539802576259086::ullitta}} is a kuṭi where the {{43207183369398794::interior (walls and ceiling)}} has been plastered and painted with {{0643610338002567::clay or lime}} {{8539802576259086::avalitta}} is a kuṭi where the {{43207183369398794::exterior (walls and roof)}} has been plastered and painted with {{0643610338002567::clay or lime}} plastering with {{004164983884983098::burnt chaff or cow dung}} is not considered {{8539802576259086::ullitta / avalitta}}
                • Lime (material) - Wikipedia ‒ calcium oxide in various forms
                • ullitta √lip↔pp. plastered; (comm) plastered inside; lit. smeared up #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
                • avalitta √lip↔pp. plastered; painted; whitewashed; (comm) plastered outside; lit. smeared down #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • in order for the kuṭi to be considered ullitta / avalitta / both, it is essential that the plaster of the inner walls and ceiling or the plaster of the outer walls and the roof be→combined and attached to each other #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • 2 characteristics of the kuṭi vatthu (construction site)
              • anārambha (without harm / danger)
                • devoid of hazards
                • devoid of danger for animals
                • not a cultivation area
              • saparikkamana bhūmi / saupacāra bhūmi
                • a site where after having built the kuṭi there would still be enough space for a bullock cart (of 2 to 4 bulls) to have one wheel at the line made by rainwater as it falls from the roof and the other wheel outwards
                • a man should be able to carry a ladder around the house without impediment
            • kuṭivatthu desanā
              • procedure followed by the bhikkhu building the kuṭi
                • clear and clean the land on which the kuṭi is to be built #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • invite the Saṅgha to inspect the land
                  • if all the Saṅgha wishes to inspect the land all of them should do so
                  • if no one wishes to the Saṅgha must appoint 2 or 3 bhikkhus who are well versed in the Vinaya to inspect the site subsequent to a vinayakamma #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • the Saṅgha inspects the site
                  • If the saṅgha determines that the site is sārambha (unsafe) or aparikkamana (there is not adequate space) the bhikkhus must state: "do not build a kuṭi here"
                  • If the kuṭi is anārambha and saparikkamana the saṅgha must be informed of it #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • the monk invites the Saṅgha to recite the kuṭivatthu
                  • the Saṅgha does so by using the ñatti dutiya kammavācā as indicated in the Vinaya Pāḷi
                  • the kuṭi vatthu can be recited at the site itself if all the Saṅgha inspects the kuṭi site and there is adequate space to perform the Vinaya kamma at that location

At that time, one of the devotees of Ven. {{9305106507041636::Channa}} informed him about his desire to {{9305106507041636::build him a kuṭi}}; the ven., while preparing a suitable land for his future residence, made the workers to {{9305106507041636::cut a sacred tree that was highly venerated by locals}}; people criticized and the Buddha promulgated the rule introducing {{9305106507041636::protocols that should be followed when a monk is building a kuṭi with the help of a sponsor}}

          • Assignment 29/12/2022 - due 02/01/2023
            • (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
            • What are the important conditions including the verbal utterance for the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem (tisaraṇāgamana) to be established?
              • The conditions to be met for the refuge (saraṇa) to be established are faith in the Triple Gem as the ultimate shelter, refuge, and assistance, faith in the genuine qualities of the Triple Gem such as faith in the enlightenment of the Buddha, faith in the Dhamma as being the truth and the path, and faith in the Saṅgha as possessed of higher virtues and as practicing the right way. The verbal utterance that follows and expresses such mental refuge is:
              • "Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi
              • Dhammaṁ saranaṁ gacchāmi
              • Saṅghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi
              • Dutiyampi Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi
              • Dutiyampi Dhammaṁ saranaṁ gacchāmi
              • Dutiyampi Saṅghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi
              • Tatiyampi Buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi
              • Tatiyampi Dhammaṁ saranaṁ gacchāmi
              • Tatiyampi Saṅghaṁ saraṇaṁ gacchāmi"
            • Describe what pollutes and what breaks the triple refuge.
              • The triple refuge is twofold as mundane (lokiyasaraṇāgamana), the refuge taken by a puthujjana, and supramundane (lokuttarasaraṇāgamana), the refuge of a Noble disciple. The mundane refuge is polluted and weakened by impure understanding of the Triple Gem and by holding wrong views about the Triple Gem. It is completely broken by rejecting the Triple Gem, by taking other teachers as refuge and by death. Of these three cases the first two are blameworthy and connected with unwholesome states while the third is blameless. The supramundane refuge of a Noble disciple is established with the first Noble Path and cannot be polluted or broken.
            • Mention the types of refuge-taking in the Buddha and describe the advantages (results) of going to the Triple Gem for refuge.
              • The taking of refuge can be classified into 4 kinds:
                • Attasannīyātana saraṇagamana (Self-relinquishment to the Triple Gem)
                • Tapparāyana saraṇagamana (verbal utterance taking refuge in the Triple Gem)
                • Sissabhāvopagamana saraṇagamana (Determination to be a disciple of the Triple Gem)
                • Paṇipātana saraṇagamanaṁ (Prostration accepting the Triple Gem as the greatest refuge)
              • The puthujjana who goes to the Triple Gem for refuge accrues as result worldly benefits such as possessions, good destinations and the support for supramundane attainments. Supramundane refuge on its turn has supramundane dhammas (paths, fruits and Nibbāna) as benefit.
            • How do you explain and define the Gem of the Dhamma according to the Theravāda standpoint?
              • The Gem of the Dhamma is the body of teachings expounded by the Buddha, the Truths, the aggregates, the faculties, the enlightenment factors, the inspiring accounts, exhortations, examples, the monastic discipline, and so on. The Dhamma is also the mundane and supramundane paths, the three trainings consisting of morality, concentration and wisdom in their mundane and supramundane manifestations. Above all Dhamma is the goal, the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna.
            • Write and essay on behaving towards the Triple Gem as a part of inner development.
              • The good person possessed of merit who approaches the Triple Gem respectfully, listens carefully and attentively to its message, investigates its meaning, establishes confidence in it and takes the triple refuge should cultivate such association often. This good person should repeatedly reflect about such truths as the Four Noble Truths, ultimate dhammas, the triple training, and so on, and should approach well versed bhikkhus respectfully and pose them intelligent questions. This person should as well associate the Triple Gem bodily and verbally by visiting holy places, supporting the Saṅgha with the necessities of their practice, making offerings of material things and offerings of Dhamma by printing Dhamma books, organizing Dhamma talks and study groups, and by performing such activities connected with what is wholesome and conducive to the Path. While doing so the good person should do it faithfully and respectfully by rising to greet venerables, paying respect, paying close attention to Dhamma discussions in a respectful posture, wearing suitable attire avoiding covering the head and wearing shoes, and by performing such good bodily and verbal deeds which are the natural practice of wise individuals. This good person should furthermore put the teaching into practice by diligently developing samatha objects such as mindfulness of breathing, kasiṇas, foulness meditation, four elements meditation and so on, by suppressing the hindrances, dwelling in the jhānas, discerning ultimate dhammas, their specific and general characteristics, and by penetrating the Noble Truths with insight cutting off defilements.
              • With such respect, with such faith, with such practices one would surely achieve growth and fruition in their path of inner development as a Noble disciple.

                • saṅgāma catukka (war tetrad, actually just two)
                  • in the war, killing parents accidentaly while intending to kill another person: {{29701005067742536::no ānantariya kamma}} (because the attack is not intended to kill the parents) in the war intentionally killing parents (even if one shoots through another person): {{29701005067742536::ānantariya kamma}} (because one's intention of killing such being is fulfilled)
                • palāla catukka (straw tetrad, also just two)
                  • one pierces a stack of straws to clean the weapon but ends up killing parents: {{8782644168397833::no ānantariya kamma}} one pierces the stack of straws intending to kill someone there and it ends up being one's parents: {{8782644168397833::ānantariya kamma}}
                  • palālaṃ (nt.)↔straw #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • killing cannot be done with a mind of compassion. Killing a being in suffering is causing an even greater suffering since there is nothing dearer to beings than their life. One wishes to kill them because one is unable to bear seeing their suffering (with dosa mind, not compassion; even though compassion may arise the killing is only done with dosa)
            • Is suicide pāṇaghātakamma?→no
            • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja depends on:
              • virtues: of the being killed
              • means: method used
              • defilements: the more intense the more blameworthy
            • vipāka and adīnava
              • pāṇaghātakamma produces result in{{5706627995903792:: the four apāya}}, ānatariyakamma produces result {{5706627995903792::in avīci. Saṅghabhedakamma produces vipāka in avīci until the end of the kappa and the other ānantariyakammas produce vipāka in avīci but for a shorter period.}}
              • other results: causes one to be ill, die at a young age, be deformed, thin, bad looking, weak, have few friends and many enemies, sadness, fear, subject to death due to the actions of others, and so on.
          • Adinnādāna (adattādānakamma)
            • Definition
              • Taking any property which belongs to another human with the intention to steal without consent by deception, threat, force, etc.
            • 5 sambhāra
              • Parapariggahitaṃ (belonging to other (human)
              • parapariggahitasaññitā (perceiving that it belongs to someone else)
              • theyyacittaṃ (intention or volition to steal it)
              • upakkamo (effort for stealing)
              • tena haraṇaṃ (taking it by means of that effort)
            • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja of adinnādāna and abhijjhā
              • virtues of the owner
              • means employed
              • intensity of defilements
              • value of the object stolen
            • Some examples of ādīnavas and vipākas of adattādānakamma→being insulted, beaten, punished, being poor, being born in woeful states such as hell, petas, and animals who have to carry heavy things for those whom they stole from.
          • Kāmesumicchācāra (kāmesumicchācārakamma)
            • definition
              • sex with an unsuitable woman/man and opposed to world customs
            • cattāro sambhārā (factors):
              • agamanīyavatthu (a woman/man who should not be approached)
                • only between a man and a protected woman (pariggahita)
                • what about other types of sexual acts considered by society as sexual misconduct such as raping another man or child? #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ (intention to have sex with that woman)
                • is perception a factor here or not? No #q🙋🏼‍♂
              • sevanappayogo (the act of engaging in a sexual activity with that person (only sāhatthika))
              • maggena-magga-paṭipattiadhivāsanaṃ (the penis enter the nimitta)
            • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja
              • virtues of the other
              • means: raping is more blameworthy than with consent
              • intensity of defilements associated
            • some vipākas and adīnavas of kāmesumicchācāra
              • being insulted, being killed, imprisoned, rebirth in hell and made to climb up and down Imbul trees with thorns as big as 16 aṅgulis, suffering death at conception, becoming eunuchs, females, having a disfigured body, many enemies, prone to sickness...
          • wrong speech
            • Musāvāda
              • definition
                • intentionally misrepresenting the truth by body, speech or by ordering another and being understood by the listener.
              • 4 sambhāra
                • atathaṃ vatthu: Being a false information according to what one perceives to be the truth
                • visaṃvādanacittaṃ: Intention of deceiving the other person
                • tajjo vāyāmo: Effort (bodily, verbal, by giving a command) to convey what is not the truth to the other person.
                  • When ordering another if the messenger knows it is a lie both lied, if the messenger does not know it is a lie only the one who ordered lied.
                  • in the case of āṇattika (by ordering another) if the messenger does not know it is a lie he {{8899316564804831::does not commit this kamma, only the sender.}} If the messenger knows it is a lie {{8899316564804831::he also commits the kamma together with the sender}}
                • parassatadatthavijānanaṃ: The listener accepts the conveyed meaning
                  • According to Ven. Janakābhivaṁsa (Myanmar) if the listener understands but is not deceived (knows it is a lie) the precept is broken but the kammapatha is not complete.
              • Factors for being appasāvajja or mahāsāvajja:
                • virtue of the being deceived
                • means the method used for conveying the lie
                • intensity of the defilements involved
                • purpose
                  • lies uttered for fun, to avoid parting with something one owns, to lull children and to hide wrong deeds are less blameworthy;
                  • making false promises, uttering lies that cause injustice, loss or harm to others are more blameworthy
              • vipākas and adīnavas of musāvāda, pisuṇavācā, pharusavācā and byāpāda
                • rebirth in the 4 apāya.
                • in hell: having to drink molten iron for example
                • one suffers for acts one has not done
                • have weak intellect
                • mouth ailments: mute, have bad breath, deformed teeth, teeth fall early, mouth ailments, disfigurements, unpleasant voice
                • one is not trusted by others
                • others: poor, childless, only female children and disobedient children.
                • ādīnavas: being insulted, imprisoned, punished, not trusted
              • Stanza on lying: (Dhp 176) "ekaṃ dhammaṃ{{5616054710494365:: atītassa, musāvādissa jantuno, vitiṇṇaparalokassa, natthi pāpaṃ akāriyaṃ}}"
                • jantu (m.) √jan 'jāyatīti jantu'↔man; person; being; lit. who is born #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
                • vitiṇṇa √tar↔pp. crossed beyond; overcome; given up; abandoned; neglected; rejected #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • Pisuṇavācā (divisive speech / causing schisms / malicious tale bearing / backbiting / slandering)
              • definition:
                • True or untrue speech intended on dividing / causing dissention between two or more beings or intended on befriending the listener while making another the listener's enemy; and which is accepted by the listener
                  • pare pana abhinne kammapathabhedo natthi
              • 4 sambhāra:
                • 1. bhinditabbo paro (someone to be divided)
                • 2. bhedapurekkhāratā vā piyakamyatā vā (the intention to cause dissension or to make oneself dear to the listener)
                • 3. tajjo vāyāmo (the effort to convey the idea to cause dissension)
                  • sāhatthika or āṇattika
                • 4. tassa tadatthavijānanaṃ (the listener accepts it)
              • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja
                • virtue of the beings being divided
                • by telling the truth it is appasāvajja and by telling lies it is mahāsāvajja
                • the intensity of the defilements involved
            • Pharusavācā (harsh speech)
              • definition→speech uttered with ill-will which is intended on hurting the feelings of others
              • 3 sambhāra
                • akkositabbo paro (a person to be insulted)
                • kupitacittaṃ (a mind associated with ill-will)
                • akkosanā (insulting the other; the other's feelings must be hurt for the kammapatha)
              • dasa akkosavatthu
                • jāti (birth: you outcaste!)
                • nāma (name)
                • gotta (family)
                • kamma (deed/activity)
                • sippa (occupation)
                • ābādha (disease)
                • liṅga (gender)
                • kilesa (defilement)
                • āpatti (offense)
                • hīnasaṅkhāta (calling another by something reckoned as low: you pig!)
                • saṅkhāta (vis.) √khā↔reckoned; so called; what is called
              • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja
                • virtue of the being insulted
                • intensity of the defilements (ill-will)
            • Samphappalāpa (frivolous speech)
              • definition→Speech that has no wholesome benefit and results in merely building up defilements and wasting time
              • 2 sambhāra
                • niratthakakathāpurekkhāratā (intention to engage in speech which is of no benefit to the speaker or listener)
                • tathārūpī kathā kathanañca (engaging in such speech)
                • (according to handbook of the buddhist only if the listener believes the frivolous speech the kammapatha is complete) #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • niratthaka (vis.) √ar↔useless; worthless; pointless; meaningless; nonsensical #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • appasāvajja and mahāsāvajja
                • In general frivolous speech is of minor severity but it may become more blameworthy according to #q🙋🏼‍♂
                • virtue of the listener
                • intensity of defilements involved
                • the harm it causes to the listener
          • Abhijjhā (covetousness)
            • definition→the desire to acquire for oneself the property of another. Based on covetousness stealing and sexual misconduct may occur.
            • 2 sambhāra
              • parabhaṇḍaṃ (being a property of another person)
              • attano pariṇāmanaṃ (the greedy wish to acquire it for oneself)
          • Byāpāda (ill-will)
            • definition→the thought of hatred wishing for the death of another being; based on byāpāda killing may occur, but killing is not necessarily preluded by it
            • 2 sambhāra
              • parasatto (being another living being)
              • tassa ca vināsanacintā (wishing destruction of it with hatred)
            • Byāpāda can lead to pāṇaghāta but pāṇaghāta is not necessarily preluded by byāpāda
          • Micchādiṭṭhi (wrong view)
            • definition as kammapatha→holding on with strong conviction to a wrong idea that rejects mainly kamma and vipāka (including past and future lives, merit and demerit, hell and heavens and nibbāna) - ahetukadiṭṭhi, akiriyadiṭṭhi or natthikadiṭṭhi
            • 2 sambhāra
              • vatthuno ca gahitākāraviparītatā (holding on to a distorted view about such matters as kamma and kammavipāka)
              • yathā ca taṃ gaṇhāti tathābhāvena tassupaṭṭhānaṃ (strong conviction in such wrong view after much consideration)
            • 3 levels of micchādiṭṭhi according to what they hinder (āvaraṇa)
              • saggāvaraṇaṁ maggāvaraṇaṁ ca (it hinders being reborn in the heavens and attaining the path): ahetukadiṭṭhi, akiriyādiṭṭhi and natthikadiṭṭhi
              • na saggāvaraṇaṁ maggāvaraṇaṁ (it doesn't hinder heaven but hinders the path): antaggāhikadiṭṭhi (sassata / uccheda)
              • nevasaggāvaraṇanamaggāvaraṇa (it neither hinders heaven nor the path): sakkāyadiṭṭhi
            • 3 views which are akusalakammapatha
              • ahetukadiṭṭhi (uncausedness): no cause for the defilement or purification of beings, kusala and akusala do not lead to good and bad results respectively; beings go through saṁsāra a certain period (84.000 kappas) and end suffering without a cause. (expounded by Makkhali Gosala)
              • akiriyadiṭṭhi (inefficacy of action): no demerit accrues by doing bad deeds, no merit accrues by doing good deeds (expressed by Pūraṇa Kassapa)
              • natthikadiṭṭhi (anihilation): no consequences of kusala or akusala kamma; no living being is reborn after death, no threefold training (expressed by Ajitakesakambala)
            • sutta related to the topic: apannakapaṭipadā
            • Pāḷi about micchādiṭṭhi as mahāsāvajja: "nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ {{15616811615919124::ekadhammampi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi. micchādiṭṭhiparamāni, bhikkhave, mahāsāvajjānī"ti}} This is said with regard to the 3 niyatamicchādiṭṭhis: ahetuka, akiriya and natthikadiṭṭhi
            • some vipākas and adīnavas of micchādiṭṭhi
              • sugati and nibbāna is not achievable and only rebirth in the 4 apāya can occur
              • based on such view one commits many unwholesome kammas
              • these views result in consequences that may be even worse than anantariyakamma (heinous crime) since ānantariyakamma leads to rebirth in hell until the end of the kappa but niyatāmicchādiṭṭhi may go even beyond that.
            • The 3 views which are akusalakammapatha are also called {{811249018390682::niyatāmicchādiṭṭhi}} since they certainly lead to rebirth in apāya.
            • "akalyāṇajanaṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ, tasmā ārakā parivajjeyya, bhūtikāmo vicakkhaṇo"ti.
          • surāmerayapānaṃ (using intoxicants)
            • definition→intentionally consuming any substance that causes intoxication. Intoxication here is a mental state of pride, delusion and heedlessness
            • 4 sambhāra
              • majjabhāvo (being drug or liquor which destroys the normal mental state and causes māda and pamāda)
              • pātukamyatācittaṃ (intention to use that drug or liquor)
              • tajjo vāyāmo (effort to do so)
              • ajjhoharaṇaṃ (it enters the body)
            • why surāmerayapānaṁ is not included in the akusalakammapathas?→it is only included by ancient teachers as associated to sexual misconduct because it is anekantika kamma which may or may not cause rebirth and all kammapathas surely cause rebirth
            • vipāka and adīnavas of surāmerayapānaṁ
              • rebirth in 4 apāya (when associated with other kammapathas)
              • if born as a human one is ummattaka (crazy)
              • this is a anekantika (not definite) kamma that may or may not cause rebirth. It produces rebirth when associated with other kammapathas (example: drinking before, while or after killing - this drinking can cause rebirth)
            • Obs: Asuras in Tāvatiṁsā lost their realm to the devas because of drinking.
          • duccaritavipākasuttaṃ (aṭṭhakanipātapāḷi)
            • "pāṇātipāto, bhikkhave, āsevito bhāvito bahulīkato nirayasaṃvattaniko tiracchānayonisaṃvattaniko pettivisayasaṃvattaniko. yo sabbalahuso [sabbalahusoti sabbalahuko (syā. aṭṭha.)] pāṇātipātassa vipāko, manussabhūtassa appāyukasaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • "adinnādānaṃ, bhikkhave, āsevitaṃ...bhogabyasanasaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • "kāmesumicchācāro, bhikkhave, āsevito...sapattaverasaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • "musāvādo, bhikkhave, āsevito...abhūtabbhakkhānasaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • "pisuṇā, bhikkhave, vācā āsevitā...pisuṇāya vācāya vipāko, manussabhūtassa mittehi bhedanasaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • "pharusā, bhikkhave, vācā āsevitā...amanāpasaddasaṃvattaniko hoti."
            • "samphappalāpo, bhikkhave, āsevito...anādeyyavācāsaṃvattaniko hoti.
            • surāmerayapānaṁ, bhikkhave, āsevitaṃ...ummattakasaṃvattaniko hotī"ti
          • 5 ānantariyakamma
            • definition→garuka akusala kamma which certainly produces result in avīci immediately after death
            • 5 ānantariyakamma
              • mātughātaka
              • pitughātaka
              • arahantaghātaka
              • lohituppādaka
              • saṅghabhedaka
            • Why are niyatāmicchādiṭṭhi, which certainly produce result in apāya after death, not ānantariyakamma?→because if given up before death one can be born in a good destination while one who has committed ānatariyakamma cannot avoid niraya
            • Order of heaviness of the 5 ānantariyakammas
              • from heaviest to lightest:
                • saṅghabhedakamma
                • lohituppādakamma
                • arahantaghātakakamma
                • matughātakakamma
                • pitughātaka (if the parents' sīla is the same) (In case the father's sīla is higher than the mother it is heavier kamma to kill him)
            • order of importance of cetiyas (more to less important)
              • saririka
              • paribhogika
              • uddesika
              • application: one may for example prune branches of a bodhi tree (paribhogika) to protect a cetiya with dhātus (saririka) but not for protecting walls or stands for offering flowers.
          • "sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhuṃ, sādhuṃ pāpena dukkaraṃ, pāpaṃ pāpena sukaraṃ, pāpamariyehi dukkaraṁ"

        • 4 agatigamanāni (wrong paths / evil motives) #edited
          • chandāgatiṁ (wrong path due to greed): favoring those we are attached to over others
          • dosāgatiṁ (wrong path due to hatred): propriety
          • mohāgatiṁ (wrong path due to delusion)
          • bhayāgatiṁ (wrong path due to fear)
          • Pāḷi: cattārimāni, bhikkhave, agatigamanāni. katamāni cattāri? chandāgatiṃ gacchati, dosāgatiṃ gacchati, mohāgatiṃ gacchati, bhayāgatiṃ gacchati – imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri agatigamanānī"ti
          • "chandā dosā bhayā mohā, yo dhammaṃ ativattati, nihīyati tassa yaso, kāḷapakkheva candimā" ("due to greed, hate, delusion or fear, whoever oversteps righteousness, one's fame dwindles, like the moon in the waning fortnight")
          • Obs: All ariyapuggalas are free from these 4 agatigamana
        • 5 nīvaraṇa #edited
          • kāmacchanda (sense desire)
          • byāpāda (ill-will)
          • thinamiddha (sloth & torpor)
            • kicca (function): {{8763148188986944::līnatā}}{{8763148188986944:: (sliggishness)}} āhāra (cause): {{8763148188986944::arati tandi vijambhitā bhattasammado cetaso ca līnattaṃ}} vipakkha (opposite): {{8763148188986944::viriya}}
          • uddhaccakukkucca (restlessness & remorse)
            • why are they combined as one hindrance?→because both result in the loss of tranquility
            • kicca: {{7803416385419264::cetaso avūpasamo}} āhāra: {{7803416385419264::thinking of commissions and omissions}} vipakkha: {{7803416385419264::samatha}}
          • vicikicchā (doubt)
          • notes:
            • They are referred to as "hindrances" because they {{9032087808038098::obstruct and weaken wisdom}}
            • Simile of the water pot for the 5 nīvaraṇas which prevent one from seeing one's image clearly:
              • kāmacchanda: colored water
              • byāpāda: boiling water
              • thinamiddha: water covered by moss
              • uddhaccakukkucca: water disturbed by wind
              • vicikicchā: muddy water
            • Some synonyms to nīvaraṇas (SN.5 āvaraṇasutta; nīvaraṇa vagga)
              • nīvaraṇa sutta:
                • andhakaraṇā/ acakkhukaraṇā/ aññāṇākaraṇā/ paññānirodhikā (synonyms for impediment of wisdom)
                • vighātapakkhiyā (troublesome)
                • anibbānasaṃvattanikā (not conducive to attainment of the Nibbāna)
              • āvaraṇā (obstruction)
              • cetaso upakkilesā (impurities of the mind)
              • paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā (weaken wisdom)
              • onāhana (covering, shroud, veil)
              • pariyonāhana (binding, wrapping)
            • Simile of the impurities of gold for the 5 nīvaraṇas
              • There are five impurities of gold which cause it not to be pliant, wieldy, radiant, firm and wrought well:
                • Iron, copper, tin, lead and silver
              • But if the gold has been freed from these five impurities, then it will be pliant, wieldy, radiant and firm, and can be wrought well. Whatever ornaments one wishes to make from it, be it a diadem, earrings, a necklace or a golden chain, it can serve that purpose.
            • nourishment for the nīvaraṇas (frequently giving unwise attention to):
              • kāmacchanda: subhanimitta (the sign of beauty)
              • byāpāda: paṭighanimitta (the sign of aversion)
              • thinamiddha: arati, tandi, vijambhitā, bhattasammado, cetaso ca līnattaṃ (dissatisfaction, laziness, yawning and stretching, drowsiness after meals, mental sluggishness)
              • uddhaccakukkucca: cetaso avūpasamo (restlessness of mind)
              • vicikicchā: vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā dhammā (things which are a base for doubt)
              • Pāḷī (kāyasutta):
                • "sāvatthinidānaṃ. seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, anāhāro no tiṭṭhati, evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañca nīvaraṇā āhāraṭṭhitikā, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhanti, anāhārā no tiṭṭhanti.
                • "ko ca, bhikkhave, āhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya? atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ. tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro – ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya.
                • ...byāpādassa...paṭighanimittaṃ...

    • introduction and saraṇagamana #edited
      • A brief introduction to Suttanta #edited
        • Suttanta has five nikāyas:
          • Dīgha Nikāya
          • Majjhima Nikāya
          • Saṁyutta Nikāya
          • Aṅguttara Nikāya
          • Khuddhaka Nikāya
        • Khuddhakapāṭha (Short passages) is the first book in the Khuddhaka Nikāya, arranged for newcomers or novices and has 9 short passages that are traditionally commit to memory. The 9 and their functions are:
          • Saraṇagamana (refuge taking) as the entrance to the sāsana
          • Dasasikkhāpadāni (the ten training rules) for the undertaking of virtue
          • Dvattiṁsākāra (the thirty two body parts) for removing lust
          • Sāmaṇerapañhā / Kumārapañhā (the novice's questions) for removing delusion
          • Maṅgalasutta (The discourse on blessings) for self-protection
          • Ratanasutta (The discourse on gems) for protecting onself and others
          • Tirokuḍḍasutta (The discourse on hungry ghosts outside the walls) for showing the dangers of unwholesome
          • Nidhikaṇḍasutta (The discourse on treasure) for showing the benefits of the wholesome
          • Mettāsutta (The discourse on benevolence) for removing hatred

        • What is the Triple Gem and why is it so called?
          • Buddha: the originator, producer, declarer, knower, discoverer of the path, the one skilled in it. He teaches it to others and thus they can attain freedom from suffering.
          • Dhamma: the nature, the law of nature, the truth and the virtue. Weather Buddhas arise or not the Dhamma persists.
          • Saṅgha: the community of those who practice and who have reached the truth.

          • "with conflict": said in Araṇavibhaṅgasutta with regard to the pursuit of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga)
            • According to saddattha (meaning of the word): {{6832072344151698::"}}{{6832072344151698::hiṁsatīti saraṇaṁ}}{{6832072344151698::"}} ⇒ That which destroys is saraṇa. Here in the sense of destruction of defilements.
            • raṇaṁ (nt.) √raṇ↔conflict; trouble; harm; (comm) defilement #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • saraṇa (adj.)↔harmful; malign; unpeaceful; (comm) defiled; lit. with conflict #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • "dwelling"
          • "something used as protection"
            • According to vohārattha (meaning of the expression) it means something used as protection.
          • "protection"
            • saraṇaṁ (nt.) √sar↔shelter; refuge; help; lit. going to; remembering #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]

        • 2 types of saraṇagamana
          • lokiyasaraṇagamana (the taking of refuge after the suppression of skepticism and wrong views)
            • attasanniyyātanasaraṇagamana (self-dedication/relinquishment)
              • "From today onwards may the Venerable remember me thus: I offer my life to the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha"
            • tapparāyanatāsaraṇagamana (taking the Triple Gem as the main, chief object in one's life)
              • "I rely on the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha."
              • Often appear in the canon: "Esāhaṃ, bhante, {{6760686463014212::taṃ bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata"nti.}}
              • Aḷavakayakkha: "so ahaṃ {{3260348050260553::vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ,namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammata"nti.}}
              • One of the three types of upasampadā
            • sissabhāvūpagamanasaraṇagamana (by becoming a student)
              • "I am an apprentice of the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha"
              • Mahākassapa: {{08833407558187734::"}}{{08833407558187734::Satthā me bhante bhagavā sāvakohamasmi.}}{{08833407558187734::"}}
            • paṇipāta saraṇagamana (tappoṇatta) (by means of prostration and adoration)
              • "From today onwards may the Venerable remember me thus: I will salute, revere, pay homage and respect the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha."
              • "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa"
              • tappoṇa (adj.)↔sloping towards that #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
              • poṇa (adj.) [pa + ava + √nam + a]↔(+acc) sloping down (to); inclining down (to); leading (to) #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • lokuttarasaraṇagamana (supramundane refuge established in the first noble path)
            • 3 defilements eradicated at sotāpattimagga
              • sakkāyadiṭṭhi (personality view)
              • vicikicchā (skepticism)
              • sīlabbataparāmāsa (adherence to rites and rituals)
            • 7 ariyadhana (noble treasures)
              • saddhā (faith)
              • sīla (morality)
              • hiri (moral shame)
              • ottappa (moral dread)
              • suta (learning)
              • cāga (generosity)
              • paññā (wisdom)
        • After having taken refuge in one of those 4 ways (attasanniyātana...etc) one is considered an upāsaka as it is said: "yato kho, mahānāma, {{8822059346491682::buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ... saṅghaṁ... – ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako hotī"ti.}}
        • 4 causes of pollution of mundane refuge
          • Aññāṇa: taking refuge without understanding the Triple Gem
          • Saṁsaya: taking it with doubt
          • Micchāñāṇa = taking the refuge with misunderstanding such as begging or wishing to get something from the Buddha, etc.
          • Anādara = taking the refuge without respect.
        • 2 types of break up of mundane refuge
          • anavajja (blameless): by death
          • sāvajja (blameworthy): by rejecting the Triple Gem and accepting other as refuge.
            • even though one pays homage to other religious people thinking they are our relatives or to learn some arts or knowledge the refuge is not broken. The refuge is broken by taking something else as the ultimate refuge.
        • Four causes of prostration (paṇipāta):
          • ñāti (relative),
          • bhaya (fear),
          • ācariya (teacher),
          • dakkhiṇeyya (one who is worthy of gift): refuge taking is done by prostrating to dakkhiṇeyyas only, not to the others.
        • 5 similes for the Tiple Gem
          • The Buddha like the moon, the sun, a rain cloud, a charioteer, a surgeon
          • The Dhamma like the moonlight, the sunlight, the rain, the method to tame the horses, the method to pull out the dart of wrong views.
          • The Saṅgha like the world receiving the moon/sunlight/rain which settles dust, like tamed horses, like those who have been cured
        • 4 meanings of dhamma
          • dhamma - this refers to truth, nature, principle or reality such as nāmas and rūpas
          • dhammatā - this refers to natural laws which are categorized into 5:
            • utuniyāma - law of temperature
            • bījaniyāma - law of seeds 🌱
            • cittaniyāma - law of consciousness
            • kammaniyāma - law of volitional actions
            • dhammaniyāma - law of dhammas
          • dhammadesanā - refers to the theoretical aspect of the Teaching, the study of texts (pariyatti)
          • dhammacariyā - refers to the practical aspect of the Teaching (paṭipatti)

          • 5 factors are mentioned as nāma in Vibhaṅgasutta

          • Both nāma and rūpa change but the change of nāma is {{5423901194280127::less evident}} than that of rūpa.
          • It is said that it would be better to hold rūpa as the self over nāma because {{3309962080083133::the change is more evident in rūpa so it is easier to erradicate such delusion}}.
        • Rūpa - Definition in Khajjanīyasutta {{7753437832715937::Ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpan'ti vuccati (It is deformed, bhikkhus, therefore it is called form)}}.
          • Which dhammas are rūpa in brief―the 4 Great Elements (Cattāro mahābhūtā) and the 24 derived materialities (upādāyarūpa)
            • Cattāro mahābhūtā
              • Paṭhavīdhātu = solidity or earth element
              • Āpodhātu = fluidity or water element
              • Tejodhātu = heat or fire element.
              • Vayodhātu = motion or air element.
            • Upādāyarūpa
              • 5 Pasādarūpa (sensitive materiality): cakkhu (eye), sota (ear), ghāna (nose), jivhā (tongue), and kāya (body).
              • 4 Gocararūpa / visayarūpa (sense objects): rūpa (form), sadda (sound), gandha (smell), and rasa (taste).
              • 2 Bhavarūpa (material qualities of sex): pumbhāva (masculinity) and itthibhāva (femininity).
              • Hadayarūpa (physical basis of mind or heart base).
              • Jīvitindriya (life faculty).
              • Āhārarūpa (nutriment or edible food).
              • Paricchedarūpa (material quality of delimitation = ākāsadhātu (space element)).
              • 2 Viññatti (material quality of communication): kāyaviññatti (bodily intimation or gesture) and vacīviññatti (verbal intimation or speech).
              • 3 Vikārarūpa (material qualities of plasticity or alterability): lahutā (lightness), mudutā (softness), kammaññatā (adaptability).
              • 4 Lakkhaṇarūpa (material qualities of characteristic): upacaya (growth or arise), santati (continuity), jaratā (decay) and aniccatā (impermanence)
          • ruppati↔changes, molests, deforms #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • ruppanaṁ (nt.)↔constant change #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • vikāro (m.)↔change, alteration, transformation, deformity (s.w. v) #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • visadisuppatti↔genesis of dissimilarity (when rūpas affect each other and change the way they arise) #q🙋🏼‍♂ #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
      • "tīṇi nāma kiṃ? {{8504937223275102::tisso vedanā}}" (What is three? The three feelings) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • Vedanākkhandha
          • Definition: {{6228425150884112::"Vedayatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā vedanā'ti vuccati" - It feels so it is called feeling}}
          • vedayati √vid↔(+acc) feels; experiences; senses; lit. causes to know
          • Feeling has the characteristic of {{851627918601487::experiencing the object}} and has the function of {{851627918601487::sensing the flavour of the object}}
          • Since feeling accompanies every citta it could be said that there are 89 or 121 feelings as well.
          • 3 types of feeling
            • sukha (pleasant)
            • dukkha (painful / unpleasant)
            • adukkhamasukha / upekkhā (neither painful nor pleasant / neutral)
          • Feeling does not like or dislike the object only feels it in a "passive" manner. Liking and disliking are functions of formations.
          • Feeling itself feels the flavor of the object not me, a self, a soul or a being. This shows the doctrine of anatta.
          • The term upekkhā can be used to refer to two dhammas:
            • tatramajjhattatā cetasika (specific neutrality) which is in the aggregate of formations
            • adukkhamasukhavedanā (neither painful nor pleasant feeling) which is in the aggregate of feeling.
          • "cakkhuñca paṭicca {{3338980297692842::rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṁ, tiṇṇaṁ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā...}}"
            • paṭicca↔1: ger. (+acc) dependent; depending (on); because (of); supported (by) #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • The main cause for vedanā is phassa as it is said: "phassapaccayā vedanā"
          • If the object is {{35010590704983335::desirable}} pleasant feeling arises; if the object is {{35010590704983335::undesirable}} painful feeling arises and when the object is {{35010590704983335::not very evident}} neuter feeling arises.
          • Lust may arise for the {{035093530598061085::desirable object}}, hatred for the {{035093530598061085::undesirable object}} and delusion for the {{035093530598061085::obscure object}}.
          • All feelings are considered as {{6610795235253306::suffering}} by the Buddha as it is said: {{6610795235253306::“yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasmiṃ"}} (whatever feeling it may be, it is included in suffering).
          • Why are all three types of feeling suffering? It is because {{2546705989716995::feelings are conditioned states. Conditioned states have the nature of impermanence and whatever is impermanent is suffering (yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ).}}
            • Vajirā bhikkhunī said:
              • “It’s only suffering that comes to be, Suffering that stands and falls away Nothing but suffering comes to be Nothing but suffering ceases.”
          • Feeling itself should not be abandoned. What should be abandoned is {{7979421828147701::the craving for it.}}
          • In which of the 4 Noble Truths is feeling classified?→1st Noble Truth which should be fully understood.
          • What should be done with regard to pleasant, unpleasant and neutral feeling?
            • The pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering and the underlying tendency to lust to it should be abandoned. The unpleasant feeling should be seen as as a dart and the underlying tendency to aversion to it should be abandoned. The neutral feeling should be seen as impermanent and the underlying tendency to delusion to it should be abandoned.
      • "cattāri nāma kiṃ? {{9326141875476994::cattāri ariyasaccāni}}" (What is four? The four noble truths) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • cattāri ariyasaccāni (4 Noble Truths) #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • What are the Four Noble Truths
            • Dukkhaṁ ariyasaccaṁ (the noble truth of suffering)
              • Rebirth is suffering; old age...death...sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress...not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.
            • Dukkhasamudayaṁ ariyasaccaṁ (the noble truth of the origin of suffering)
              • It’s the craving:
                • kāmataṇhā (craving for sense pleasures)
                • bhavataṇhā (craving for existence)
                • vibhavataṇhā (craving for non-existence)
            • Dukkhanirodhaṁ ariyasaccaṁ (the noble truth of the cessation of suffering)
              • It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving with nothing remaining.
            • Dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṁ (the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering)
              • Noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
          • Why are they called Noble Truths? (3)
            • because the Noble Ones penetrate them
              • i.e. the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas and Arahants, etc.
            • because they are the Truths of Noble Ones
              • as it is said “{{7093514509050844::sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya tathāgato ariyo, tasmā ‘ariyasaccānī’ti vuccanti".}}" (In this world, with its devas, Māra, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the noble one)
            • because the Noble Truths are always real, truth and cannot be changed
            • mem aid: pen of unchanging
          • The four functions regarding the Four Noble Truths
            • The Noble Truth of suffering should be fully understood (pariññeyya ⇒ pariññāta)
            • The Noble Truth of the origin of Suffering should be abandoned (pahātabba ⇒ pahīna)
            • The Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized (sacchikātabba ⇒ sacchikata)
            • The Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering should be developed (bhāvetabba ⇒ bhavita)
          • The three ñāṇa (knowledges), three parivaṭṭa (rounds/levels) and twelve ākāra (aspects): "yāvakīvañca me, bhikkhave, imesu catūsu ariyasaccesu evaṃ tiparivaṭṭaṃ dvādasākāraṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ na suvisuddhaṃ ahosi..."
            • The three ñāṇas (knowledges) with regard to the 4NT
              • saccañāṇa (knowledge of the truths): knowledge of the Four Noble Truths as they really are
                • idaṁ dukkhaṁ ariyasaccaṁ
                • ayaṁ dukkhasamudayaṁ ariyasaccaṁ
                • ayaṁ dukkhanirodhaṁ ariyasaccaṁ
                • ayaṁ dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā ariyasaccaṁ
              • kiccañāṇa (knowledge of the functions): knowledge of the function that should be done with regard to each of the Noble Truths; 4 kiccañāṇa:
                • pariññeyyaṁ
                • pahātabbaṁ
                • sacchikātabbaṁ
                • bhāvetabbaṁ
              • katañāṇa (knowledge of what has been done): knowledge of having accomplished the duties with respect to the Four Noble Truths; 4 katañāṇa:
                • pariññātaṁ
                • pahīnaṁ
                • sacchikataṁ
                • bhāvitaṁ
            • The three parivaṭṭa (rounds / circles) of the 4NT
              • first parivaṭṭa is saccañāṇa
              • second parivaṭṭa is kiccañāṇa
              • third parivaṭṭa is katañāṇa
            • The 12 ākāra of the 4NT
              • saccañāṇa with regard to each NT (4)
              • kiccañāṇa with reagard to each NT (4)
              • katañāṇa with regard to each NT (4). Total = 12
          • All teachings of the Buddha can be condensed into the Four Noble Truths
          • Are the aggregates of arahats included in the 4NT? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • What is vibhavataṇhā? Is it the desire to end existence, or is it attachment to the anihilation view, or is it desire for fine material existence or immaterial ones? Sumana: one who commits suicide, for example, in most cases does so with a dosa mind but it is due to craving. #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • why the third NT is defined as the cessation of craving and not suffering? Could it be said then the third NT is the cessation of the 2nd NT? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • All conditioned things are suffering because they cannot remain as they are. They are oppressed by change.
          • The 7 opposing factors of the 7 bojjhangas? which opposes which? #q🙋🏼‍♂
      • "pañca nāma kiṃ? {{16238758955605137::pañcupādānakkhandhā}}" (What is five? The five clinging aggregates) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • 5 Khandha (aggregates)
          • rūpa
            • rūpakkhandha (a. of materiality)
          • nāma
            • vedanākkhandha (a. of feeling)
            • saññākkhandha (a. of perception)
              • Definition: "
              • primary recognition:
              • papañcasaññā (proliferation-perception): associated with diṭṭhi, māna and rāga (TBC)
              • vijjābhāgiyasaññā: Concept conducive to knowledge. Perception of impermanence, suffering and non-self.
            • saṅkhārakkhandha (a. of formations)
            • viññāṇakkhandha (a. of consciousness)
        • saññākkhandha
          • Definition in khajjanīyasutta: {{1759259675448288::"sañjānātīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘saññā’ti vuccati."}} (It perceives/recognizes, bhikkhus, therefore it is called perception/recognition)
            • kiñca sañjānāti? nīlampi sañjānāti, pītakampi sañjānāti, lohitakampi sañjānāti, odātampi sañjānāti. sañjānātīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘saññā’ti vuccati.
          • 6 according to object
            • Rūpasaññā (perception of form): blue, yellow, red, white, etc.
            • Saddasaññā (perception of sound): loud, low, high-pitched, bass, etc.
            • Gandhasaññā (perception of scent): fragrant, foul, smelly, etc.
            • Rasasaññā (perception of flavor): sweet, sour, bitter, spicy, salty, etc.
            • Phoṭṭhabbasaññā (perception of touch): hard, soft, smooth, rough, hot, cold, etc.
            • Dhammasaññā (perception of mental objects): beautiful, ugly, permanence, impermanence, self, non-self, etc.
        • saṅkhārakkhandha
          • Definition in Khajjanīyasutta: {{07251246270225997::"saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘saṅkhārā’ti vuccati.}} (They construct the conditioned, bhikkhus, therefore they are called volitional formations)
            • abhisaṅkharoti↔(+acc) creates; constructs; generates; forms; fabricates #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • kiñca saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti. rūpaṃ rūpattāya [rūpatthāya (ka.)] saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, vedanaṃ vedanattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, saññaṃ saññattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, saṅkhāre saṅkhārattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, viññāṇaṃ viññāṇattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti. saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘saṅkhārā’ti vuccati.
            • rūpatta (nt.) √rūp↔state of being material; state of having form; lit. matter state #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
          • What saṅkhāra means in different cases:
            • Saṅkhārakkhandha in the case of the five aggregates refers to{{8026697247813424:: mental formations (50 cetasikas) lead by volition (cetanā), therefore the term “cetanā” sometimes represents all the mental formations.}} Saṅkhāra in the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering and non-self (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā...) refers to {{8026697247813424::all five aggregates.}} Saṅkhāra in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is defined in the context of practical application and operative function and refers to {{8026697247813424::kāya-saṅkhāra (bodily volitional activity), vacī-saṅkhāra (verbal volitional activity), and citta-saṅkhāra (mental volitional activity).}}
              • {{6121482731138959::"cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi. cetayitvā kammaṃ karoti – kāyena vācāya manasā" }}(O monks, It is volition that I call “kamma”. Having intended one performs kamma through body, speech or mind)
              • 6 types of cetanā according to object
                • Rūpasañcetanā (intention with regard to form)
                • Saddasañcetanā (intention with regard to sound)
                • Gandhasañcetanā (intention with regard to odour)
                • Rasasañcetanā (intention with regard to flavor)
                • Phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā (intention with regard to tangibles)
                • Dhammasañcetanā (intention with regard to mental objects)
        • viññāṇakkhandha
          • Definition in khajjanīyasutta: {{534797851982334::"vijānātīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘viññāṇa’nti vuccati."}} (It cognizes, bhikkhus, therefore it is called consciousness)
            • kiñca vijānāti? ambilampi vijānāti, tittakampi vijānāti, kaṭukampi vijānāti, madhurampi vijānāti, khārikampi vijānāti, akhārikampi vijānāti, loṇikampi vijānāti, aloṇikampi vijānāti. vijānātīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘viññāṇa’nti vuccati.
          • Its function is {{5675705751683913::to cognize / know / be aware of / focus on the object}}
            • Its primary function is in the sense of knowing the object initially. For instance, one sees a cat (i.e., eye-consciousness arises); then one may feel happy seeing the cat (vedanā), one may identify whose cat it belongs to (saññā) and one may love that cat (saṅkhāra). #q🙋🏼‍♂
            • Its secondary function is to know the object afterwards which means one knows in conjunction with the other aggregates. For instance, when one feels happy or sad, one knows that one is happy or sad (viññāṇa). One perceives the object as good or bad (saññā). One engages in various thoughts and intention (saṅkhāra). #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • 6 types according to dvāra (door)
            • Cakkhuviññāṇa (eye-consciousness)
            • Sotaviññāṇa (ear-consciousness)
            • Ghānaviññāṇa (nose-consciousness)
            • Jivhāviññāṇa (tongue-consciousness)
            • Kāyaviññāṇa (body-consciousness)
            • Manoviññāṇa (mind-consciousness)
      • "cha nāma kiṁ? {{02415588529570023::cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni}}" (What is six? The six internal sense-spheres) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • the six sense doors (dvāra) / doors of contact (phassadvāra):
          • cakkhudvāra (eye door)
          • sotadvāra (ear door)
          • ghānadvāra (nose door)
          • jivhādhāra (tongue door)
          • kāyadvāra (body door)
          • manodvāra (mind door)
        • the six sense objects (ārammaṇa):
          • rūpārammaṇa (forms / visible data / color)
          • saddārammaṇa (sounds)
          • gandhārammaṇa (odors)
          • rasārammaṇa (flavors)
          • phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa (tangibles)
          • dhammārammaṇa (mental objects)
        • the three doors / channels of action (kamma-dvāra):
          • kāya-dvāra (body door or channel of bodily actions),
          • vacī-dvāra (the speech-door or channel of verbal actions) and
          • mano-dvāra (mind door or channel of mental actions)
        • The actions through each of the three doors of action are called {{8479852844391549::kāya-kamma (bodily action), vacī-kamma (verbal action) and mano-kamma (mental action) respectively.}}
        • meanings of āyatana #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • In the scriptures, the term “āyatana” is used in the context of “dvāra (door)”.
          • The term “āyatana” means (3)
            • base: “the base for consciousness and an object”
            • link: the “cognitive link,”
            • sphere: “the sphere of cognition”, “source of awareness.”
            • Visuddhimagga : “the point of transmission for the mind and mental factors (cetasika), i.e. the locus of their active engagement; the point of expansion for the mind and mental concomitants; the agents behind the continuation of the protracted suffering in the round of rebirth (saṁsāradukkha); the source; the domain; the point of convergence; etc.” see. Vsm.I.122
              • locus n. (pl. loci ) English definition↔the effective or perceived location of something abstract
            • āyatanaṁ (nt.) √yat↔1: nt. sense base; sense field; sense range; lit. stretching out; 2: realm; sphere; dimension; range; 3: support; basis; grounds. #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
        • They are six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana) as follows:
          • cakkhāyatana (eye / visual base)
          • sotāyatana (ear / auditory base)
          • ghānāyatana (nose / olfactory base)
          • jivhāyatana (tongue / gustatory base)
          • kāyāyatana (body / tactile base)
          • manāyatana (mind / mental base)
        • The objects (form, sound, odour...) which impinge at those internal bases (eye, ear...) are also called “āyatana” because they are {{05927448880916297::co-operative in a cognitive link or source of awareness}}. There are therefore 6 bāhirāyatana (external sense bases):
          • rūpāyatana (form base)
          • saddāyatana (sound base)
          • gandhāyatana (odour base)
          • rasāyatana (flavor base)
          • phoṭṭhabbāyatana (tangible base)
          • dhammāyatana (mental object base)
        • According to Madhupiṇḍikasutta there are two levels of engagement with the world:
          • They are the doorways for experiencing the world. This is the basic function which can lead to knowledge (ñāṇamattāya)
          • They are the channels for responding to the world: This is the extra function which can lead to enjoyment.
            • perception + vitakka + papañca ⇒ papañcasaññā
        • Kāmaguṇa↔pleasing objects of the senses
      • "satta nāma kiṃ? {{7102108843998314::satta bojjhaṅgā}}" (What is seven? The seven enlightenment factors) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • Definition in bhikkhusutta: {{7897067346863744::"bodhāya saṁvattantīti kho bhikkhu tasmā bojjhaṅgāti vuccati"}}{{7897067346863744:: (They lead to enlightenment, monk, therefore they are called factors of enlightenment)}}
        • "sam" in sambojjhaṅga means {{8901833453494368::"good, exalted"}}
        • They are called bojjhaṅgas because they are (3)
          • the factors which lead to enlightenment
          • factors of enlightened ones
            • Bodhi means enlightenment or also enlightened ones
          • Factors which support mental health
        • What are the opposing factors of the bojjhaṅgas? #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • sati ⇒
          • dhammavicaya ⇒
          • vīriya ⇒ inactivity
          • pīti ⇒
          • passaddhi ⇒ restlessness
          • samādhi ⇒ sense indulgence
          • upekkhā ⇒
        • 7 sambojjhaṅgas are:
          • satisambojjhaṅga (mindfulness)
            • Function→to recall, to reflect upon, to fix the attention on, to pull the mind to and to keep it on the object.
            • As a bojjhaṅga mindfulness covers both mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness and ordinary recollection of what was done and said long ago.
            • Mindfulness without clear comprehension (wisdom) is not strong enough to produce enlightenment.
              • "Appamādo {{02691365372848309::amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ, appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā."}}
              • “Mindfulness is the way to the deathless, heedlessness is the way to death The mindful do not die the heedless are as if already dead” (Dhammapada 21).
          • dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga (investigation of truth)
            • Function→to deliberate on, to ponder over and enquire.
          • vīriyasambojjhaṅga (effort)
            • Function→to move or push forward without giving up.
            • four right efforts (cattāro sammappadhāna)
              • "Idha bhikkhave bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati, uppannānaṃ...pahānāya...anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya...uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā...(to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to generate un-arisen wholesome states and to develop arisen wholesome states)
          • pītisambojjhaṅga (joy)
            • It is {{40137157635675424::satisfaction, delight, appreciation and rapture}} with regard to the object.
              • Like our body our mind needs nourishment. Pīti is an important nutrient of the mind. #q🙋🏼‍♂
          • passaddhisambojjhaṅga (tranquility)
            • It means {{5409462858457972::relaxation, calmness and coolness.}} This factor is divided into both {{5409462858457972::bodily and mental tranquility}}
          • samādhisambojjhaṅga (concentration)
            • Samādhi means {{27093530895080575::one-pointedness, concentration, firm establishment of the mind on a particular object without distraction or wavering}}. In the sutta right concentration refers to the four jhānas.
          • upekkhāsambojjhaṅga (equanimity)
            • Upekkhā is {{3041294917192965::evenness, neutrality of mind}} (not vedanā) and is accompanied by knowledge.
        • Balancing the bojjhaṅgas according to aggisutta
          • If the mind is sluggish {{21460085464909762::(līnaṃ cittaṃ)}} ⇒ develop the 3 activating factors which are {{21460085464909762::dhammavicaya, vīriya and pīti}}. If the mind is agitated {{21460085464909762::(uddhataṃ cittaṃ)}} ⇒ develop the three restraining factors of {{21460085464909762::passaddhi, samādhi and upekkhā}}. Mindfulness is always necessary ({{21460085464909762::satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmi}})
      • "aṭṭha nāma kiṃ? {{3751586355346057::ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo}}" (What is eight? The Noble eightfold path) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • Different meanings of ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga (4) #[[khuddaka exam]]
          • ‘Eightfold Path of Noble Beings’ (Nobles' path)
          • ‘Eightfold Path Leading One to Become a Noble Being’ (Ennobling Path)
          • ‘Eightfold Path Discovered by the Noble One (Noble's Path)
          • ‘Supreme Path Comprised of Eight Factors
          • tattha ariyoti {{4662255825007615::nibbānatthikehi abhigantabbo, apica ārakā kilesehi vattanato, ariyabhāvakaraṇato, ariyaphalapaṭilābhato cāpi ariyoti veditabbo.}}
          • The Noble Eightfold Path, also called {{6578953930322107::'The middle way' }}does not mean that there are eight paths or eight ways and that one has to practice them separately but it is only a path consisting of eight factors.
          • Why is it called the Middle Way?→because this is the way which is corresponding to the laws of nature, that gives results according to the natural cycle of cessation, that deviates from the two extremes of sensual pleasure and self-mortification and leads to the goal, Nibbāna.
        • The eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path are:
          • Sammādiṭṭhi (right view): knowing the 4NT
          • Sammāsaṅkappa (right thought): It is the thought of:
            • nekkhammasaṅkappo (renunciation)
            • abyāpādasaṅkappo (good will)
            • avihiṁsāsaṅkappo (harmlessness)
          • Sammāvācā (right speech): abstinence from
            • musāvādā veramaṇī (false speech)
            • pisuṇāyavācāya veramaṇī (divisive speech)
            • pharusāyavācāya veramaṇī (harsh speech)
            • samphappalāpā veramaṇī (idle chatter)
          • Sammākammanta (right action): abstinence from
            • pāṇātipātā veramaṇī (destruction of life)
            • adinnādānā veramaṇī (stealing)
            • kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī (sexual misconduct)
          • Sammāājīva (right livelihood)
          • Sammāvāyāma (right effort): 4 kinds of right effort
            • "Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṁ janeti, vāyamati, vīriaṁ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; (A bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives)
            • uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti...(He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states….)
            • anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṁ janeti...(He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states…)
            • uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṁ janeti...(He generates desire for the development of arisen wholesome states, for their non decay, increase, expansion, and fulfilment by development...)
          • Sammāsati (right mindfulness): 4 Foundations of mindfulness
            • kāyānupassanā
              • "idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; (A bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world)
            • vedanānupassanā
              • vedanāsu vedanānupassī…pe…(He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings...)
            • cittānupassanā
              • citte cittānupassī…pe… (mind in mind...)
            • dhammānupassanā
              • dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati...pe..." (phenomena in phenomena...)
          • Sammāsamādhi (right concentration): The 4 jhānas
            • paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ
              • "vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. (Having secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.)
            • dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ
              • vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. (With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration.)
            • tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ
              • pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. (With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.’ )
            • catutthaṁ jhānaṁ
              • sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. (With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity.)
        • The 8 factors of the Noble Path can be divided into the three higher trainings thus:
          • adhisīlasikkhā (the training in higher morality): Sammāvācā, sammākammanto and sammāājīvo.
          • adhicittasikkhā (the training in higher mind): sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati and sammāsamādhi.
          • adhipaññāsikkhā (the training in higher wisdom): sammādiṭṭhi and sammāsaṅkappo
        • Why is Right view mentioned first?→because it is the essential factor from beginning until liberation and it supports the other seven factors towards the right path.
      • "nava nāma kiṃ? {{49257408098880684::nava sattāvāsā}}" (What is nine? The nine abodes of beings) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • 7 viññāṇaṭṭhiti and 2 āyatanāni (Seven stations of consciousness and two dimensions)
          • 7 viññāṇaṭṭhiti (stations of consciousness) according to Mahānidānasutta (DN)
            • Nānattakāya-Nānattasaññī (Beings with different bodies and different rebirth linking perceptions)
              • Humans
                • Body: different
                • Perception: ahetuka, dvihetuka or tihetuka
              • Deities in the 6 kāmāvacara deva realms
                • Body: different
                • Perception: ahetuka, dvihetuka or tihetuka (lower cātummahārājika deities including vinipātika asuras, vemānika asuras, etc); and dvihetuka and tihetuka for the rest of deities.
            • Nānattakāya-Ekattasaññī (different bodies, similar rebirth linking perceptions)
              • 1st jhāna brahma realms (brahma pārisajja, brahma purohita and mahābrahma)
                • Body: same appearance but the higher the realm the bigger their size
                • Perception: tihetuka (all have the vipākacitta of the 1st jhāna)
              • 4 apāya beings (niraya, tiracchānagata, petivisaya, asurakāya)
                • Body: different bodies
                • Perception: ahetuka (all have the akusala vipāka upekkhā santīraṇa citta)
            • Ekattakāya-Nānattasaññī (similar bodies, different rebirth linking perceptions)
              • 2nd jhāna brahmas (parittābhā, appamāṇābhā, ābhassarā)
                • Bodies: similar in each realm but not between realms
                • Perception: tihetuka (either vipāka of the 2nd or 3rd jhānas according to the abhidhamma method)
            • Ekattakāya-Ekattasaññī (similar bodies, similar rebirth linking perceptions)
              • 3rd jhāna brahmas and Vehapphala brahmas (parittāsubhā, appamāṇasubhā, subhākiṇhā and vehapphala)
                • Body: similar
                • Perception: tihetuka (all with either the vipāka of the 4th rūpāvacara jhāna or the 5th using the abhidhamma method)
              • For Suddhāvāsa beings: beings in this realm are Anāgāmī; therefore, they are reborn there only when a Buddha arises in the world. In the Buddhasuññakappa (Kappa in which there is no single Buddha), they do not arise there.
            • Ākāsānañcāyatana (Ākāsānañcāyatana brahmas)
            • Viññāṇañcāyatana (Viññāṇañcāyatana brahmas)
            • Ākiñcaññāyatana (Ākiñcaññāyatana brahmas)
            • What is a viññāṇaṭṭhiti (station of consciousness)?→they are places for the rebirth liking consciousness to occur. Those 7 places are called viññāṇaṭṭhiti.
            • nānattakāya and ekattakāya refer to what?→It refers to the difference / similarity of body in terms of size and appearance
            • nānattasaññī and ekattasaññī refer to what?→It refers to the difference / similarity of perception in the rebirth linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) with regard to associated roots (ahetuka: rootless, dvihetuka: with two roots, and tihetuka: with three roots)
          • The 2 āyatanāni (dimensions)
            • Asaññasattāyatana (the dimension of impercipient beings): it is not included in the 7 viññāṇaṭṭhiti since beings of that realm do not possess mind.
            • Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana:(the dimension of the base of neither perception nor non-perception): not in viññāṇaṭṭhiti since the rebirth liking consciousness in that realm is extremely subtle.
          • What does viññāṇaṭṭhiti refers to in the ultimate sense?→it refers to the aggregates other than the viññāṇakkhandha. More specifically: In the pañcavokāra realms (beings with 5 aggregates) the four aggregates of rūpa, vedanā, saññā and saṅkhārakkhandhas In the catuvokāra realms (except Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana realm) the three aggregates of vedanā, saññā and saṅkhārakkhandhas.
      • "dasa nāma kiṃ? {{1744791480832295::dasahaṅgehi samannāgato ‘arahā’ti vuccatī"ti}} (What is ten? One who is possessed of 10 factors is called an arahat) #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • The 10 factors of righteousness (sammatta) or the ten qualities of an adept or of one who does not require any further training (asekha):
          • The 8 factors of the Noble Eightfold path
          • Sammāñāṇa (right knowledge): arahattaphalañāṇa and 19 paccavekkhaṇañāṇas
          • Sammavimutti (right liberation): it is equivalent to the arahattaphalavimutti (deliverance of the fruition of arahatship)
        • However in Paṭhamaanāthapiṇḍikasutta they are also ascribed to Anāthapiṇḍika, a stream-enterer.

              • "The deluded fellow leads one to ruin, he enjoins one in reckless ways, he is hard to guide to the good, spoken rightly he gets upset, he does not know discipline, it is good not to see such a one"

            • Majjhadesa (In Cammakkhandhaka) Pāḷi:
                • IIT - Nissayamuttaka Course
              • The middle region (majjhadesa) is {{7216004251867876::300}} yojanās in length, {{7216004251867876::250}} in width and {{7216004251867876::900}} in curcumference. 14 out of 16 mahājanapadās (big cities) are in this area (except {{7216004251867876::Gandhāra and Kamboja}} which belong to the Uttarāpaṭha). Sammāsambuddhas, paccekabuddhas and aggasāvakabuddhas as well as universal monarchs arise only in this area.
            • The place is a blessing because it is a condition for beings to perform wholesome deeds and meet the six unsurpassed things:
              • Dassanuttariya (supreme sight): The Buddha and Saṅgha and things that cause wholesome minds to arise
              • Savanānuttariya (supreme hearing): hearing the Dhamma
              • Lābhānuttariya (supreme gain): faith
              • Sikkhānuttariya (supreme training): three trainings
              • Pāricariyānuttariya (supreme service or ministry): towards the Triple Gem
              • Anussatānuttariya (supreme memory): recaling the qualities of the Triple Gem

              • bhaginīsamā (a wife like a sister) = a wife who respects her husband as a younger sister her elder brother, who is conscientious and follows her husband’s will is called a wife and a sister.
              • sakhīsamā (a wife like a friend) = a wife who rejoices seeing her husband like a friend seeing another friend who has come after a long time, who is well raised, virtuous and devoted is called a wife and a friend.
              • dāsīsamā (a wife like a slave) = a wife who has no anger, remains calm and endures when threatened with violence by the rod and who follows her husband’s will is called a wife and a slave. Among these seven, the first three are considered as bad, immoral and go to hell after death but the last four are good and go to heaven after death.
