              • vajjaṃ (nt.)→fault, blame (s.w. v)
              • anavajja (na + na + vajja ⇒ an + a + vajja) even though it is double negation it still means blameless (avajja)
            • There are two kinds of faults:
              • Loka-vajja (secular or worldly fault or offense): this can be committed by both monks and lay people such as stealing, killing, sexual misconduct, etc. They are necessarily done with unwholesome mind.
              • Paṇṇatti-vajja (fault by regulation): even if lay people do these kinds of faults, it is not wrong. It is only an offense for monks such as eating after noon, digging the earth, wearing robes without marks, etc. These are not necessarily done with unwholesome mind.
            • The difference between anākula-kamma (unentangled action) and anavajja-kamma (blameless action):
              • Anākula-kamma refers to a proper means of livelihood or occupations and it is not concerned with social services.
              • Anavajja-kamma refers to the action mainly associated with welfare of others and social services
            • 4 criteria for blameless work (anavajjakamma) #[[khuddaka exam]]
              • not against the law
              • not against the culture
              • not against morality
              • not against dhamma
      • Khuddhaka Nikāya - Ven. Sumana - Assignment #edited #[[khuddaka exam]]
        • by (Brasil) Ariyañāṇa Bhikkhu
        • Based on the hermit "Akitti" what are the characteristics of the fool and that of the wise?
          • The 5 characteristics of the fool and their counterparts were expressed by the hermit Akitti in the following stanzas uttered as a respons to Sakka's question in Akittijātaka:
            • "anayaṃ nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati, dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati, vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassanaṃ."
            • "The deluded fellow leads one to ruin, he enjoins one in reckless ways, he is hard to guide to the good, spoken rightly he gets upset, he does not know discipline, it is good not to see such a one"
            • "nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati, sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati, vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo"
            • "the wise fellow leads one to what is right, he does not enjoin one in reckless ways, he is easy to guide to the good, spoken rightly he is not upset, he understands discipline, it is good to encounter such a one"
        • Explain how the principles of support (saṅgahavatthu) relate to the four sublime states (brahmavihāra)?
          • The first three saṅgahavatthus of dāna, piyavācā and atthacariyā can be related to the first 3 brahmavihāras of mettā, karuṇā and muditā while the fourth saṅgahavatthu of samānattatā can be related to the fourth brahmavihāra of upekkhā:
          • One may give a gift to a friend out of loving-kindness, medicines to the sick out of compassion or a gift to a friend who was successful in his studies out of muditā. In such ways dāna can be understood to be related to the 3 brahmavihāras of mettā, karuṇā and muditā.
          • One may speak kind words when meeting a dear family member out of loving-kindness, kind words of advice to one facing difficulties out of compassion or words of praise to a donor for his merit out of muditā. In such ways piyavācā can be understood to be related to the 3 brahmavihāras of mettā, karuṇā and muditā.
          • One may establish unvirtuous parents in virtue out of loving-kindness, clean the bedroom of a sick friend out of compassion or prepare the meal of a monk because of rejoicing in his practice. In such ways atthacariyā can be understood to be related to the 3 brahmavihāras of mettā, karuṇā and muditā.
          • A good leader may perform his duties treating people according to their status, with the same stable attitude when facing good or bad fortunes. In such a way samānattatā can be understood to be related to upekkhā brahmavihāra.
        • What are the five factor of well-spoken speech?
          • 5 qualities of well-spoken speech
            • sacca - it should be true
            • atthasañhita - it should be beneficial
            • kāla - it should be utter at the proper time
            • mettacitta - it should be uttered with loving-kindness
            • saṇha - it should be gentle
        • Elucidate why parents are called "brahma, pubbācariya, pubbadeva and āhuneyya"?
          • Parents are possessed of the four brahmavihāra states of mettā, karuṇā, muditā and upekkhā towards their children therefore they are called brahma.
          • Parents are the first ones to teach what should and should not be done, what is good and bad and show their children the world therefore they are called pubbācariya.
          • Parents are those who desire benefits for their children and the first ones their children pay respect to therefore they are called pubbadevatā.
          • Parents are those who provide their children with material and emotional support therefore they are worthy of respect/offerings (āhuneyya )

            • santuṭṭhī ca
              • santuṭṭhi (or santosa) is satisfaction with whatever material things one has. It is further classified into three (or 12): #[[khuddaka exam]]
                • yathālābhasantuṭṭhī (contentment according to one’s gains): one is content with whatever one gets
                • yathābalasantuṭṭhī (contentment according to one’s strength): if one receives requisites that do not fit or do not suit oneself (too big, too small, too heavy...) one exchanges it with another and is content
                • yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhī (contentment according to suitability): suitability in terms of one’s status, quality, and goal of life
                  • status: a monk does not wish for something which is not suitable for a monk’s life
                  • quality: if one gets something of higher quality one reflects that such requisite is suitable for an elder monk and gives it away
                  • goal: even if one gets something which is suitable for oneself but it is more useful for another one is willing to give it up to that person
                • Each of the 3 types of santuṭṭhi can be applied to each of the 4 requisites amounting to 12
                • Vocab: #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
                  • santuṭṭhi / santosa √tus (f.)↔satisfaction; contentment
                  • sāruppa √rūp (vis.)↔(+dat) suitable (for); proper (for); appropriate (for); lit. with same form

                • pubbakārī - one who takes the initiative in helping others without expectation
                • kataññū katavedī - one who is grateful and repays favors
              • gratitude is of five types (these five types are not mentioned in the Tipiṭaka; they are explained by tradition)
                • Upattiguṇa = gratitude for giving birth or for giving this body and life
                • Upathambhaguṇa = gratitude for bringing up, raising or supporting with food, drink, etc
                • Ārakkhaguṇa = gratitude for protecting or caring such as preventing from dangers, providing for treatments, etc
                • Sāsaguṇa = gratitude for teachings, admonishing, giving advices
                • Piyaguṇa = gratitude for loving and caring
                • Parents usually have these 5, teachers the last 3

              • "Akkosaṁ vadhabandhañca, aduṭṭho yo titikkhati; khantībalaṃ balānīkaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ" (Abuse, killing, imprisonment: they endure these without anger; patience is their powerful army: that’s who I call a brahmin)
            • the sage Sarabhaṅga said:
              • "One bears the speech of a higher-status person out of respect, one bears the speech of someone of equal status to avoid conflict, but it is said that the highest form of forbearance is to bear the speech of a lower-status person, according to the wise"
              • “Having slain anger, one never sorrows; the sages praise the abandoning of contempt. One should endure harsh words from everyone; the good call this the highest patience”
            • Sakka: “When a person endowed with strength patiently endures a weakling, they call that the supreme patience; the weakling must always be patient.”
          • sovacassatā ({{9606032974834746::being easy to admonish}})
            • When one is being admonished one does not show anger, speak harshly, or think of one’s own good qualities and the faults of others, but listens with high respect and humility
            • 2 types of suvaca
              • āmisahetusuvaco
              • dhammagāravahetusuvaco
            • there are two types of people in this world (according to suvaca)
              • sovacassatā = being easy to admonish or being obedient such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Rāhula, etc.
                • āmisahetu-suvaco = one who is easily admonished due to their interest in profits or material benefits. If he does not get those material benefits, then he is not easy to admonish. The Buddha mentioned that this kind of person is not called “Suvaca” person.
                • dhammagāravahetu-suvaco = one who is easy to admonish because of their respect for the dhamma. This kind of person is called “Suvaca” person
              • dovacassatā = being hard to admonish or being resistant to admonition such as the ascetic Sañjaya, the Venerable Channa, etc.
          • samaṇānañca dassanaṁ ({{5303194055514895::seeing monks}})
            • samaṇa means
              • a recluse, one who went forth; samaṇa literally means one who is calm. “Not by a shaven head does a man become a recluse, if he lacks morality and austere practices, and tells lies; how could he who is full of desire and greed be a reluse”; “One who subdued all evil deeds, great or small, because of stopping bad deeds one is said to be a recluse.”
            • 3 types of seeing
              • seeing with eyes: one seeing the calm and peaceful appearance and deportment of a recluse, just as the Venerable Sāriputta sees the Venerable Assaji for the first time and The king Pasenadi Kosala sees the behavior of monks in the Dhammacetiyasutta
              • seeing with mind: one recollects the good qualities of a recluse without really seeing them, but he sees them by hearing and learning, etc.
              • seeing with wisdom: one knows the good qualities of a recluse since he himself practices and has those qualities. In brief, he sees the truth like a recluse
          • kālena dhammasākacchā ({{6512850641283081::timely discussion of the Dhamma}})
            • sākacchā (saha > sa + kath + ya > kaccha)
            • kālena (things that should be done from time to time)
              • dhammasavanaṁ
              • dhammasākacchā
              • sammasanā/samathā
              • vipassanā
            • “when you are sitting together, you should do one of two things: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence ({{49537746112900005::dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo}})
            • 3 principles for more beneficial Dhamma discussions with no quarreling
              • discussing about Dhamma: The talk should be within the scope of Dhamma, as outlined in Kathāvatthu 10
              • discussing with Dhamma: Both sides must respect each other; if one is wrong, the other must correct with gentle speech; if one is right, the other must appreciate, and both bodily and verbal actions must be appropriate
              • discussing for Dhamma: Both sides must discuss for the purpose of deepening their understanding of Dhamma, or with the intention to help another understand Dhamma. One must not discuss Dhamma to show off their knowledge or for material gain, among other inappropriate reasons
      • 9th verse #editing
        • "{{8006152948090204::tapo ca brahmacariyañca, ariyasaccāna dassanaṁ, nibbānasacchikiriyā ca, etaṁ maṅgalamuttamaṁ}}" Purpose: {{8006152948090204::practice for the eradication of defilements}} - {{8006152948090204::4}} blessings
          • tapo ({{08124160854521856::austerity}})
            • tapa↔burning up, heating (the defilements) by indriyasaṁvara and vīriya #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • yañña↔sacrifice #[[pāḷi vocab (1st year) ]]
            • 4 meanings of tapo
              • indriyasaṁvara (the restraint of the six sense faculties): because of burning up abhijjhā and domanassaṁ (vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ)
              • viriya (effort): 4 right efforts to burn laziness
              • khanti (forbearance): “Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā"; it is tolerance which is the strength and endurance that makes oneself firm on the way that leads to one's goal
              • adhicittasikkhā (training in higher mind): includes all samādhi bhāvanā
          • brahmacariyañca ({{0571409877281428::holy life}})
            • 10 types of brahmacariya + 1 extra
              • dāna (generosity)
              • veyyāvacca (service)
              • pañcasīla (the 5 precepts)
              • appamaññā (4 sublime abodes)
              • sadārasantosa (contentment with one's spouse)
              • methunavirati (abstention from sex)
              • vīriya (effort)
              • uposathaṅga (8 precepts)
              • ariyamagga (Noble Eightfold Path)
              • sāsana (dispensation)
              • samaṇadhamma
            • 4 meanings of brahmacariya according to Maṅgalasuttaṭṭhakatha
              • methunavirati-brahmacariya (practicing holy life by refraining from sexual intercourse)
              • samaṇadhamma-brahmacariya (all practices of monks)
              • sāsana-brahmacariya (the Buddha’s dispensation)
              • magga-brahmacariya (the Noble Eightfol Path)
              • Here in this verse all the first three meanings are taken because the last meaning will be included in the next blessing “seeing the noble truths.” In Maṅgaladīpanī, even Sāsana-brahmacariya is included blessing factor “Subhāsitā ca yā vācā.”
            • 3 levels of practicing the holy life: “Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati; Majjhimena ca devattaṁ, uttamena visujjhati.” #editing
          • "ariyasaccāna dassanaṁ"
          • "nibbānasacchikiriyā ca" ({{26525860464777073::realization of nibbāna}})
            • ni (out, without, finished) and vāna (to blow, to go or taṇhā – craving), therefore it can be translated as the blowing out, extinguishment, quenching, cooling like the extinguishment of a fire, or as without craving, craving-free state, craving-less
            • nibbāna here means arahattaphala which is free from craving and therefore free from the jungle (vana) of the 5 destinations
            • 2 types of nibbāna
              • saupādisesa nibbāna (nibbāna with remaining fuel): upādi is the five aggregates since they are governed by impure actions or are the subject of grasping
              • anupādisesa nibbāna (nibbāna without remaining fuel): refers to parinibbāna
      • 10th verse #editing
        • “{{06493245725605257::phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi, cittaṃ yassa na kampati; asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ}}.” Purpose: {{06493245725605257::The result of practice}} - {{06493245725605257::4}} blessings
          • phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi, cittaṁ yassa na kampati ({{8421693667889627::to have the mind which is not shaken by the eight worldly conditions}})
            • The noble person’s mind does not shake, waver or tremble by the eight worldly conditions:
              • lābha = gain
              • 5.1.2. Alābha = loss
              • 5.1.3. Yasa = fame
              • 5.1.4. Ayasa = disrepute
              • 5.1.5. Pasaṃsā = praise
              • 5.1.6. Ninda = blame
              • 5.1.7. Sukha = happiness 5.1.8.
              • Dukkha = suffering
          • asokaṁ ({{5316352389975825::to have the mind which is free from sorrow}})
          • virajaṁ ({{9665400156688393::to have the mind which is undefiled}})
          • khemaṁ ({{4828245653588408::to have the mind which is secure}})
      • Concluding verse
        • “Etādisāni katvāna, sabbatthamaparājitā; sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttaman’ti.
        • “Having completed these things, undefeated everywhere; everywhere they go in safety: this is their highest blessing.”

      • analysis of each sikkhāpada
        • Pārājika
          • Calculating the boundaries of villages:
            • Walled villages
              • according to abhidhamma
                • beyond the village's gate posts it is forest
              • according to suttanta
                • a forest abode is at least 500 bow lengths from the village's gate posts to the monastery wall by following the road #[[Measurements / Dimensions]]
            • Villages without a wall
              • according to vinaya
                • a woman standing a the door of the outermost house throws water with a pot to shoo away a crow. That marks the house precincts. From the house precincts an underhand (?) stone-throw by an average sized man marks the village boundaries. From there another stone-throw marks the village precincts. Beyond that it is forest.

          • S 9 Aññabhāgiyasikkhāpada
            • 10 points which are a mere pretext (dasa lesā)
              • jātileso (birth)
              • nāmaleso (name)
              • gottaleso (family)
              • liṅgaleso
              • āpattileso (offense)
              • pattaleso (bowl)
              • cīvaraleso (robes)
              • upajjhāyaleso (preceptor)
              • ācariyaleso (teacher)
              • senāsanaleso (dwelling)
              • kiñci desaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāyāti leso nāma dasa lesā – jātileso , nāmaleso, gottaleso, liṅgaleso, āpattileso, pattaleso, cīvaraleso, upajjhāyaleso, ācariyaleso, senāsanaleso.
          • S 10 Sanghabhedasikkhāpada
            • 9 factors for saṅghabheda
              • dipati: one of the 18 saṅghabheda vatthu is brought up amongst the saṅgha
              • disputes start
              • ruci gaṇhāti: others approve
              • apakassati: the schismatic gains followers
              • anusāvati: he informs others his intention to split the saṅgha
              • salākagaṇhāti: distributes voting tickets
              • at least 4 on his side
              • at least 4 accept his proposal
              • avenikammaṁ karoti: they perform vinaya kamma separately

          • 4 types of parivāsa
            • Appaṭicchanna parivāsa: Tesu “Yo, bhikkhave, aññopi aññatitthiyapubbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhati pabbajjaṃ, ākaṅkhati upasampadaṃ, tassa cattāro māse parivāso dātabbo”ti (mahāva· 86) evaṃ mahākhandhake vutto titthiyaparivāso appaṭicchannaparivāso nāma.
            • Paṭicchanna parivāsa
            • Suddhanta parivāsa: the bhikkhu does not remember number of offenses, nights concealed, or has doubts about these two (2 kinds)
              • Cūḷasuddhanta parivāsa: remember periods of purity and periods of impurity
              • Mahāsuddhanta parivāsa: does not remember any periods of purity so must take parivāsa for as long as one has been ordained.
            • Samodhāna parivāsa: multiple offenses, concealed for different periods, of multiple bases

                  • Unallowable root/rhizome and why
                    • Turmeric (Curcuma longa), because it fades quickly
                  • Unallowable stems/woods and why
                    • Rubia tinctorum (aka Rubia manjistha, Indian madder) Rubia tinctorum - Wikipedia
                    • Rottleria tinctoria (aka Kamala tree)
                      • Mallotus philippensis - Wikipedia
                    • because they are the wrong color

                  • Unallowable bark and why
                    • Mucuna pruriens
                      • Mucuna pruriens - Wikipedia
                    • Symplocos racemosa (aka tirIta tree)
                    • because they are the wrong color
                    • Mnemonic: tree trunk oozing resin (like mucus) and pasted with tiritas (band-aids)
                  • Unallowable leaves and why

                    • Indigo tinctoria: because it is the wrong color

                  • Unallowable flowers and why

                    • Butea frondosa (aka Coral Tree)
                    • because they are too red

      • 10 antarāya to the Pātimokkha (obstacles)
        • Rājantarāyo (King)
        • Corantarāyo (Criminal)
        • Agyantarāyo (Aggi antara) (Fire)
        • Udakantarāyo (Water)
        • Manussantarāyo (People): such as an angry mob
        • Amanussantarāyo (Non-humans): one bhikkhu is possessed
        • Vāḷanatarāyo (wild animals)
        • Sarīsapantarāyo (serpent)
        • Jīvitantarāyo (life): Bhikkhu gilāno vā hoti, kālaṃ vā karoti, verino vā taṃ māretukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ ¶ jīvitantarāyo.
        • Brahmacariyantarāyo (holy life, chastity): manussā ekaṃ vā bahū vā bhikkhū brahmacariyā cāvetukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo.
        • performing shorter uposatha kamma not existing any of these obstacles is a {{2112234374137596:: Dukkaṭa }} āpatti.
        • rājantarāyotiādīsu sace bhikkhūsu “Uposathaṃ karissāmā”ti nisinnesu rājā āgacchati, ayaṃ rājantarāyo. Corā āgacchanti, ayaṃ corantarāyo. Davadāho vā āgacchati, āvāse vā aggi uṭṭhahati, ayaṃ aggantarāyo. Megho vā uṭṭheti, ogho vā āgacchati, ayaṃ udakantarāyo. Bahū manussā āgacchanti, ayaṃ manussantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ amanussantarāyo. Byagghādayo caṇḍamigā āgacchanti, ayaṃ vāḷantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ sappādayo ḍaṃsanti, ayaṃ sarīsapantarāyo. Bhikkhu gilāno vā hoti, kālaṃ vā karoti, verino vā taṃ māretukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ ¶ jīvitantarāyo. manussā ekaṃ vā bahū vā bhikkhū brahmacariyā cāvetukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo.
      • Hatthapāsa for vinaya kamma→Hatthapāso nāma diyaḍḍhahatthappamāṇo. (1 1/2 cubits) (opinions)
      • Hatthapāsa for piṇḍapāta (bhojana)
